lessons.title: Tables, rows and your first query
tldr: A relational database keeps data in **tables** of **rows** and named, typed **columns**, and `SELECT … FROM` is how you ask it for some of that data.
Every report, screen and API you will build starts as a query like this, so knowing exactly what a query reads and returns is the first skill to learn.

visualizer.title: Anatomy of a table and a first SELECT
visualizer.caption: Step through from the server down to one cell. Watch which columns each query reads, compare the result, and click any cell to inspect it.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id       int PRIMARY KEY,
  name     text NOT NULL,
  category text NOT NULL,
  price    numeric(8,2) NOT NULL,
  stock    int            -- NULL means "not counted yet"
);
INSERT INTO products (id, name, category, price, stock) VALUES
  (1, 'Desk lamp',    'home',     24.00,   12),
  (2, 'Coffee mug',   'kitchen',   9.50,   40),
  (3, 'Chef knife',   'kitchen',  45.00,    0),
  (4, 'Wool blanket', 'home',     60.00,    5),
  (5, 'Teapot',       'kitchen',  18.00, NULL),
  (6, 'Notebook',     'office',    4.50,  120),
  (7, 'Desk chair',   'office',  150.00,    3),
  (8, 'Pen set',      'office',   15.00, NULL),
  (9, 'Plant pot',    'home',     15.00,   25);

presets.label: Everything
presets.sql: SELECT * FROM products;
presets.note: 9 rows, 5 columns. Two rows show **NULL** for stock: the value is unknown, not zero.

presets.label: Pick columns
presets.sql:
SELECT name, price
FROM products;
presets.note: Only the two columns you listed, in that order. Swap them and run again.

presets.label: Expressions and AS
presets.sql:
SELECT name,
       price,
       price * 1.2          AS price_with_tax,
       stock * 2,
       name || ' (' || category || ')' AS label
FROM products;
presets.note: `price * 1.2` returns `28.800`: three decimals. `stock * 2` has no alias, so its column is named `?column?`, and NULL stock stays NULL. `||` joins text.

presets.label: Table alias and comments
presets.note: `p` is a short name for `products` in this one query. Comments are ignored by the server.

presets.label: Where am I?
presets.sql:
SELECT current_database() AS database,
       current_schema()   AS schema,
       current_user       AS logged_in_as,
       version();
presets.note: You are in database `postgres`, schema `public`, as user `postgres`, on PostgreSQL 18.

presets.label: List my tables
presets.sql:
SELECT table_schema, table_name
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = 'public';

SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_name = 'products'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;
presets.note: The database describes itself with ordinary tables you can query. `stock` is the only nullable column.

production.title: An export that stops breaking
production.context: A data analyst exports the product catalog to a spreadsheet every week with `SELECT * FROM products`. A finance script reads the file by column position.
production.problem: A developer adds a `supplier_id` column between `category` and `price`. The next export shifts every column one place to the right, and the finance script reads supplier ids as prices.
production.solution: Name the columns, give computed values clear aliases, and sort the output so the file is the same shape and order every week.
production.sql:
SELECT id,
       name,
       category,
       price,
       price * 1.2 AS price_with_tax
FROM products
ORDER BY id;
production.outcome: The export keeps exactly 5 columns in a fixed order no matter how the table changes. New columns appear only when someone adds them to the query on purpose.

pitfalls.title: Assuming rows come back in insert order
pitfalls.symptom: A list looks sorted in testing, then shows up in a different order in production after some updates.
pitfalls.cause: A table is an unordered set of rows. Without `ORDER BY`, PostgreSQL returns rows in whatever order is cheapest, which changes as data moves.
pitfalls.fix: Add `ORDER BY` whenever order matters, for example `ORDER BY id`. The next lesson covers sorting.

pitfalls.title: SELECT * in application code
pitfalls.symptom: An app slows down or breaks after someone adds a large or renamed column.
pitfalls.cause: `*` expands to whatever columns exist right now, so the query silently changes when the table does, and it may fetch big columns you never use.
pitfalls.fix: Use `SELECT *` for exploring. In code, list the columns you need.

pitfalls.title: Double quotes around text values
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: column "home" does not exist` from `SELECT name FROM products WHERE category = "home"`.
pitfalls.cause: Double quotes mean a **name** (a column or table). Text values use **single quotes**.
pitfalls.fix: Write `'home'`. To put a quote inside text, double it: `'it''s'`.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT name FROM products WHERE category = 'home';

pitfalls.title: The statement never runs
pitfalls.symptom: In `psql` you press Enter and the prompt changes from `postgres=#` to `postgres-#`, and nothing happens.
pitfalls.cause: A statement ends at the semicolon, not at the end of the line. `psql` is waiting for the rest.
pitfalls.fix: Type `;` and press Enter. Ending every statement with `;` also lets you put several in one script.

pointers: Cluster → database → schema → table → row → column. A connection works in one database. New tables land in schema `public`.
`SELECT columns FROM table;` Use `*` to explore and named columns in real code.
Expressions in the select list compute new columns. Name them with `AS`, or they are called `?column?`.
Rows have **no order** unless you ask for one with `ORDER BY`. `NULL` means unknown, not zero or empty.
**Going deeper:** [What PostgreSQL is](/m1/what-is-postgres) follows one query from your client through the server and back.

lessons.title: Creating tables and inserting rows
tldr: `CREATE TABLE` defines a table once (its columns, their types and the rules each row must obey), and `INSERT` adds rows that PostgreSQL checks against those rules.
Types and constraints such as `NOT NULL`, `PRIMARY KEY` and `DEFAULT` let the database itself reject bad data, so every program that writes to it gets the same protection.

visualizer.title: Build a table, one statement at a time
visualizer.caption: Step through CREATE TABLE and six INSERTs. Watch defaults fill in, bad rows bounce off the constraints, and the identity counter skip a number.

presets.label: Create the table
presets.sql:
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id        bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email     text    NOT NULL,
  name      text    NOT NULL,
  vip       boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  credit    numeric(10,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  joined_on date    NOT NULL DEFAULT current_date,
  joined_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable, column_default
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_name = 'customers'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;
presets.note: The second query reads the table definition back. `id` shows no default: identity columns are generated, not defaulted.

presets.label: Insert one, RETURNING
presets.note: You sent two values; the row came back complete. `id` = 1, `vip` = false, `credit` = 0.00, and today's date.

presets.label: Many rows, DEFAULT keyword
presets.sql:
INSERT INTO customers (email, name, vip, credit)
VALUES ('ben@example.com',   'Ben',   true,    25.50),
       ('chloe@example.com', 'Chloe', DEFAULT, DEFAULT)
RETURNING id, name, vip, credit;
presets.note: One statement, two rows, ids 2 and 3. `DEFAULT` inside VALUES asks for the column default.

presets.label: Rules that reject rows
presets.note: Four different errors: **23502** NOT NULL, **428C9** identity, **22P02** bad input for a boolean, **42703** unknown column. Eve then gets id **5**: the first failed insert used up 4.

presets.label: INSERT … SELECT
presets.note: Rows can come from a query instead of VALUES. `source = 'friend'` is a true/false expression, so Hana becomes a VIP.

presets.label: Quotes and names
presets.note: Unquoted names are folded to lower case, so `Orders` means `orders` and is not found (**42P01**). Only `"Orders"` with quotes finds it. Stick to lower-case names.

presets.label: Drop a table
presets.note: `DROP TABLE` removes the definition **and** all its rows at once. `IF EXISTS` turns "not found" into a notice instead of an error.

production.title: Sign-up in one round trip
production.context: A web app inserts a customer at sign-up and then needs the new id to create a welcome coupon and a session.
production.problem: The first version inserted the row, then ran `SELECT max(id) FROM customers` to find it. Under load two sign-ups interleaved and one user got the other's id, so the coupon went to the wrong account.
production.solution: Let the database generate the id and send it back from the same statement with `RETURNING`. No second query, no guessing. (`$1` and `$2` are placeholders: the application sends the email and name separately from the SQL text, so user input can never change the statement.)
production.outcome: Each sign-up costs one statement instead of two, and the id returned is always the row that statement inserted, however many sign-ups run at once.

pitfalls.title: Expecting ids without gaps
pitfalls.symptom: Ids go 1, 2, 3, 5, and someone files a bug about the missing 4.
pitfalls.cause: An identity number is taken before the row is checked. A failed or rolled-back insert does not give it back.
pitfalls.fix: Treat ids as unique labels, not counters. If you need a gapless sequence (invoice numbers), build it separately; to count rows, use `count(*)`.

pitfalls.title: Typing ids by hand into an identity column
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column "id"` while loading old data.
pitfalls.cause: `GENERATED ALWAYS` refuses user-supplied values.
pitfalls.fix: For a one-off load, write `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE` after the column list, then move the counter past the highest id. Otherwise omit the column.

pitfalls.title: Money in a float column
pitfalls.symptom: A balance shows `0.30000000000000004` or totals drift by a cent.
pitfalls.cause: `real` and `double precision` store binary approximations. Many decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly.
pitfalls.fix: Use `numeric(12,2)` (exact) for money and anything that must add up to the cent.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT 0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8 AS float_sum, 0.1::numeric + 0.2::numeric AS numeric_sum;

pitfalls.title: Mixed-case table names
pitfalls.symptom: `relation "orders" does not exist`, although you can see `Orders` in a GUI tool.
pitfalls.cause: The table was created as `"Orders"` with quotes, which keeps the capital. Every query must then quote it the same way.
pitfalls.fix: Use lower-case names with underscores (`order_items`). If one exists already, rename it: `ALTER TABLE "Orders" RENAME TO orders;`.

pointers: `CREATE TABLE t (col type constraints, …)`. Everyday types: `int`/`bigint`, `text`, `numeric(p,s)`, `boolean`, `date`, `timestamptz`.
`PRIMARY KEY` = unique + not null. `NOT NULL` forbids missing values. `DEFAULT` fills omitted columns.
`bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` numbers rows for you; numbers are unique but can have **gaps**.
`'single quotes'` are values, `"double quotes"` are names. `RETURNING` sends the inserted row back.
**Going deeper:** [Primitive types, alignment and padding](/m2/primitive-types) shows how each type is laid out in bytes on disk.

lessons.title: Filtering and sorting
tldr: `WHERE` keeps only the rows whose condition is **true**, `ORDER BY` sorts them, and `LIMIT` keeps the first few.
Those three clauses turn "the whole table" into "the ten rows this screen needs", and the rules around `NULL`, operator precedence and ties decide whether you get the rows you meant.

visualizer.title: Filter lab: true, false and NULL
visualizer.caption: Pick a WHERE condition and see each row's verdict. Then sort, move NULLs, and drag LIMIT. The table on the right shows how NULL combines with AND, OR and NOT.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id       int PRIMARY KEY,
  name     text NOT NULL,
  category text NOT NULL,
  price    numeric(8,2) NOT NULL,
  stock    int            -- NULL means "not counted yet"
);
INSERT INTO products (id, name, category, price, stock) VALUES
  (1, 'Desk lamp',    'home',     24.00,   12),
  (2, 'Coffee mug',   'kitchen',   9.50,   40),
  (3, 'Chef knife',   'kitchen',  45.00,    0),
  (4, 'Wool blanket', 'home',     60.00,    5),
  (5, 'Teapot',       'kitchen',  18.00, NULL),
  (6, 'Notebook',     'office',    4.50,  120),
  (7, 'Desk chair',   'office',  150.00,    3),
  (8, 'Pen set',      'office',   15.00, NULL),
  (9, 'Plant pot',    'home',     15.00,   25);

presets.label: Compare
presets.sql:
SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price < 20;
SELECT name, category FROM products WHERE category <> 'office';
presets.note: `<>` (or `!=`) means "not equal". Text comparisons are exact and case-sensitive: `category = 'Office'` would match nothing.

presets.label: AND / OR precedence
presets.note: Five rows, then three. Without parentheses AND is applied first, so cheap kitchen items sneak in.

presets.label: IN, BETWEEN, LIKE
presets.note: `BETWEEN` includes both ends: five rows, from 15.00 up to 45.00. `_` matches one character: names whose second letter is `e`.

presets.label: NULL traps
presets.note: `stock < 10` misses the two unknowns; `= NULL` finds nothing; `IS NULL` finds them. `NULL = NULL` is itself NULL.

presets.label: Sort, NULLs first or last
presets.note: NULLs sort as if larger than any value: last when ascending, first when descending, unless you say `NULLS FIRST/LAST`. The last query sorts by category, then by price within each category.

presets.label: LIMIT, OFFSET, WITH TIES
presets.note: Pen set and Plant pot tie at 15.00. `LIMIT 3` picks one of them; `WITH TIES` returns both (4 rows); adding `id` as a tiebreaker makes `LIMIT 3` repeatable. `OFFSET 3` skips the first three.

presets.label: DISTINCT
presets.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products ORDER BY category;
SELECT DISTINCT stock IS NULL AS unknown_stock FROM products;
presets.note: `DISTINCT` removes duplicate result rows. Three categories out of nine rows.

production.title: A low-stock alert that missed items
production.context: A shop runs a nightly job that emails the buyer a list of products to reorder: `WHERE stock < 10`.
production.problem: New products are created with `stock` NULL until the first stock count. They never appeared in the alert, because `NULL < 10` is not true, and some sold out before anyone noticed they had never been counted.
production.solution: Say what to do with unknowns explicitly, and sort so the most urgent rows come first, NULLs included.
production.sql:
SELECT id, name, stock
FROM products
WHERE stock < 10 OR stock IS NULL
ORDER BY stock NULLS FIRST, name;
production.outcome: On the sample data the alert grows from 3 rows to 5: Teapot and Pen set, which have never been counted, now come first. The rows are in the same order every night.

pitfalls.title: col = NULL finds nothing
pitfalls.symptom: `WHERE deleted_at = NULL` returns zero rows although many rows have no `deleted_at`.
pitfalls.cause: Any comparison with NULL gives NULL (unknown), and WHERE keeps only true.
pitfalls.fix: Use `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`. To compare two columns that may both be NULL, use `a IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b`.

pitfalls.title: OR without parentheses
pitfalls.symptom: A filter for "kitchen or home items over 20" returns cheap kitchen items.
pitfalls.cause: `AND` binds tighter than `OR`: `a OR b AND c` means `a OR (b AND c)`.
pitfalls.fix: Put parentheses around every OR group: `(a OR b) AND c`.

pitfalls.title: NOT IN with a NULL in the list
pitfalls.symptom: `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)` suddenly returns no rows at all.
pitfalls.cause: If the list holds a NULL, `x NOT IN (…)` is never true: it means `x <> a AND x <> NULL`, and the last part is unknown.
pitfalls.fix: Use `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)`, or filter NULLs out of the list.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT 5 NOT IN (1, 2) AS no_null, 5 NOT IN (1, NULL) AS with_null;

pitfalls.title: LIMIT without a full ORDER BY
pitfalls.symptom: Page 2 of a list repeats an item from page 1, or an item is never shown.
pitfalls.cause: Without ORDER BY, or with ties in the sort key, the database may return tied rows in any order, and each query can choose differently.
pitfalls.fix: Always sort by a unique tiebreaker last: `ORDER BY price, id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20`.

pointers: `WHERE` keeps rows whose condition is **true**. False and NULL (unknown) are both dropped.
Precedence: `NOT`, then `AND`, then `OR`. When mixing AND and OR, use parentheses.
`IN (…)`, `BETWEEN a AND b` (inclusive), `LIKE` (`%` any, `_` one; case-sensitive), `ILIKE` (any case), `IS [NOT] NULL`.
`ORDER BY a, b DESC`; NULLs are last ascending and first descending unless `NULLS FIRST/LAST`. Use a unique tiebreaker before `LIMIT`.
**Going deeper:** [Designing indexes](/m4/index-design) shows how an index can answer a WHERE and ORDER BY without reading the whole table.

lessons.title: Counting, summing and grouping
tldr: An **aggregate** such as `count`, `sum` or `avg` turns many rows into one value, and `GROUP BY` computes it once per group of rows that share a key.
Most questions people ask of data ("how many", "how much", "per what") are aggregates, and knowing the order the clauses run in tells you where each filter belongs.

visualizer.title: How a grouped SELECT is evaluated
visualizer.caption: Step through the clauses in the order they run. Watch rows drop at WHERE, fold into buckets at GROUP BY, and buckets drop at HAVING. Click a bucket name to see all its aggregates.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id       int PRIMARY KEY,
  name     text NOT NULL,
  category text NOT NULL,
  price    numeric(8,2) NOT NULL,
  stock    int            -- NULL means "not counted yet"
);
INSERT INTO products (id, name, category, price, stock) VALUES
  (1, 'Desk lamp',    'home',     24.00,   12),
  (2, 'Coffee mug',   'kitchen',   9.50,   40),
  (3, 'Chef knife',   'kitchen',  45.00,    0),
  (4, 'Wool blanket', 'home',     60.00,    5),
  (5, 'Teapot',       'kitchen',  18.00, NULL),
  (6, 'Notebook',     'office',    4.50,  120),
  (7, 'Desk chair',   'office',  150.00,    3),
  (8, 'Pen set',      'office',   15.00, NULL),
  (9, 'Plant pot',    'home',     15.00,   25);
-- A tiny helper so the error presets show the message instead of stopping.
CREATE FUNCTION try_sql(q text) RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN EXECUTE q; RETURN 'ok';
EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN RETURN SQLSTATE || ': ' || SQLERRM;
END $$;

presets.label: count(*) vs count(col)
presets.sql:
SELECT count(*)     AS all_rows,
       count(stock) AS rows_with_stock,
       sum(stock)   AS units,
       min(price)   AS cheapest,
       max(price)   AS dearest,
       avg(price)   AS avg_price,
       round(avg(price), 2) AS avg_rounded
FROM products;
presets.note: `count(*)` = 9 rows, `count(stock)` = 7: the two NULL stocks are skipped. `avg` prints 16 decimals (37.8888888888888889); `round(…, 2)` gives 37.89.

presets.label: GROUP BY
presets.sql:
SELECT category,
       count(*)              AS products,
       sum(stock)            AS units,
       round(avg(price), 2)  AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY category;
presets.note: One output row per category. Each aggregate is computed over that category's rows only.

presets.label: The GROUP BY rule
presets.note: Error **42803**: a bucket has many names, so `name` must be grouped or aggregated. `string_agg` is an aggregate that joins them into one text value.

presets.label: WHERE vs HAVING
presets.sql:
SELECT try_sql('SELECT category FROM products WHERE count(*) >= 3 GROUP BY category') AS aggregate_in_where;

SELECT category, count(*) AS n, round(avg(price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products
WHERE price < 100
GROUP BY category
HAVING count(*) >= 3
ORDER BY avg_price DESC;
presets.note: Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE (**42803**): WHERE runs before groups exist. WHERE drops the Desk chair row; HAVING drops the office group (only 2 rows left).

presets.label: The full pipeline
presets.sql:
SELECT category, count(*) AS n, round(avg(price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products
WHERE price < 100
GROUP BY category
HAVING count(*) >= 3
ORDER BY avg_price DESC
LIMIT 1;

SELECT try_sql('SELECT category, avg(price) AS a FROM products GROUP BY category HAVING a > 30') AS alias_in_having;
presets.note: The visualizer's query: **home | 3 | 33.00**. ORDER BY may use the alias `avg_price`, but HAVING may not (**42703**), because it runs before SELECT names the columns.

presets.label: Group by an expression
presets.sql:
SELECT price >= 20 AS pricey, count(*), round(avg(price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY price >= 20
ORDER BY pricey;

SELECT stock IS NULL AS stock_unknown, count(*)
FROM products
GROUP BY stock IS NULL;
presets.note: Any expression can be a group key. 5 products are under 20.00 and 4 are not; 2 have unknown stock.

presets.label: Aggregates over no rows
presets.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS n, sum(stock) AS units, avg(price) AS avg_price,
       coalesce(sum(stock), 0) AS units_or_zero
FROM products
WHERE category = 'garden';
presets.note: No garden products: `count` gives 0, but `sum` and `avg` give **NULL**. `coalesce(x, 0)` replaces NULL with 0.

production.title: A category summary for a dashboard
production.context: A shop dashboard shows one tile per category: number of products, units in stock and average price.
production.problem: The first version loaded every product into the app and counted in code. It sent every row over the network on each page view, and the "units" tile was wrong because the code added NULL stock as 0 and counted those products as stocked.
production.solution: Let the database aggregate and send only the summary rows. Count uncounted products separately so the gap is visible.
production.sql:
SELECT category,
       count(*)                         AS products,
       count(stock)                     AS counted,
       count(*) - count(stock)          AS not_counted,
       coalesce(sum(stock), 0)          AS units,
       round(avg(price), 2)             AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY category;
production.outcome: The app receives 3 rows instead of 9 (and the saving grows with the catalog: always one row per category). Kitchen and office each show 1 product as "not counted" (Teapot and Pen set) instead of hiding it.

pitfalls.title: A column that is neither grouped nor aggregated
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: column "products.name" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function`.
pitfalls.cause: After GROUP BY each output row stands for a whole bucket. A bucket has many names, so `name` alone has no single value.
pitfalls.fix: Add the column to GROUP BY if you want a row per value, or wrap it in an aggregate (`min(name)`, `string_agg(name, ', ')`).

pitfalls.title: count(col) when you meant count(*)
pitfalls.symptom: A "products per category" number is lower than the real count.
pitfalls.cause: `count(col)` skips rows where `col` is NULL. `count(*)` counts rows.
pitfalls.fix: Use `count(*)` to count rows. Use `count(col)` only when "rows that have a value" is what you mean.

pitfalls.title: Filtering groups in WHERE
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE`.
pitfalls.cause: WHERE runs before GROUP BY, when there are no groups to count yet.
pitfalls.fix: Filter rows in WHERE, and filter groups in HAVING: `HAVING count(*) >= 3`. Repeat the expression; HAVING cannot see SELECT aliases.

pitfalls.title: sum() of nothing is NULL, not 0
pitfalls.symptom: A total shows blank for a category with no matching rows, or app code crashes on a null.
pitfalls.cause: Every aggregate except `count` returns NULL when it sees no rows.
pitfalls.fix: Wrap it: `coalesce(sum(stock), 0)`.

pointers: `count(*)` counts rows; `count(col)` counts non-NULL values; `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max` skip NULLs and return NULL on zero rows.
With GROUP BY, every selected column must be in the GROUP BY or inside an aggregate.
WHERE filters **rows** before grouping. HAVING filters **groups** after. Aggregates belong in HAVING.
Run order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. WHERE and HAVING cannot use SELECT aliases; ORDER BY can.
**Going deeper:** [Aggregates, FILTER and GROUPING SETS](/m3/aggregates-grouping) adds subtotals and conditional counts; [From SQL text to rows](/m4/query-pipeline) shows the plan that runs a query.

lessons.title: Updating and deleting safely
tldr: `UPDATE` changes and `DELETE` removes every row its `WHERE` matches, and a transaction (`BEGIN` … `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`) lets you look at the result before it becomes permanent.
A single missing `WHERE` changes the whole table with no warning, so a habit of preview, transaction, check and only then commit is the cheapest insurance you will ever buy.

visualizer.title: The safe-change routine
visualizer.caption: Pick a scenario and step through it. Compare the safe UPDATE with the forgotten WHERE, and watch ROLLBACK put every value back.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id       int PRIMARY KEY,
  name     text NOT NULL,
  category text NOT NULL,
  price    numeric(8,2) NOT NULL,
  stock    int            -- NULL means "not counted yet"
);
INSERT INTO products (id, name, category, price, stock) VALUES
  (1, 'Desk lamp',    'home',     24.00,   12),
  (2, 'Coffee mug',   'kitchen',   9.50,   40),
  (3, 'Chef knife',   'kitchen',  45.00,    0),
  (4, 'Wool blanket', 'home',     60.00,    5),
  (5, 'Teapot',       'kitchen',  18.00, NULL),
  (6, 'Notebook',     'office',    4.50,  120),
  (7, 'Desk chair',   'office',  150.00,    3),
  (8, 'Pen set',      'office',   15.00, NULL),
  (9, 'Plant pot',    'home',     15.00,   25);
-- A tiny helper so the error presets show the message instead of stopping.
CREATE FUNCTION try_sql(q text) RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN EXECUTE q; RETURN 'ok';
EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN RETURN SQLSTATE || ': ' || SQLERRM;
END $$;

presets.label: 1. Preview
presets.note: Three rows, and the prices they would get. Nothing has changed yet.

presets.label: 2. Try it, then ROLLBACK
presets.note: RETURNING shows 10.45, 49.50 and 19.80. After ROLLBACK the last query shows the original 9.50, 45.00 and 18.00 again.

presets.label: 3. Do it, then COMMIT
presets.note: Same UPDATE, now committed: the three kitchen prices stay raised. Every other row is untouched.

presets.label: 4. The forgotten WHERE
presets.note: `UPDATE` with no WHERE hits all **9** rows. Inside the transaction 9 products cost 0; after ROLLBACK, 0 do.

presets.label: 5. DELETE … RETURNING
presets.note: Preview finds Chef knife; DELETE removes exactly that row and lists it. 8 products remain.

presets.label: 6. An error aborts the transaction
presets.note: Here the helper catches the error, so the transaction survives. In psql, after a real error every later statement fails with **25P02** ("current transaction is aborted") until you run ROLLBACK.

presets.label: 7. TRUNCATE inside a transaction
presets.note: TRUNCATE empties the table in one step (0 rows), and ROLLBACK brings every row back. Outside a transaction it would be final.

production.title: Fixing a mispriced category in production
production.context: A support engineer learns that every kitchen product was imported 10% too cheap and must fix the prices on the live database while customers are shopping.
production.problem: A plain `UPDATE` typed into a console commits the moment it finishes. A typo in the WHERE, or no WHERE at all, would reprice the whole store instantly and customers would see it.
production.solution: Preview the rows, change them inside a transaction, compare the row count with the preview, and only then commit. Setting a short lock timeout makes the change give up, instead of queueing, if another transaction is holding locks on those rows.
production.outcome: The change is checked before anyone sees it: 3 rows previewed, 3 rows updated, then one commit makes all 3 visible together. A mistake costs one `ROLLBACK`, not a restore from backup.

pitfalls.title: UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE
pitfalls.symptom: The tag says `UPDATE 48213` when you meant to change one row.
pitfalls.cause: WHERE is optional. Without it the statement applies to every row, and in autocommit mode it is committed immediately.
pitfalls.fix: Write the WHERE first and test it in a SELECT. Run changes inside `BEGIN` and compare the tag with the preview before `COMMIT`. In psql, `\set AUTOCOMMIT off` makes psql issue `BEGIN` for you, so nothing is saved until you `COMMIT`.

pitfalls.title: A transaction left open
pitfalls.symptom: Other sessions hang when they try to change the rows you changed, and your changes are not visible to anyone.
pitfalls.cause: After `BEGIN`, changes stay private and the changed rows stay locked until `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`. Closing a tool window may not end the transaction.
pitfalls.fix: Always finish with COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` so a forgotten session is ended automatically.
pitfalls.sql: SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5min';

pitfalls.title: current transaction is aborted
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block` on every statement.
pitfalls.cause: Any error inside a transaction marks it failed. PostgreSQL refuses all further work in it so you cannot commit half a change.
pitfalls.fix: Run `ROLLBACK;` and start again. (A `SAVEPOINT` lets you undo just part of a transaction.)

pitfalls.title: TRUNCATE where DELETE was needed
pitfalls.symptom: An app freezes while a cleanup job runs, or an audit trigger never fired.
pitfalls.cause: `TRUNCATE` takes the strongest table lock (even reads wait), runs no `ON DELETE` triggers, and cannot take a WHERE.
pitfalls.fix: Use `DELETE … WHERE` to remove some rows or when triggers must run. Use `TRUNCATE` (with `RESTART IDENTITY` to reset ids) only to empty a table nobody is using.

pointers: `UPDATE t SET col = expr WHERE …` and `DELETE FROM t WHERE …`. No WHERE means **every row**.
Preview with a `SELECT` using the same WHERE. The number of rows it returns is the number the change will touch.
`BEGIN` → change → check the tag and `RETURNING` → `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`. Outside BEGIN, each statement commits by itself.
`TRUNCATE` empties a table fast and frees space at once, but locks it completely and skips DELETE triggers.
**Going deeper:** [ACID and transactions](/m5/acid-transactions) explains how COMMIT and ROLLBACK work; [INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE](/m3/dml-lifecycle) shows what UPDATE does to the stored rows.

lessons.title: Text and strings
tldr: PostgreSQL ships dozens of **string functions** that join, measure, change case, trim, slice, search and rewrite text, plus **regular expressions** for patterns.
Real data arrives messy, with stray spaces, mixed case and odd formats, so you clean and compare it in SQL instead of shipping every row to application code.

visualizer.title: String workbench: every character and its bytes
visualizer.caption: Pick an input (or type your own) and step through the functions. Watch which characters are kept, removed or changed, and compare **length** with **octet_length**.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id         int PRIMARY KEY,
  first_name text,
  last_name  text,
  email      text,
  phone      text,
  city       text
);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES
  (1, '  ann ', 'LEE',    'Ann.Lee@Example.COM',    '(555) 123-4567',  'new york'),
  (2, 'Bob',    NULL,     'bob@example.com',        '555.987.6543',    'LONDON'),
  (3, 'josé',   'García', 'jose@ejemplo.es',        '+34 600 111 222', 'sevilla'),
  (4, 'Chen',   'Wei',    'CHEN.WEI@example.com ',  NULL,              'são paulo'),
  (5, 'dee',    'o''neil','dee@sample.org',         '555 000 1111',    'new york'),
  (6, 'ann',    'lee',    'ann.lee@example.com',    '5551234567',      'New York');

presets.label: Joining strings
presets.sql:
SELECT id,
       first_name || ' ' || last_name      AS with_pipes,
       concat(first_name, ' ', last_name)  AS with_concat,
       concat_ws(' ', first_name, last_name) AS with_ws
FROM customers ORDER BY id;
presets.note: Bob has no last name. With `||` one NULL makes the whole result NULL. `concat` and `concat_ws` skip NULLs, and `concat_ws` puts the separator only between real values.

presets.label: Characters vs bytes
presets.note: `são paulo` is 9 characters but 10 bytes, because `ã` takes 2 bytes in UTF-8. The emoji string is 12 characters and 17 bytes.

presets.label: Clean up names
presets.sql:
SELECT id,
       '[' || first_name || ']'          AS raw_first,
       initcap(trim(first_name))         AS first_clean,
       initcap(last_name)                AS last_clean,
       initcap(city)                     AS city_clean
FROM customers ORDER BY id;
presets.note: The brackets show the stray spaces around `ann`. `trim` removes them and `initcap` fixes the case: `LEE` → `Lee`, `o'neil` → `O'Neil`, `são paulo` → `São Paulo`.

presets.label: Slice and search
presets.sql:
SELECT email,
       position('@' IN email)          AS at_pos,
       split_part(email, '@', 1)       AS local_part,
       split_part(email, '@', 2)       AS domain,
       substring(email FROM 1 FOR 3)   AS first3,
       split_part(email, '.', -1)      AS tld
FROM customers ORDER BY id;
presets.note: Positions start at 1. `split_part` with `-1` takes the last field. Row 4 has a trailing space, so its `tld` is `com ` (with a space): dirty data shows up as soon as you slice it.

presets.label: Regular expressions
presets.sql:
SELECT id, phone,
       regexp_replace(phone, '\D', '', 'g')   AS digits_only,
       phone ~ '^\(?555'                     AS starts_555,
       regexp_match(email, '^([^@]+)@(.+)$')  AS parts
FROM customers ORDER BY id;

SELECT id, regexp_matches(phone, '\d{4}', 'g') AS four_digit_groups
FROM customers ORDER BY id;
presets.note: `\D` = any non-digit. The second query returns rows only for customers whose phone contains a 4-digit group: `regexp_matches` silently **drops** rows with no match (ids 3 and 4 vanish).

presets.label: format() for messages and SQL
presets.note: `%s` inserts a value, `%I` quotes an identifier only when needed (`"Customer List"`), `%L` quotes a literal safely. This is how dynamic SQL avoids injection.

presets.label: Case-insensitive matching
presets.note: Plain `=` finds 1 row; normalising with `lower(trim(...))` finds both Ann rows. `ILIKE`, the `citext` type and a **nondeterministic collation** are three more ways to ignore case.

production.title: Duplicate sign-ups that differ only by case
production.context: A newsletter service stores whatever email the sign-up form sends. Mobile keyboards capitalise the first letter and some users paste a trailing space.
production.problem: `Ann.Lee@Example.COM` and `ann.lee@example.com` are different strings, so the `UNIQUE (email)` constraint lets both in. Users get two copies of every mail, and unsubscribe only removes one.
production.solution: Find the duplicates by grouping on a normalised value. Merge them, store the normalised form, and enforce uniqueness on `lower(email)` with an **expression index** so the database rejects new case-variants.
production.outcome: In the playground data, step 1 finds one duplicate group (ids 1 and 6) and step 2 removes id 6. After the index exists, inserting `ANN.LEE@example.com` fails with a unique violation, and lookups written as `WHERE lower(email) = lower($1)` can use the index.

pitfalls.title: One NULL blanks the whole label
pitfalls.symptom: A report shows empty names for some customers even though the first name is filled in.
pitfalls.cause: `||` returns NULL if any piece is NULL. One missing `last_name` makes `first_name || ' ' || last_name` NULL.
pitfalls.fix: Use `concat_ws(' ', first_name, last_name)` or wrap the nullable pieces in `coalesce(col, '')`.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT concat_ws(' ', first_name, last_name) FROM customers;

pitfalls.title: Counting characters when the limit is in bytes
pitfalls.symptom: A value that passed a 255-character check is rejected by a downstream system with a 255-byte limit.
pitfalls.cause: `length` and `varchar(n)` count **characters**. Accented letters take 2 bytes and emoji take 4 in UTF-8.
pitfalls.fix: Check `octet_length` when the limit is in bytes, for example `CHECK (octet_length(bio) <= 255)`.

pitfalls.title: regexp_matches silently drops rows
pitfalls.symptom: Adding a regex column to a SELECT makes some rows disappear from the result.
pitfalls.cause: `regexp_matches` is a set-returning function: it returns zero rows when there is no match, which removes the row.
pitfalls.fix: Use `regexp_match` (one result or NULL) when you want the first match, or wrap it: `(SELECT regexp_matches(col, pat))`.

pitfalls.title: Case-insensitive search that scans the whole table
pitfalls.symptom: `WHERE lower(email) = $1` is slow on a big table even though `email` has an index.
pitfalls.cause: An index on `email` stores the original values. It cannot answer a question about `lower(email)`.
pitfalls.fix: Create an expression index on exactly the expression you filter by, or use the `citext` type.
pitfalls.sql: CREATE INDEX ON customers (lower(email));

pointers: `||` returns NULL if any piece is NULL. `concat` and `concat_ws` skip NULLs.
**length** counts characters and **octet_length** counts bytes. String positions start at **1**.
`~` matches a regex anywhere in the string. `LIKE` must match the whole string. Add `g` to `regexp_replace` to replace every match.
For case-insensitive equality, normalise with `lower()`, use `ILIKE`, the `citext` type or a nondeterministic collation. Back it with a matching index.
Going deeper: the Internals lesson [Designing indexes](/m4/index-design) shows how an expression index on `lower(email)` serves these lookups.

lessons.title: Numbers and arithmetic
tldr: PostgreSQL has three families of number types: **integers** (whole numbers), **numeric** (exact decimals) and **floating point** (fast binary approximations).
The type decides what arithmetic means, so `7 / 2` is 3, `0.1 + 0.2` may not equal 0.3, and picking the right type keeps money and ratios correct.

visualizer.title: Three number experiments
visualizer.caption: Divide integers and watch the fraction vanish, add 0.1 ten times in binary and in decimal, then squeeze values into a **numeric(p, s)** column.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE line_items (
  id           int PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id     int,
  product      text,
  price        numeric(10,2),   -- exact money
  qty          int,
  weight_kg    real,            -- approximate measurement
  discount_pct int
);
INSERT INTO line_items VALUES
  (1, 100, 'coffee beans',  12.99, 3, 0.25, 10),
  (2, 100, 'grinder',       49.95, 1, 1.4,   0),
  (3, 101, 'filter papers',  3.10, 7, 0.1,  15),
  (4, 101, 'mug',            8.50, 2, 0.35,  0),
  (5, 102, 'kettle',        34.00, 1, 1.2,   5);

presets.label: Integer division
presets.note: `7 / 2` is **3** and `-7 / 2` is **-3**: integer division truncates toward zero. One decimal operand (`7.0`) switches to numeric division.

presets.label: What type is this?
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_typeof(42)          AS "42",
       pg_typeof(3000000000)  AS "3000000000",
       pg_typeof(4.2)         AS "4.2",
       pg_typeof(1e3)         AS "1e3",
       pg_typeof(42 + 4.2)    AS "42 + 4.2",
       pg_typeof(42::float8 + 4.2) AS "float8 + 4.2";

SELECT pg_typeof(sum(qty)) AS sum_int, pg_typeof(avg(qty)) AS avg_int, pg_typeof(sum(price)) AS sum_numeric
FROM line_items;
presets.note: A whole-number literal is `integer` (or `bigint` if it is too big), and any literal with a point or exponent is `numeric`. Mixing types promotes to the "wider" one.

presets.label: Float vs numeric
presets.note: Floats are binary, so `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004` and ten 0.1s make `0.9999999999999999`. A `real` keeps about 6 digits: widening its sum shows `3.3000000193715096`.

presets.label: Rounding family
presets.note: `round(2.5)` on numeric is **3** (ties away from zero), but on double precision it is **2** (ties to even). `trunc` cuts toward zero; `floor` always goes down.

presets.label: numeric(p, s) limits
presets.note: Extra decimals are rounded, but too many digits before the point is an **error** (`numeric field overflow`). Try `SELECT 2147483647 + 1;` yourself: integers never wrap around silently.

presets.label: Money math
presets.sql:
SELECT product, price * qty AS gross,
       round(price * qty * (100 - discount_pct) / 100, 2) AS net,
       price * qty * (discount_pct / 100)                 AS discount_wrong
FROM line_items ORDER BY id;

SELECT order_id, sum(qty) AS items, count(*) AS lines,
       sum(qty) / count(*)                       AS avg_truncated,
       round(sum(qty)::numeric / count(*), 2)    AS avg_exact,
       round(100.0 * sum(price * qty) / (SELECT sum(price * qty) FROM line_items), 1) AS pct_of_revenue
FROM line_items GROUP BY order_id ORDER BY order_id;
presets.note: `discount_pct / 100` is integer division, so it is 0 for every row and `discount_wrong` is always 0.00. Multiply first or use `100.0`. Order 101 averages 4.5 items, not 4.

presets.label: Random numbers
presets.note: `random()` returns a double in [0, 1). `random(1, 6)` includes both ends. After `setseed` the sequence repeats, which helps tests. It is not secure: use `gen_random_uuid()` or pgcrypto for tokens.

production.title: An invoice that is off by one cent
production.context: A billing team prints invoices with a tax line for each item, then charges the card for the order total. Prices are already `numeric(10,2)`.
production.problem: The invoice shows each line rounded to cents, but the charge rounds only the final sum. With five lines at 8.25% tax the two disagree, and customers spot the difference.
production.solution: Decide where rounding happens and do it once per line, in `numeric`, then sum the rounded lines. Never use `float8` for money: it adds binary error on top of the rounding question.
production.sql:
SELECT sum(round(price * qty * 1.0825, 2))  AS sum_of_rounded_lines,
       round(sum(price * qty * 1.0825), 2)  AS rounded_total,
       sum(price::float8 * qty * 1.0825)    AS float_total
FROM line_items;
production.outcome: On the playground data the printed lines add up to **174.96** while the rounded total is **174.95**, and the float total is `174.95365`. Charging `sum_of_rounded_lines` makes the invoice and the card charge match exactly.

pitfalls.title: Ratios that are always zero
pitfalls.symptom: A conversion rate or percentage column shows 0 for every row, or whole numbers only.
pitfalls.cause: Both sides are integers (`count(*)`, `int` columns), so `/` truncates: `3 / 7` is 0.
pitfalls.fix: Make one side numeric before dividing: `100.0 * a / b` or `a::numeric / b`, then `round(..., 1)`.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT 3 / 7 AS wrong, round(100.0 * 3 / 7, 1) AS pct;

pitfalls.title: Storing money in float
pitfalls.symptom: Totals end in `…99999999` or reports disagree by a cent with the accounting system.
pitfalls.cause: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, and every operation rounds again.
pitfalls.fix: Use `numeric(12,2)` (or integer cents) for money. Keep `real`/`double precision` for measurements where tiny errors do not matter.

pitfalls.title: Integer overflow on a growing counter
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: integer out of range` from a multiplication or addition on `integer` values once the numbers grow.
pitfalls.cause: `integer` stops at 2,147,483,647. PostgreSQL raises an error rather than wrapping around.
pitfalls.fix: Use `bigint` for ids and large counters. Cast before multiplying big values: `a::bigint * b`.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT 2147483647::bigint + 1 AS fits_in_bigint;

pitfalls.title: Comparing floats with =
pitfalls.symptom: `WHERE weight = 0.1` finds nothing even though the value was inserted as 0.1.
pitfalls.cause: A `real` column holds the nearest float4 to 0.1, while the literal 0.1 becomes numeric and is compared as a double: they differ in the last bits.
pitfalls.fix: Compare with a tolerance (`abs(weight - 0.1) < 1e-6`) or store the value as `numeric` if exact equality matters.

pointers: **integer / integer** truncates toward zero. Add a decimal point or cast to get fractions.
**numeric** is exact and right for money. **real**/**double precision** are fast binary approximations.
`numeric(p, s)` rounds extra decimals but **errors** when the integer part is too long. Integer overflow is also an error.
`round` on numeric rounds ties away from zero; on double precision it usually rounds ties to even (the exact rule depends on the platform).
Going deeper: the Internals lesson [Primitive types, alignment and padding](/m2/primitive-types) shows how many bytes each number type takes on disk.

lessons.title: Dates, times and time zones
tldr: PostgreSQL has `date`, `timestamp` (wall-clock time), `timestamptz` (a real instant, stored in UTC) and `interval`, plus functions to truncate, extract, bucket and convert them.
Time zones and daylight saving time make "the same time" ambiguous, so choosing **timestamptz** and **half-open ranges** keeps reports and schedules correct everywhere.

visualizer.title: One instant, many clocks
visualizer.caption: Step through eight scenes. The x axis is real time; each lane is a local clock with its DST jumps. Switch the **session TimeZone** to see that only the display changes.

presets.label: TimeZone and now()
presets.note: The same stored instant prints as `17:00:00+00` or `22:30:00+05:30`. Inside a transaction `now()` never moves; `clock_timestamp()` does (elapsed is about 0.2 s).

presets.label: timestamp vs timestamptz
presets.note: A `timestamp` literal **silently drops** the `+02`. The timestamptz version converts it: 12:00 at +02 is 10:00 UTC.

presets.label: AT TIME ZONE
presets.note: timestamptz → timestamp (wall clock) and timestamp → timestamptz (an instant). Careful: the text `'+05'` is a POSIX zone meaning **UTC−5** (07:00); the interval form means UTC+5 (17:00).

presets.label: DST arithmetic
presets.note: 02:30 does not exist and becomes 03:30-04. `1 day` lands on 12:00 but `24 hours` on 13:00. The fall-back day lasts `1 day 01:00:00`: 25 hours.

presets.label: Dates, months and age
presets.sql:
SELECT date '2026-01-31' + interval '1 month'  AS jan31_plus_month,
       date '2024-01-31' + interval '1 month'  AS leap_year,
       date '2026-11-14' + 30                  AS in_30_days,
       date '2026-12-25' - date '2026-11-14'   AS days_to_go,
       age(date '2026-11-14', date '1990-05-20') AS age;
presets.note: Adding a month clamps to the last day (Feb 28, or Feb 29 in 2024). `date + integer` adds days; `date - date` is an integer number of days.

presets.label: Truncate, extract, bin
presets.sql:
SELECT happened_at,
       date_trunc('hour', happened_at)  AS hour,
       date_trunc('week', happened_at)  AS week_monday,
       extract(dow FROM happened_at)    AS dow_sun0,
       extract(isodow FROM happened_at) AS isodow_mon1,
       date_bin('15 minutes', happened_at, timestamptz '2026-01-01') AS bin15
FROM events ORDER BY id LIMIT 5;

SELECT extract(week FROM date '2027-01-01')    AS iso_week,
       extract(isoyear FROM date '2027-01-01') AS iso_year;
presets.note: `date_trunc('week')` snaps to Monday. `dow` counts Sunday as 0, `isodow` Monday as 1. 2027-01-01 belongs to ISO **week 53 of 2026**: always pair `week` with `isoyear`.

presets.label: Daily report, half-open
presets.note: Each day is `[start, start + 1 day)`: every event lands in exactly one bucket. Grouped by New York days the counts shift, and the 2026-03-08 bucket starts at 05:00 UTC but the next at 04:00 UTC (a 23-hour day).

production.title: A daily revenue report that is off by a day
production.context: An online shop stores `happened_at timestamptz`. Its finance team works in New York and reads a daily revenue report built with `happened_at::date`.
production.problem: The database session runs in UTC, so `::date` cuts days at midnight **UTC**, which is 19:00 or 20:00 in New York. Evening orders show up on the next day and the totals never match the till.
production.solution: Bucket by the business time zone explicitly with the three-argument `date_trunc`, and filter with half-open ranges built in that zone, so the result does not depend on the session TimeZone.
production.sql:
-- wrong: days in the session time zone (UTC)
SELECT happened_at::date AS day, count(*), sum(amount)
FROM events GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

-- right: New York business days
SELECT (date_trunc('day', happened_at, 'America/New_York')
          AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York')::date AS ny_day,
       count(*), sum(amount)
FROM events GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
production.outcome: On the playground data the UTC report shows 2026-03-06 with 15 events and 110.00; the New York report shows 14 events and 115.00 for that day, plus 4 events from the evening of 2026-03-05 that the UTC report had moved forward.

pitfalls.title: Using timestamp for events
pitfalls.symptom: Rows written by servers in different regions sort in the wrong order, and an hour of data looks duplicated every November.
pitfalls.cause: `timestamp` stores digits without a zone. Two clocks reading `01:30` may be hours apart, and the fall-back hour repeats.
pitfalls.fix: Store real moments as **timestamptz**. Use `timestamp` only for wall-clock values such as "store opens at 09:00 local".

pitfalls.title: BETWEEN on dates misses the last day
pitfalls.symptom: A monthly report written as `BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-31'` is missing almost all of March 31.
pitfalls.cause: The date `2026-03-31` becomes the timestamp `2026-03-31 00:00`. `BETWEEN` includes that single instant, not the whole day.
pitfalls.fix: Use a **half-open range**: `>= start AND < next_start`. It never overlaps and never leaves a gap.

pitfalls.title: A DEFAULT frozen at table creation
pitfalls.symptom: Every row has the same `created_at`: the moment the table was created.
pitfalls.cause: `DEFAULT 'now'` or `DEFAULT timestamptz 'now'` is a constant. It is converted once, when the CREATE TABLE is parsed.
pitfalls.fix: Use the function: `created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()`.

pitfalls.title: POSIX offsets point the wrong way
pitfalls.symptom: `AT TIME ZONE '+05'` gives a time 10 hours away from what you expected.
pitfalls.cause: A text zone like `'+05'` follows POSIX rules, where positive means **west** of Greenwich (UTC−5). ISO 8601 uses the opposite sign.
pitfalls.fix: Use a zone name (`'Asia/Karachi'`) or an interval (`AT TIME ZONE INTERVAL '+05:00'`).

pointers: **timestamptz** stores an instant (in UTC) and displays it in the session **TimeZone**. **timestamp** is wall-clock digits only.
`AT TIME ZONE` flips the type: timestamptz → timestamp (read a clock), timestamp → timestamptz (pin to a zone).
`+ interval '1 day'` keeps the local time of day; `+ interval '24 hours'` adds elapsed time. They differ across DST.
Filter time with **half-open ranges** `>= start AND < end`, and pass the business zone to `date_trunc`.
Going deeper: the Internals lesson [Declarative partitioning and pruning](/m7/partitioning) uses the same half-open bounds to split tables by time.

lessons.title: Conditional logic
tldr: `CASE`, `COALESCE`, `NULLIF`, `GREATEST`/`LEAST` and aggregate `FILTER` let one query choose a value per row, replace missing data and count different things in a single pass.
They exist so that labels, defaults and guarded calculations such as division by zero live in SQL, right next to the data, instead of in a loop in application code.

visualizer.title: Evaluate a conditional expression row by row
visualizer.caption: Choose an expression and press **Next row**. Branches light up in order: true, false, NULL or not evaluated at all. In **FILTER** mode, watch four aggregates fill up in one pass.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id       int PRIMARY KEY,
  customer text NOT NULL,
  status   text NOT NULL,          -- paid / refunded / pending
  total    numeric(8,2),           -- NULL = not known yet
  qty      int,
  coupon   numeric(6,2),
  promo    numeric(6,2)
);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES
  (1, 'Ann', 'paid',     120.00, 4, NULL,  5.00),
  (2, 'Bob', 'refunded',  64.50, 3, 10.00, NULL),
  (3, 'Cy',  'paid',      NULL,  2, NULL,  NULL),
  (4, 'Dee', 'pending',   18.00, 2, NULL,  2.50),
  (5, 'Eve', 'paid',      50.00, 0, NULL,  NULL);

presets.label: Searched CASE
presets.sql:
SELECT id, customer, total,
       CASE WHEN total >= 100 THEN 'gold'
            WHEN total >= 50  THEN 'silver'
            WHEN total IS NULL THEN 'unknown'
            ELSE 'bronze'
       END AS tier
FROM orders ORDER BY id;
presets.note: The first true branch wins. For Cy the comparisons are NULL (not true), so CASE falls through to `IS NULL`. Without that branch Cy would be `bronze`.

presets.label: Simple CASE and NULL
presets.note: A simple CASE compares with `=`, and `NULL = NULL` is not true, so it does **not** match. A CASE with no ELSE and no true branch returns NULL.

presets.label: COALESCE, GREATEST, LEAST
presets.sql:
SELECT id, coupon, promo,
       COALESCE(coupon, promo, 0) AS discount,
       GREATEST(coupon, promo)    AS best_offer,
       LEAST(total, 100)          AS capped_total
FROM orders ORDER BY id;
presets.note: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument. GREATEST and LEAST **ignore NULLs**, so Ann's best offer is 5.00, and they return NULL only when every argument is NULL.

presets.label: Safe division with NULLIF
presets.sql:
SELECT id, total, qty,
       round(total / NULLIF(qty, 0), 2)                AS per_item,
       COALESCE(round(total / NULLIF(qty, 0), 2), 0)  AS per_item_or_zero
FROM orders ORDER BY id;
presets.note: Eve has `qty = 0`. `NULLIF(qty, 0)` returns NULL, so the division returns NULL instead of an error. Try `SELECT total / qty FROM orders;` to see the error it prevents.

presets.label: FILTER: many metrics, one pass
presets.sql:
SELECT count(*)                                     AS orders,
       count(*)   FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')     AS paid,
       sum(total) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')     AS paid_revenue,
       count(*)   FILTER (WHERE total IS NULL)       AS missing_total,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'refunded') / NULLIF(count(*), 0), 1) AS refund_pct
FROM orders;
presets.note: Five metrics from one scan. `sum` skips Cy's NULL total, so paid revenue is 170.00 from three paid orders.

presets.label: Booleans as columns
presets.sql:
SELECT id, total,
       total >= 50                  AS big_order,
       status = 'paid' AND qty > 0  AS shippable,
       (status = 'paid')::int       AS paid_flag
FROM orders ORDER BY id;

SELECT sum((status = 'paid')::int) AS paid_count,
       bool_or(total IS NULL)      AS any_missing,
       coalesce(sum(total) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled'), 0) AS cancelled_revenue
FROM orders;
presets.note: A comparison is a value of type boolean, so it can be a column. Cy's `big_order` is NULL, not false. A sum over zero rows is NULL; `coalesce(..., 0)` turns it into 0.

presets.label: CASE needs one result type
presets.note: `1` and `2.5` unify to numeric. Mixing a number with a word does not: `CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 'n/a' END` fails, so cast the number to text first.

production.title: A KPI tile query that crashed on an empty day
production.context: An operations dashboard shows today's orders, paid share and refund rate. The first version ran one query per tile and computed rates with plain division.
production.problem: Four queries scanned the table four times, and right after midnight there were no orders: `refunded / count(*)` divided by zero and the whole dashboard showed an error.
production.solution: One query with **FILTER** aggregates computes every tile in a single pass. `NULLIF(count(*), 0)` makes empty days return NULL, and `COALESCE` turns that into a display value.
production.sql:
SELECT count(*)                                            AS orders,
       coalesce(sum(total) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid'), 0) AS paid_revenue,
       coalesce(round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'refunded')
                      / NULLIF(count(*), 0), 1), 0)           AS refund_pct
FROM orders
WHERE status <> 'cancelled';      -- on an empty result: 0, 0, 0 instead of an error
production.outcome: On the playground data the query returns 5 orders, 170.00 paid revenue and a 20.0% refund rate. With a filter that matches no rows it returns 0, 0 and 0 instead of failing, and the dashboard needs one scan instead of four.

pitfalls.title: CASE branches in the wrong order
pitfalls.symptom: Every large order is labelled "silver"; no order is ever "gold".
pitfalls.cause: CASE returns the **first** true branch. If `total >= 50` comes before `total >= 100`, it catches the big orders too.
pitfalls.fix: Order WHEN branches from most specific to least specific, and test the edge values.

pitfalls.title: CASE x WHEN NULL never matches
pitfalls.symptom: Rows with a NULL status fall into ELSE even though there is a `WHEN NULL` branch.
pitfalls.cause: A simple CASE compares with `=`, and `NULL = NULL` is NULL, not true.
pitfalls.fix: Use a searched CASE: `CASE WHEN status IS NULL THEN … END`.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT CASE WHEN NULL IS NULL THEN 'matched' END;

pitfalls.title: Division by zero in a ratio
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: division by zero` from a report, often only on some days or for new customers.
pitfalls.cause: A denominator such as `count(*)` or `qty` can be 0. Every numeric type raises an error.
pitfalls.fix: Divide by `NULLIF(denominator, 0)` and wrap the result in `COALESCE` if you need a number.

pitfalls.title: A constant error inside an unused CASE branch
pitfalls.symptom: A query fails with division by zero even though the CASE branch with `1/0` can never be chosen.
pitfalls.cause: CASE skips branches at run time, but the planner simplifies constant expressions first, and `1/0` fails during planning.
pitfalls.fix: Do not rely on CASE to hide constant errors; compute guarded values with NULLIF instead.

pointers: Searched **CASE** returns the first **true** branch. NULL is not true. No ELSE means NULL.
**COALESCE** picks the first non-NULL argument and stops there. **NULLIF(a, b)** turns a chosen value into NULL.
`x / NULLIF(y, 0)` is the standard guard against division by zero.
`count(*) FILTER (WHERE …)` computes many conditional metrics in one pass. Sums over no rows are NULL.

Going deeper: the Internals lesson [From SQL text to rows](/m4/query-pipeline) follows a query through parsing, rewriting and planning, the stages that run before the executor evaluates CASE row by row.

lessons.title: Type conversion
tldr: A **cast** converts a value from one type to another, written `CAST(x AS type)` or `x::type`, and functions like `to_char`, `to_number` and `to_date` handle custom formats.
Data often arrives as text from forms and files, so you need to know which conversions succeed, which round, which fail, and how to test input before it breaks a whole load.

visualizer.title: The cast matrix
visualizer.caption: Every cell is a real cast result. Click a cell for its SQL and error, or press **Next interesting cell** for a guided tour. Switch to **From a number** to compare numeric and double precision rounding.

playground.setup:
-- raw rows from a CSV upload: everything is text
CREATE TABLE staging_orders (
  line      int PRIMARY KEY,
  raw_qty   text,
  raw_price text,
  raw_date  text,
  raw_paid  text
);
INSERT INTO staging_orders VALUES
  (1, '3',     '12.50',     '2026-11-14', 'yes'),
  (2, ' 2 ',   '8',         '2026-11-15', 'no'),
  (3, '1',     '$1,299.00', '2026-11-15', 'true'),
  (4, 'four',  '9.99',      '2026-11-16', '1'),
  (5, '',      '7.25',      '2026-02-30', 't'),
  (6, '40000', '0.10',      '11/16/2026', 'f'),
  (7, '2',     '5.00',      '2026-11-17', 'maybe');

CREATE TABLE orders_clean (
  line       int PRIMARY KEY,
  qty        smallint      NOT NULL,
  price      numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
  ordered_on date          NOT NULL,
  paid       boolean       NOT NULL
);

presets.label: Three ways to cast
presets.sql:
SELECT CAST('42' AS integer) AS cast_syntax,
       '42'::integer          AS double_colon,
       integer '42'           AS typed_literal,
       42::text || '!'        AS number_to_text,
       pg_typeof('42'::integer) AS result_type;
presets.note: All three spellings do the same conversion. `::` is PostgreSQL shorthand; `CAST(… AS …)` is standard SQL.

presets.label: Literals adapt, columns do not
presets.note: A quoted literal starts as type `unknown` and takes whatever type its neighbour needs. Two texts compare character by character, so `'10' < '9'` is true and text numbers sort 1, 10, 2, 9.

presets.label: What would fail?
presets.sql:
SELECT line,
       raw_qty,   pg_input_is_valid(raw_qty,   'smallint') AS qty_ok,
       raw_price, pg_input_is_valid(raw_price, 'numeric')  AS price_ok,
       raw_date,  pg_input_is_valid(raw_date,  'date')     AS date_ok,
       raw_paid,  pg_input_is_valid(raw_paid,  'boolean')  AS paid_ok
FROM staging_orders ORDER BY line;

SELECT s.line, s.raw_qty, e.message, e.sql_error_code
FROM staging_orders s, pg_input_error_info(s.raw_qty, 'smallint') AS e
WHERE e.message IS NOT NULL ORDER BY s.line;
presets.note: `pg_input_is_valid` tests a value **without raising an error**. `pg_input_error_info` returns the message the cast would have raised: `four` and `''` are invalid syntax, `40000` is out of range.

presets.label: Rounding and truncation
presets.sql:
SELECT 2.5::integer          AS numeric_to_int,
       2.5::float8::integer  AS float_to_int,
       (-2.5)::integer       AS negative,
       3.99::integer         AS rounds_up,
       trunc(3.99)::integer  AS truncated,
       'abcdef'::varchar(3)  AS cut_to_3,
       1234.5678::numeric(6,2) AS two_places,
       '2026-11-14 15:42:07.987'::timestamp(0) AS whole_seconds;
presets.note: Casting a number to integer **rounds**, it does not truncate: 3.99 becomes 4. numeric ties go away from zero (3), double ties go to even (2). An explicit cast to `varchar(3)` silently cuts the text.

presets.label: to_char, to_number, to_date
presets.sql:
SELECT to_char(1234567.891, 'FM9,999,999.00')            AS money_text,
       to_char(42, '000')                                  AS zero_padded,
       to_char(12345, '999')                               AS too_narrow,
       to_char(date '2026-11-14', 'FMDay, FMDD FMMonth YYYY') AS long_date,
       to_char(timestamptz '2026-11-14 15:42+00', 'YYYY-MM-DD"T"HH24:MI:SS"Z"') AS iso_8601;

SELECT to_number('$1,299.00', 'L9G999D99')  AS parsed_price,
       to_date('14/11/2026', 'DD/MM/YYYY')   AS parsed_date;
presets.note: `to_char` formats numbers and dates as text; `FM` removes padding. A format too narrow prints `###`. `to_number` and `to_date` parse text that a plain cast rejects.

presets.label: Validate, then load
presets.sql:
INSERT INTO orders_clean (line, qty, price, ordered_on, paid)
SELECT line,
       trim(raw_qty)::smallint,
       CASE WHEN pg_input_is_valid(raw_price, 'numeric') THEN raw_price::numeric
            ELSE to_number(raw_price, 'L9G999D99') END,
       raw_date::date,
       raw_paid::boolean
FROM staging_orders
WHERE pg_input_is_valid(trim(raw_qty), 'smallint')
  AND pg_input_is_valid(raw_date, 'date')
  AND pg_input_is_valid(raw_paid, 'boolean');

SELECT * FROM orders_clean ORDER BY line;
presets.note: Only rows that pass every check are cast, so the INSERT cannot fail halfway. Lines 1, 2 and 3 load (line 3 via `to_number`). Lines 4 to 7 stay in staging for a human to fix.

presets.label: DateStyle and JSON values
presets.note: The same `03/04/2026` is April 3 or March 4 depending on **DateStyle**: prefer ISO `YYYY-MM-DD`. `->>` always returns text, so cast it before doing arithmetic.

production.title: Importing a messy CSV without losing the good rows
production.context: A wholesale team uploads order spreadsheets every morning. A job copies them into a text-only staging table and then into typed tables.
production.problem: The first version ran `INSERT … SELECT raw_qty::smallint, …`. One cell with `four` raised `invalid input syntax for type smallint` and the **whole statement** rolled back: no orders loaded until someone found the bad row.
production.solution: Test every value with `pg_input_is_valid` first. Load the rows that pass, and copy the rest, with the exact message from `pg_input_error_info`, into a quarantine table that the team reviews.
production.sql:
CREATE TABLE import_errors AS
SELECT s.line, 'raw_qty' AS field, s.raw_qty AS value, e.message
FROM staging_orders s, pg_input_error_info(trim(s.raw_qty), 'smallint') AS e
WHERE e.message IS NOT NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT s.line, 'raw_date', s.raw_date, e.message
FROM staging_orders s, pg_input_error_info(s.raw_date, 'date') AS e
WHERE e.message IS NOT NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT s.line, 'raw_paid', s.raw_paid, e.message
FROM staging_orders s, pg_input_error_info(s.raw_paid, 'boolean') AS e
WHERE e.message IS NOT NULL;

SELECT * FROM import_errors ORDER BY line, field;
production.outcome: On the playground data 3 of 7 rows load and 5 problems in 4 rows are reported (line 5 has both an empty quantity and February 30). Before the change, one bad cell meant zero rows loaded.

pitfalls.title: One bad value aborts the whole load
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: invalid input syntax for type smallint: "four"` and nothing is inserted, not even the valid rows.
pitfalls.cause: A statement is atomic. The first failing cast raises an error and rolls back every row of that INSERT.
pitfalls.fix: Filter with `pg_input_is_valid(value, 'type')` before casting, and route invalid rows to a review table.

pitfalls.title: Numbers stored as text sort wrongly
pitfalls.symptom: Order numbers come back as 1, 10, 2, 9, and `WHERE code > '9'` misses 10.
pitfalls.cause: Text compares character by character: `'1'` < `'9'`, so `'10'` sorts before `'9'`.
pitfalls.fix: Store numbers in numeric columns. As a stopgap, cast in the query: `ORDER BY code::int`.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT x FROM (VALUES ('1'), ('10'), ('2'), ('9')) AS v(x) ORDER BY x::int;

pitfalls.title: Casting to integer rounds, and not always the same way
pitfalls.symptom: An "items per box" calculation is off by one, and two code paths disagree on 2.5.
pitfalls.cause: `::integer` rounds instead of truncating. From numeric, ties go away from zero; from double precision, ties go to even.
pitfalls.fix: Say what you mean before casting: `trunc(x)::int`, `floor(x)::int`, `ceil(x)::int` or `round(x)::int`.

pitfalls.title: Explicit varchar casts truncate silently
pitfalls.symptom: Long names are cut to a few characters in an export, with no error.
pitfalls.cause: Inserting `'abcdef'` into a `varchar(3)` column is an error, but an explicit `::varchar(3)` cast quietly keeps only 3 characters.
pitfalls.fix: Do not cast to a shorter length to "make it fit". Check `length(x)` first, or widen the column.

pointers: `CAST(x AS t)`, `x::t` and `t 'literal'` are the same conversion. Quoted literals start as `unknown` and adapt to their context.
Text → number accepts spaces but not decimal points (for integers), commas or empty strings. Out of range is an error, never a wrap.
Number → integer **rounds**: ties away from zero from numeric, to even from double precision. Be explicit with `trunc`/`round`.
Check input with `pg_input_is_valid` and `pg_input_error_info` before casting; use `to_char`/`to_number`/`to_date` for custom formats.
Going deeper: the Internals lesson [JSON vs JSONB](/m2/json-jsonb) shows how JSON values are stored and why `->>` hands you text.

lessons.title: Working with JSON
tldr: PostgreSQL can build JSON documents from ordinary rows, query them with path expressions, turn them back into rows, change parts of them and validate them with constraints.
Applications speak JSON, so doing this shaping in one SQL statement replaces many round trips and loops in application code, as long as you pick the right function and the right index.

visualizer.title: Rows, paths and indexes
visualizer.caption: **Rows → document**: press **Fold one level** and watch join rows nest into one document; switch the empty-group handling to see what a customer with no orders gets. **Path explorer**: click a node. **Index guide**: pick a query shape.

presets.label: Rows become JSON
presets.sql:
SELECT to_jsonb(c)     AS as_jsonb,
       row_to_json(c)  AS as_json
FROM customers c WHERE id = 1;

SELECT o.id,
       jsonb_build_object(
         'order',  o.id,
         'status', o.status,
         'items',  jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('sku', i.sku, 'qty', i.qty) ORDER BY i.sku)) AS doc
FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.id ORDER BY o.id;

SELECT jsonb_object_agg(status, n) AS orders_by_status
FROM (SELECT status, count(*) AS n FROM orders GROUP BY status) s;
presets.note: `to_jsonb(row)` turns a whole row into an object keyed by column name. `jsonb_build_object` picks the keys, `jsonb_agg(… ORDER BY …)` folds rows into an ordered array, and `jsonb_object_agg(key, value)` folds rows into one object.

presets.label: Empty groups: [null], NULL or []
presets.sql:
SELECT c.name,
       jsonb_agg(o.id ORDER BY o.id)                                  AS plain,
       jsonb_agg(o.id ORDER BY o.id) FILTER (WHERE o.id IS NOT NULL)  AS filtered,
       COALESCE(jsonb_agg(o.id ORDER BY o.id) FILTER (WHERE o.id IS NOT NULL), '[]') AS safe,
       jsonb_agg_strict(jsonb_build_object('id', o.id))               AS strict_objects
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

SELECT jsonb_object_agg(name, city)        AS keeps_null_values,
       jsonb_object_agg_strict(name, city) AS drops_null_values
FROM customers;
presets.note: Dara has no orders. Plain `jsonb_agg` gives `[null]`, `FILTER` gives SQL NULL, and `COALESCE(…, '[]')` gives an empty array. `jsonb_agg_strict` skips NULL values but not an object full of nulls. A NULL **key** in `jsonb_object_agg` is an error; a NULL value is kept unless you use the `_strict` form.

presets.label: SQL/JSON standard functions
presets.sql:
SELECT JSON_OBJECT('order': o.id, 'status': o.status,
         'items': JSON_ARRAYAGG(JSON_OBJECT('sku': i.sku, 'qty': i.qty) ORDER BY i.sku RETURNING jsonb)
         RETURNING jsonb) AS doc
FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.id = 103 GROUP BY o.id;

SELECT JSON_OBJECT('a': 1, 'b': NULL)::text                AS object_keeps_null,
       JSON_OBJECT('a': 1, 'b': NULL ABSENT ON NULL)::text  AS object_drops_null,
       JSON_ARRAY(1, NULL, 'x')::text                       AS array_drops_null,
       pg_typeof(JSON_OBJECT('a': 1))                       AS default_type;

SELECT id,
       JSON_VALUE(body, '$.customer')                                       AS customer,
       JSON_VALUE(body, '$.placed' RETURNING date)                          AS placed,
       JSON_VALUE(body, '$.placed' RETURNING date DEFAULT '1900-01-01' ON ERROR) AS placed_or_default,
       JSON_VALUE(body, '$.gift' RETURNING boolean DEFAULT false ON EMPTY)  AS gift,
       JSON_QUERY(body, '$.items[*].sku' WITH WRAPPER)                      AS skus,
       JSON_EXISTS(body, '$.items[*] ? (@.price > $p)' PASSING 10 AS p)     AS has_item_over_10
FROM inbox ORDER BY id;
presets.note: The standard constructors return `json` unless you say `RETURNING jsonb`. `JSON_OBJECT` keeps NULLs by default, `JSON_ARRAY` drops them. Inbox row 2 has `13/11/2026`, which is not a valid date: `JSON_VALUE … RETURNING date` quietly returns NULL, unless you give a `DEFAULT … ON ERROR`.

presets.label: Shred JSON into rows and load it
presets.note: `jsonb_to_recordset` maps each array element to a typed row: the string `"3"` becomes the integer 3 and a missing `qty` becomes NULL. `WITH ORDINALITY` numbers the elements from 1. The `LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true` keeps inbox row 2, whose array is empty.

presets.label: Update toolkit
presets.sql:
SELECT d || '{"status": "paid"}'                        AS add_or_replace_key,
       d - 'gift'                                       AS remove_key,
       d #- '{items,0}'                                 AS remove_at_path,
       jsonb_insert(d, '{items,0}', '"gift-wrap"')       AS insert_before_first,
       jsonb_insert(d, '{items,-1}', '"card"', true)     AS insert_after_last,
       jsonb_set(d, '{meta,source}', '"web"')            AS set_missing_parent,
       jsonb_set(d, '{meta}', COALESCE(d -> 'meta', '{}') || '{"source": "web"}') AS set_parent_first
FROM (SELECT '{"order": 202, "gift": true, "items": ["mug", "tea"]}'::jsonb AS d) s;

UPDATE inbox SET body = (body || '{"status": "received"}') - 'gift'
WHERE id = 2
RETURNING body;
presets.note: `||` adds or replaces top-level keys, `-` removes a key, `#-` removes whatever sits at a path. `jsonb_insert` inserts into arrays (and refuses to overwrite an existing object key). `jsonb_set` with a missing **parent** returns the document unchanged, with no error. Mind the parentheses: `-` binds tighter than `||`.

presets.label: Validate documents
presets.sql:
SELECT v,
       v IS JSON                   AS is_json,
       v IS JSON OBJECT            AS is_object,
       v IS JSON ARRAY             AS is_array,
       v IS JSON SCALAR            AS is_scalar,
       v IS JSON WITH UNIQUE KEYS  AS unique_keys
FROM (VALUES ('{"a": 1}'), ('{"a": 1, "a": 2}'), ('[1, 2]'), ('42'), ('{a: 1}'), ('')) AS t(v);

CREATE TABLE carts (
  id  int PRIMARY KEY,
  doc jsonb NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT doc_is_object CHECK (jsonb_typeof(doc) = 'object'),
  CONSTRAINT doc_has_keys  CHECK (doc ?& ARRAY['customer', 'items']),
  CONSTRAINT items_array   CHECK (jsonb_typeof(doc -> 'items') = 'array'),
  CONSTRAINT items_valid   CHECK (NOT JSON_EXISTS(doc,
    '$.items[*] ? (!exists(@.qty) || @.qty.type() != "number" || @.qty < 1)')));

DO $$
DECLARE d text;
BEGIN
  FOREACH d IN ARRAY ARRAY[
    '{"customer": "Ben", "items": [{"sku": "tea", "qty": 2}]}',
    '[1, 2]',
    '{"customer": "Ben", "items": {"sku": "tea"}}',
    '{"customer": "Ben", "items": [{"sku": "tea", "qty": "2"}]}',
    '{"customer": "Ben", "items": [{"sku": "tea"}]}',
    '{"customer": "Ben", "items": [{"sku": "tea", "qty": 0}]}'] LOOP
    BEGIN
      INSERT INTO carts VALUES ((SELECT count(*) + 1 FROM carts), d::jsonb);
      RAISE NOTICE 'accepted %', d;
    EXCEPTION WHEN check_violation THEN
      RAISE NOTICE 'rejected % (%)', d, SQLERRM;
    END;
  END LOOP;
END $$;
presets.note: `IS JSON` tests text without raising an error; `WITH UNIQUE KEYS` catches duplicate keys that jsonb would silently collapse. The CHECK constraints accept only the first cart: watch the notices for which constraint rejected each of the others.

presets.label: Index decision guide
presets.note: Containment and `?` use the GIN indexes; `->>` equality, the numeric range and top-N need the B-tree expression indexes; the jsonpath range stays a Seq Scan. In the last two plans compare the `rows=` estimate: a guess of 100 for `->>` against 50 (the true count) for the promoted column.

production.title: One query for an account page, with no [null]
production.context: A storefront API returns each customer with their orders and the items of each order. The first version ran one query for the customers, one per customer for orders, and one per order for items.
production.problem: The page made 1 + 4 + 4 = **9** round trips for the 4 customers here, and it grew with every order. A rewrite with `LEFT JOIN` and `jsonb_agg` cut that to one, but customers without orders came back as `"orders": [{"id": null, "items": null}]` and the mobile app crashed reading the fake order.
production.solution: Aggregate items per order in a subquery, then orders per customer, with `FILTER` to drop the all-NULL row and `COALESCE` to turn "no rows" into an empty array. Put `ORDER BY` inside each aggregate so the arrays have a stable order.
production.sql:
SELECT jsonb_build_object(
         'customer', c.name,
         'orders', COALESCE(jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('id', o.id, 'status', o.status, 'items', o.items)
                                      ORDER BY o.placed_on)
                            FILTER (WHERE o.id IS NOT NULL), '[]')) AS doc
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN (SELECT o.*, jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('sku', i.sku, 'qty', i.qty, 'price', i.price)
                                 ORDER BY i.sku) AS items
           FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
           GROUP BY o.id) o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;
production.outcome: One statement replaces nine on the playground data, and the count no longer grows with the number of orders. Dara now gets `"orders": []`, which every client can loop over.

pitfalls.title: Customers with no children get [null]
pitfalls.symptom: A JSON API returns `"orders": [null]` or `[{"id": null}]` for customers without orders, and clients crash on the fake element.
pitfalls.cause: A `LEFT JOIN` produces one all-NULL row for an unmatched parent, and `jsonb_agg` aggregates it. `jsonb_agg_strict` skips only NULL values, not objects whose fields are NULL.
pitfalls.fix: Filter the fake row and default the empty case: `COALESCE(jsonb_agg(x) FILTER (WHERE child.id IS NOT NULL), '[]')`, or aggregate in a correlated subquery, which sees no fake row but still needs `COALESCE(…, '[]')`.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT c.name, COALESCE(jsonb_agg(o.id) FILTER (WHERE o.id IS NOT NULL), '[]') AS orders
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

pitfalls.title: JSON_VALUE turns bad data into NULL
pitfalls.symptom: After a load, some order dates are NULL although every document had a `placed` value.
pitfalls.cause: The default for `JSON_VALUE` and `JSON_QUERY` is **NULL ON ERROR**: a value that does not convert to the `RETURNING` type, or a path that finds an object or several items, gives NULL instead of an error.
pitfalls.fix: In loads, write `ERROR ON ERROR` so bad documents fail loudly, or `DEFAULT … ON ERROR` plus a check that counts the defaults. Use `ON EMPTY` for keys that may be missing.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT JSON_VALUE(body, '$.placed' RETURNING date ERROR ON ERROR) FROM inbox WHERE id = 2;  -- fails: "13/11/2026" is not a date

pitfalls.title: jsonb_set silently does nothing
pitfalls.symptom: An `UPDATE … SET doc = jsonb_set(doc, '{meta,source}', '"web"')` reports rows updated, but the key never appears.
pitfalls.cause: `jsonb_set` creates only the **last** step of the path. If a parent such as `meta` is missing, it returns the document unchanged, without an error.
pitfalls.fix: Create the parent first: `jsonb_set(doc, '{meta}', COALESCE(doc -> 'meta', '{}') || '{"source": "web"}')`, or rebuild the sub-object with `||`.

pitfalls.title: Expecting one index to serve every JSON query
pitfalls.symptom: A GIN index exists on the document, yet `->>` filters, numeric ranges and `ORDER BY` on a JSON key are still sequential scans.
pitfalls.cause: GIN on the column serves `@>`, `?`, `?|`, `?&` and jsonpath **equality** (`@?`, `@@`). It cannot serve an extracted expression, a range, or ordering. A `VIRTUAL` generated column cannot be indexed at all.
pitfalls.fix: Add a B-tree on the exact expression (`((attrs ->> 'sku'))`, `(((attrs ->> 'price')::numeric))`), or promote a hot key to a `STORED` generated column with its own index and statistics.
