Each pass reads only the **working table** (last pass's new rows); recursion ends when a pass produces nothing.
UNION drops rows that duplicate **any earlier row**; UNION ALL keeps everything.
`CYCLE col SET is_cycle USING path` stops loops; `SEARCH DEPTH|BREADTH FIRST BY col SET ord` gives a sortable order.
Recursive CTEs are always materialized; data-modifying statements cannot be recursive.

lessons.title: Window functions and frames
tldr: A **window function** computes a value for every row from a set of related rows (its partition, and for aggregates and value functions a **frame** inside it), without collapsing rows the way GROUP BY does.

It answers "compared with its neighbours" questions in one pass: rankings, running totals, moving averages, previous-row deltas and top-N per group, where a self-join or correlated subquery would be slower and harder to read.

visualizer.title: The window frame explorer
visualizer.caption: Click a row to make it current, then change mode, bounds, offset and EXCLUDE. Start with **Default frame** on Sony VAIO (a three-way tie at 700), then compare **Running total**.

presets.label: Rows stay, unlike GROUP BY
presets.sql:
SELECT group_name, round(avg(price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products JOIN product_groups USING (group_id)
GROUP BY group_name ORDER BY group_name;

SELECT product_name, group_name, price,
       round(avg(price) OVER (PARTITION BY group_name), 2) AS group_avg
FROM products JOIN product_groups USING (group_id)
ORDER BY group_name, price;
presets.note: GROUP BY returns 3 rows. The window version returns all 11, each with its group's average attached (Laptop 850, Smartphone 500, Tablet 350).

presets.label: Ranking with ties
presets.sql:
SELECT product_name, price,
       row_number() OVER w, rank() OVER w, dense_rank() OVER w,
       round((percent_rank() OVER w)::numeric, 2) AS pct_rank,
       round((cume_dist() OVER w)::numeric, 2) AS cume_dist,
       ntile(3) OVER w
FROM products JOIN product_groups USING (group_id)
WHERE group_name = 'Laptop'
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY price);
presets.note: Lenovo and Sony tie at 700: row_number 1,2 (arbitrary order), rank 1,1,3,4 (gap), dense_rank 1,1,2,3 (no gap). `percent_rank` = (rank − 1) / (rows − 1), so the first row is always 0. `cume_dist` = rows up to the last peer / rows: 0.5 for both 700s. `ntile(3)` over 4 rows makes buckets of 2, 1, 1: bigger buckets come first.

presets.label: The default frame trap
presets.sql:
SELECT product_name, price,
       sum(price) OVER (ORDER BY price) AS range_default,
       sum(price) OVER (ORDER BY price ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS rows_running,
       last_value(product_name) OVER (ORDER BY price) AS last_default,
       last_value(product_name) OVER (ORDER BY price
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_whole
FROM products ORDER BY price, product_id;
presets.note: All three 700 rows show `range_default` = 3550 (peers share the frame end), while `rows_running` differs across them, in an order PostgreSQL does not guarantee. `last_default` is just the current row's last peer; `last_whole` is HP Elite everywhere.

presets.label: Cheapest per group
presets.sql:
SELECT group_name, product_name, price
FROM (
  SELECT g.group_name, p.product_name, p.price,
         dense_rank() OVER (PARTITION BY g.group_name ORDER BY p.price) AS r
  FROM products p JOIN product_groups g USING (group_id)
) ranked
WHERE r = 1
ORDER BY group_name, product_name;
presets.note: Window functions run after WHERE, so filtering on the rank needs a subquery. dense_rank keeps **both** 700s in Laptop; row_number would silently pick one.

presets.label: LAG: year over year
presets.sql:
SELECT year, group_id, amount,
       lag(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY group_id ORDER BY year) AS prev,
       amount - lag(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY group_id ORDER BY year) AS delta
FROM sales ORDER BY group_id, year;
presets.note: The first year of each group has no previous row, so `lag` returns NULL (pass a third argument for a default). `lag` and `lead` ignore the frame. They look at the previous **row**, not the previous year: if 2019 were missing, 2020 would be compared with 2018. And with `ORDER BY year DESC`, `lag` returns the following year.

presets.label: Percent of total in one pass
presets.sql:
SELECT band, name, earnings,
       round(100 * earnings / sum(earnings) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_all,
       round(100 * earnings / sum(earnings) OVER (PARTITION BY band), 1) AS pct_of_band
FROM musicians ORDER BY band, earnings DESC;

-- window over grouped rows: the inner sum is the aggregate, the outer one the window
SELECT band, sum(earnings) AS band_total,
       round(100 * sum(earnings) / sum(sum(earnings)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_all
FROM musicians GROUP BY band ORDER BY band;
presets.note: `sum(…) OVER ()` puts the grand total (20.8) on every row, so no CROSS JOIN to a total subquery is needed. Changing only the window to `PARTITION BY band` switches the denominator to the band total: Stills is 30.3% of all earnings but 48.5% of CSNY. The second query works because windows run **after** GROUP BY: CSNY 62.5%, PPM 37.5%.

presets.label: Fill gaps: last known value
presets.sql:
SELECT ts, temperature, grp,
       first_value(temperature) OVER (PARTITION BY sensor_id, grp ORDER BY ts) AS filled,
       lag(temperature) OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS naive_lag
FROM (
  SELECT *, count(temperature) OVER (PARTITION BY sensor_id ORDER BY ts) AS grp
  FROM sensor_readings
) s
ORDER BY ts;
presets.note: `count(temperature)` skips NULLs, so the running count only rises on a real reading: every NULL row inherits the group of the last reading. `first_value` within that group carries 22.50 forward twice and 23.10 once. A plain `lag` is no fix: after two NULLs in a row it returns NULL.

presets.label: Moving window: ROWS vs RANGE
presets.sql:
SELECT product_name, price,
       sum(price) OVER (ORDER BY price ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING) AS rows_1,
       sum(price) OVER (ORDER BY price RANGE BETWEEN 100 PRECEDING AND 100 FOLLOWING) AS range_100,
       sum(price) OVER (ORDER BY price GROUPS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING EXCLUDE TIES) AS groups_1
FROM products ORDER BY price, product_id;
presets.note: Compare with the explorer's presets: ROWS counts rows, RANGE compares price values, GROUPS counts distinct prices.

production.title: Deduplicating a change-data feed: latest row per key
production.context: An analytics team receives a CDC feed into `customer_changes(customer_id, changed_at, payload)`, many rows per customer, and needs the current state of each customer every hour.
production.problem: The first query used a correlated subquery `WHERE changed_at = (SELECT max(changed_at) … WHERE customer_id = c.customer_id)`. It ran one subquery per row, and returned two rows when two changes shared a timestamp.
production.solution: Number the rows per customer with `row_number()` ordered by time and a tie-breaker, then keep number 1. One sort, one pass, exactly one row per key.
production.sql:
SELECT customer_id, changed_at, payload
FROM (
  SELECT *, row_number() OVER (
           PARTITION BY customer_id
           ORDER BY changed_at DESC, change_id DESC) AS rn
  FROM customer_changes
) x
WHERE rn = 1;
production.outcome: One scan and one sort instead of one subquery per row, and a deterministic answer when timestamps tie, thanks to the `change_id` tie-breaker. An index on `(customer_id, changed_at DESC, change_id DESC)` can provide the order and skip the sort.

pitfalls.title: last_value returns the current row
pitfalls.symptom: `last_value(price) OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY price)` returns each row's own price instead of the group maximum.
pitfalls.cause: With ORDER BY, the default frame is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`: it ends at the current row's last peer.
pitfalls.fix: Add `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`, or use `first_value(…)` with the ORDER BY reversed.

pitfalls.title: Running totals that jump on ties
pitfalls.symptom: A running balance shows the same total on two rows, then skips ahead.
pitfalls.cause: The default RANGE frame includes all **peers**, so rows with an equal ORDER BY value get the same sum.
pitfalls.fix: Use `ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING` and add a unique tie-breaker to the ORDER BY (`ORDER BY booked_at, id`) so the order is deterministic.

pitfalls.title: Filtering on a window function in WHERE
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: window functions are not allowed in WHERE`.
pitfalls.cause: Window functions are computed after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, just before the final ORDER BY and LIMIT.
pitfalls.fix: Compute the window function in a subquery or CTE, then filter in the outer query.

pitfalls.title: A ROWS window treated as a time window
pitfalls.symptom: A "7-day moving average" over daily rows is wrong after days with no data.
pitfalls.cause: `ROWS 6 PRECEDING` means six **rows**. Missing days silently stretch the window.
pitfalls.fix: Use `RANGE BETWEEN interval '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` on a date column, or fill the gaps with `generate_series` first.

pitfalls.title: DISTINCT does not deduplicate a row_number()
pitfalls.symptom: `SELECT DISTINCT price, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY price)` still returns every duplicate price.
pitfalls.cause: Window functions run **before** DISTINCT, and every row gets a different number, so no two output rows are equal.
pitfalls.fix: Deduplicate first, then number: `SELECT price, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY price) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT price FROM products) p` (8 rows instead of 11). Or use `dense_rank()`, which gives equal values the same number.

pitfalls.title: Top-N with LIMIT on a tie
pitfalls.symptom: "Top 4 products by price" shows Lenovo on one run and Sony or iPad on the next.
pitfalls.cause: Three products tie at 700 for the fourth place. `ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 4` returns some 4 rows that satisfy the order; which tied row makes the cut is not defined.
pitfalls.fix: Add a unique tie-breaker (`ORDER BY price DESC, product_id`), or include every tie with `FETCH FIRST 4 ROWS WITH TIES` (6 rows here) or `rank() <= 4`.

pointers: Window functions run **after** WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING and never collapse rows.
**Peers** are rows equal under the window ORDER BY; rank functions give peers the same value.
Default frame with ORDER BY: `RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING` to the current row's **last peer**; without ORDER BY: the whole partition.
`ROWS` counts rows, `RANGE` compares values (one ORDER BY column for offsets), `GROUPS` counts peer groups; `EXCLUDE` trims the result.
Frames matter for aggregates and `first_value`/`last_value`/`nth_value`, not for `row_number`, `rank`, `lag` or `lead`.

lessons.title: LATERAL joins
tldr: A `LATERAL` subquery in FROM may reference columns of the FROM items to its left, so it is evaluated **once per outer row**, like the body of a for-each loop.
It exists for questions a plain join cannot express, such as "the latest N rows for each parent" or "expand this row's array", and with the right index it is often the fastest top-N-per-group plan.

visualizer.title: LATERAL as a for-each loop
visualizer.caption: Step through the outer rows and watch the subquery re-run with each `a.id`. Compare **CROSS JOIN LATERAL** (5 rows) with **LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true** (6 rows), and try the plain JOIN to see the error.

presets.label: Without LATERAL: an error
presets.sql:
SELECT try_sql($q$
  SELECT a.name, p.item
  FROM accounts a
  JOIN (SELECT * FROM purchases WHERE account_id = a.id) p ON true
$q$) AS result;
presets.note: `42P01: invalid reference to FROM-clause entry for table "a"`. A plain FROM subquery cannot see its neighbours.

presets.label: Latest 2 per account
presets.sql:
SELECT a.name, p.item, p.created_at
FROM accounts a
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT item, created_at FROM purchases
  WHERE account_id = a.id
  ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 2
) p
ORDER BY a.id, p.created_at DESC;
presets.note: 5 rows. Umbrella has no purchases, so CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops it.

presets.label: Keep empty parents
presets.sql:
SELECT a.name, p.item, p.created_at
FROM accounts a
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT item, created_at FROM purchases
  WHERE account_id = a.id
  ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 2
) p ON true
ORDER BY a.id, p.created_at DESC;
presets.note: 6 rows: Umbrella appears with NULLs. `ON true` is required syntax for LEFT JOIN; the real condition lives inside the subquery.

presets.label: loops=4 and the index
presets.note: A **Nested Loop** whose inner side shows `loops=4`. With the index the inner side is an Index Scan that reads at most 2 entries per account, no sort.

presets.label: Functions are implicitly lateral
presets.note: A set-returning function in FROM may always reference earlier items, with or without the keyword. `WITH ORDINALITY` adds a bigint position column. Initech has no tags: dropped by the comma form, kept by LEFT JOIN.

presets.label: Split a CSV column (and the text trap)
presets.sql:
-- hourly readings stored as one comma-separated string per station
SELECT w.station, max(t) AS max_reading, min(t) AS min_reading
FROM weather_data w, unnest(string_to_array(w.temps, ',')) AS t
GROUP BY w.station ORDER BY 1;

-- cast before comparing
SELECT w.station, max(t) AS max_temp, min(t) AS min_temp, count(*) AS readings
FROM weather_data w, unnest(string_to_array(w.temps, ',')::int[]) AS t
GROUP BY w.station ORDER BY 1;

-- the hottest hour per station: ordinality + LATERAL top-1
SELECT w.station, h.hour, h.temp
FROM weather_data w
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT hour, temp
  FROM unnest(string_to_array(w.temps, ',')::int[]) WITH ORDINALITY AS u(temp, hour)
  ORDER BY temp DESC LIMIT 1
) h ORDER BY 1;
presets.note: `string_to_array` returns `text[]`, so the first query compares **strings**: North's minimum is '-1' (true value −16) and West's maximum is '9' (true 16). Casting to `int[]` fixes it. The last query numbers each reading with `WITH ORDINALITY` and keeps the top one per station: hour 8 at West (16°), hour 7 at South (33°).

presets.label: LATERAL vs a window function
presets.sql:
SELECT name, item, created_at
FROM (
  SELECT a.name, p.item, p.created_at,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY a.id ORDER BY p.created_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM accounts a JOIN purchases p ON p.account_id = a.id
) x
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY name, created_at DESC;
presets.note: Same 5 rows. The window version numbers **every** purchase and then filters; LATERAL + LIMIT with an index reads only the rows it returns. With few parents and many children per parent, LATERAL wins.

production.title: An activity feed: latest 3 events per followed user
production.context: A social app shows each user the 3 newest posts from every account they follow. `posts` has 400 M rows; a typical user follows 200 accounts.
production.problem: The original query ranked all posts of all followed accounts with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY author_id ORDER BY created_at DESC)` and then filtered `rn <= 3`. For a user following prolific accounts it sorted hundreds of thousands of rows to return 600.
production.solution: Drive the query from the follow list and fetch each author's newest 3 with LATERAL, backed by an index whose order matches the subquery.
production.outcome: The plan becomes a Nested Loop with an Index Scan inside, `loops` = number of followed accounts, and at most 3 index entries read per loop: about 600 rows touched instead of every post of those authors.

pitfalls.title: CROSS JOIN LATERAL silently drops parents
pitfalls.symptom: Accounts with no purchases are missing from a "latest purchase per account" report.
pitfalls.cause: With comma or CROSS JOIN LATERAL, an outer row whose subquery returns zero rows produces no output, just like an inner join.
pitfalls.fix: Use `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (…) p ON true` to keep every outer row, NULL-extended.

pitfalls.title: LATERAL without a supporting index
pitfalls.symptom: A LATERAL top-N query is slower than the window-function version.
pitfalls.cause: The subquery runs once per outer row. Without an index matching `WHERE … ORDER BY`, each run scans and sorts the inner table.
pitfalls.fix: Create an index on `(correlation_column, sort_column DESC)` so each loop is a short index scan, and check `loops=` in EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

pitfalls.title: Referencing the right side from a RIGHT/FULL join
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: invalid reference to FROM-clause entry` even though LATERAL is written.
pitfalls.cause: A LATERAL item may only reference items that are INNER or LEFT joined to it. In `X RIGHT JOIN LATERAL Y`, Y cannot reference X.
pitfalls.fix: Rewrite with the LATERAL item on the right side of an inner or LEFT join.

pitfalls.title: Max-then-join-back for "latest per group"
pitfalls.symptom: A "latest purchase per account" query built as `GROUP BY account_id` + `max(created_at)`, joined back on both columns, returns two rows for some accounts.
pitfalls.cause: The join back matches every row with that timestamp, so a tie on `created_at` returns all tied rows. It also reads the table twice. A common claim is that this GROUP BY form always beats LATERAL at scale; with an index on `(account_id, created_at DESC)` the LATERAL plan reads one index entry per account.
pitfalls.fix: Use LATERAL with `ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1`, or `DISTINCT ON (account_id) … ORDER BY account_id, created_at DESC, id DESC`. Both return exactly one row per key, with a deterministic tie-breaker.

pointers: `LATERAL` lets a FROM subquery reference columns of FROM items **to its left**; it runs once per outer row.
Set-returning functions in FROM are **implicitly lateral**; the keyword is optional there.
CROSS JOIN / comma LATERAL drops rows with an empty result; `LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true` keeps them.
Top-N per group: LATERAL + `ORDER BY … LIMIT n` + index on `(key, sort DESC)` → Nested Loop with Index Scan.
`WITH ORDINALITY` numbers the rows of a function in FROM (bigint, from 1).

lessons.title: Aggregates, FILTER and GROUPING SETS
tldr: An **aggregate** folds many input rows into one value per group, and `FILTER`, ordered-set aggregates and `GROUPING SETS` / `ROLLUP` / `CUBE` control which rows feed it and which groupings are produced.

Together they turn a dozen report queries (totals, subtotals, conditional counts, medians) into one pass over the data, provided you respect the NULL rules that make `count(col)` differ from `count(*)` and `sum` of nothing NULL.

visualizer.title: Grouping sets, one set at a time
visualizer.caption: Pick ROLLUP, CUBE or your own GROUPING SETS and step through each set. Watch which input rows fold together, and how `grouping()` tells a subtotal's NULL from Baz's real NULL size.

presets.label: CUBE and grouping()
presets.sql:
SELECT brand, size, sum(sales), grouping(brand, size) AS g
FROM items_sold
GROUP BY CUBE (brand, size)
ORDER BY g, brand, size;
presets.note: 12 rows. Two rows read `NULL, NULL`: sum 8 with g = 2 (Baz's real NULL size, grouped by size) and sum 58 with g = 3 (the grand total).

presets.label: Four queries, or one GROUPING SETS
presets.sql:
-- four GROUP BYs glued together: four scans
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT brand, size, sum(sales) FROM items_sold GROUP BY brand, size
UNION ALL SELECT brand, NULL, sum(sales) FROM items_sold GROUP BY brand
UNION ALL SELECT NULL, size, sum(sales) FROM items_sold GROUP BY size
UNION ALL SELECT NULL, NULL, sum(sales) FROM items_sold;

-- the same 12 rows from one scan
SELECT brand, size, sum(sales)
FROM items_sold
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((brand, size), (brand), (size), ())
ORDER BY brand, size;

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT brand, size, sum(sales) FROM items_sold
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((brand, size), (brand), (size), ());
presets.note: The UNION ALL plan is an **Append** of four aggregates, each over its own Seq Scan. GROUPING SETS returns the same 12 rows from one **MixedAggregate** (one Hash Key per set, `Group Key: ()` for the total) over a single scan. `CUBE (brand, size)` is shorthand for exactly these four sets.

presets.label: ROLLUP with labels
presets.sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN grouping(brand) = 1 THEN 'ALL brands' ELSE brand END AS brand,
       CASE WHEN grouping(size) = 1 THEN 'all sizes' ELSE coalesce(size, '(none)') END AS size,
       sum(sales)
FROM items_sold
GROUP BY ROLLUP (brand, size)
ORDER BY grouping(brand), brand, grouping(size), size;

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT brand, size, sum(sales) FROM items_sold GROUP BY ROLLUP (brand, size);
presets.note: ROLLUP gives detail rows, a subtotal per brand and a grand total. The plan is one **MixedAggregate** with a Hash Key per set: a single scan.

presets.label: count(*) vs count(col)
presets.sql:
SELECT count(*)               AS all_rows,
       count(amount)          AS with_amount,
       count(coupon)          AS with_coupon,
       count(DISTINCT region) AS regions,
       sum(amount)            AS total,
       round(avg(amount), 2)  AS avg_amount,
       round(sum(amount) / count(*), 2) AS naive_avg
FROM orders;

SELECT sum(amount) AS sum_of_nothing, count(*) AS count_of_nothing,
       coalesce(sum(amount), 0) AS fixed
FROM orders WHERE false;
presets.note: `count(*)` counts rows, `count(col)` skips NULLs (40 orders have no amount, so `avg` ignores them: 104.63). Dividing `sum` by `count(*)` counts those 40 rows as zeros and gives 102.54. Over zero rows `sum` is **NULL**, not 0; only count returns 0.

presets.label: FILTER: one pass, many counts
presets.sql:
SELECT region,
       count(*)                                    AS orders,
       count(*)    FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')     AS paid,
       sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'refunded') AS refunded,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE coupon IS NOT NULL) / count(*), 1) AS coupon_pct
FROM orders
GROUP BY region ORDER BY region;
presets.note: Each aggregate sees only the rows its FILTER allows, all in a single scan. Clearer than `sum(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`, and it works with any aggregate: `array_agg(x) FILTER (…)` skips rows, while the CASE trick would collect NULLs. FILTER is standard SQL, not a PostgreSQL extension.

presets.label: Median and mode
presets.sql:
SELECT region,
       percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) AS median_cont,
       percentile_disc(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) AS median_disc,
       mode() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY status)              AS most_common_status
FROM orders GROUP BY region ORDER BY region;
presets.note: Ordered-set aggregates sort their input. `percentile_cont` interpolates between the two middle values; `percentile_disc` returns an actual input value. There is no separate `median()`: `percentile_cont(0.5)` is the median.

presets.label: WHERE vs HAVING
presets.note: Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE (`42803`): WHERE filters input rows, HAVING filters groups after aggregation. HAVING cannot use the output alias `total` either (`42703`), because the SELECT list is computed after HAVING. Logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. ORDER BY can use output names, and so can GROUP BY as a PostgreSQL extension; WHERE and HAVING cannot.

presets.label: DISTINCT ON: first row per key
presets.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (region) region, id, amount, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE amount IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY region, amount DESC, id;
presets.note: One row per region: the first after sorting, here the largest order. The DISTINCT ON expressions must lead the ORDER BY; add a tie-breaker (`id`) for a deterministic pick.

production.title: A finance dashboard: from 9 queries to 1
production.context: A finance dashboard shows revenue by region and month, subtotals per region, per month, a grand total, and for each cell the refunded amount and the share of coupon orders.
production.problem: It ran 9 separate queries (one per breakdown and metric), each scanning the orders table, and the page took seconds. Subtotal rows were found with `WHERE month IS NULL`, which also caught orders whose month column was legitimately NULL.
production.solution: One `GROUP BY CUBE` with FILTER clauses, and `grouping()` to label the subtotal rows.
production.sql:
SELECT region, date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month,
       grouping(region, date_trunc('month', created_at)) AS level,
       sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')     AS revenue,
       sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'refunded') AS refunded,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE coupon IS NOT NULL) / count(*), 1) AS coupon_pct
FROM orders
GROUP BY CUBE (region, date_trunc('month', created_at));
production.outcome: One scan feeding one MixedAggregate instead of nine scans. For 4 regions and 2 months that is 4 × 2 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 rows. Subtotal rows are identified by `level`, so a real NULL can never be mistaken for a total.

pitfalls.title: sum() of no rows is NULL
pitfalls.symptom: A balance shows blank (or the app crashes on null) for a customer with no transactions.
pitfalls.cause: Every aggregate except `count` returns **NULL** on an empty input: `sum`, `avg`, `max`, even `array_agg`.
pitfalls.fix: Wrap it: `coalesce(sum(amount), 0)`. For arrays, `coalesce(array_agg(x), '{}')`. The same applies to FILTER: a month with no matching rows gives `sum(x) FILTER (…)` = NULL, so a CASE or FILTER rewrite of a report that used to print 0 needs the COALESCE back.

pitfalls.title: count(col) where count(*) was meant
pitfalls.symptom: A conversion rate is too high: the denominator is smaller than the number of visits.
pitfalls.cause: `count(col)` counts only non-NULL values. If the column is nullable, rows silently drop out.
pitfalls.fix: Use `count(*)` to count rows; use `count(col)` only when "rows with a value" is what you mean.

pitfalls.title: Telling subtotals apart with IS NULL
pitfalls.symptom: A ROLLUP report shows two "Total" lines for one region.
pitfalls.cause: Grouping sets fill ungrouped columns with NULL, which is indistinguishable from a real NULL in the data.
pitfalls.fix: Use `grouping(col)`: 1 means the NULL is a subtotal placeholder, 0 means it is data.

pitfalls.title: Order-sensitive aggregates without ORDER BY
pitfalls.symptom: `string_agg(name, ', ')` lists names in a different order on each run.
pitfalls.cause: Aggregate input order is unspecified. A sorted subquery usually works but is not guaranteed once the plan changes.
pitfalls.fix: Put the order inside the call: `string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name)`, `array_agg(x ORDER BY ts)`.

pitfalls.title: BETWEEN on a timestamp drops the last day
pitfalls.symptom: An October report built with `WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-10-01' AND '2026-10-31'` is missing most of October 31.
pitfalls.cause: BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends, and `'2026-10-31'` on a timestamp means midnight at the **start** of the 31st. Hourly rows for October: 721 instead of 744. In adjacent BETWEEN buckets the boundary row lands in both.
pitfalls.fix: Use a half-open range: `created_at >= '2026-10-01' AND created_at < '2026-11-01'`. It is exact for dates and timestamps, never double-counts, and an index can use it.

pitfalls.title: Integer division in ratios
pitfalls.symptom: A conversion rate prints 0 for every row, or a share prints 33 instead of 33.3.
pitfalls.cause: `count(*)` returns bigint, and integer / integer truncates: `2 / 3` is 0. A zero denominator raises `division by zero`.
pitfalls.fix: Make one operand numeric first (`100.0 * count(*) FILTER (…) / count(*)`) and guard the denominator with `NULLIF(count(*), 0)`, which turns 0 into NULL so the ratio is NULL instead of an error.

pointers: `count(*)` counts rows; `count(col)` counts non-NULL values; every other aggregate returns **NULL** on no rows.
`agg(...) FILTER (WHERE ...)` restricts one aggregate's input; WHERE restricts all rows; HAVING filters groups.
`ROLLUP (a, b)` = (a,b), (a), (); `CUBE (a, b)` = all 4 subsets; all sets run in one scan.
`grouping(a, b)` is a bitmask: bit = 1 when that column is **not** grouped in the current row's set.
Ordered-set aggregates: `percentile_cont` interpolates, `percentile_disc` picks a value, `mode()` returns the most frequent.

lessons.title: Pagination: OFFSET vs keyset
tldr: **Keyset pagination** fetches the next page with `WHERE (created_at, id) < ($last_ts, $last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT n`, so it seeks to where the previous page ended instead of counting rows from the start.
`OFFSET n` must produce and discard n rows on every request, so deep pages get linearly slower and shift when rows are inserted, while a keyset page costs the same at page 10 000 as at page 1.

visualizer.title: Skipping rows vs seeking to a key
visualizer.caption: Press **Go deeper** to jump from page 1 to page 10 000, then switch to **Keyset** and compare rows read and buffers. Below, add a row between two page loads and watch OFFSET serve a duplicate.

presets.label: OFFSET: page 1 vs page 5 000
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
SELECT id, created_at, title FROM events
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 0;

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
SELECT id, created_at, title FROM events
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 49990;
presets.note: Both use the index in order. Page 1 touches about 4 buffers. Page 5 000 shows the Index Scan with **actual rows=50000** under a Limit that returns 10: every skipped row was fetched, about 600 buffers.

presets.label: Keyset: seek to the last row seen
presets.sql:
-- the last row of page 4 999 was (2026-01-12 13:50:00+00, id 50011)
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
SELECT id, created_at, title FROM events
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-01-12 13:50:00+00', 50011)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 10;

SELECT id, created_at, title FROM events
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-01-12 13:50:00+00', 50011)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 10;
presets.note: The row comparison becomes an **Index Cond**: one descent, 10 rows, about 4 buffers. Same rows as OFFSET 49990, at roughly 1/150 of the work.

presets.label: Why the tiebreaker matters
presets.sql:
-- three events share each timestamp; compare three "next page" filters
SELECT 'row comparison' AS filter, count(*) AS rows_after_cursor
FROM events WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-01-12 13:50:00+00', 50011)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'created_at only', count(*)
FROM events WHERE created_at < '2026-01-12 13:50:00+00'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'created_at AND id', count(*)
FROM events WHERE created_at < '2026-01-12 13:50:00+00' AND id < 50011;

SELECT id, created_at FROM events
WHERE created_at = '2026-01-12 13:50:00+00' ORDER BY id DESC;
presets.note: The row comparison keeps **50 010** rows. `created_at` alone silently drops id 50010, which shares the cursor's timestamp, and the AND version drops it too (and, with other data, many more). Always end the sort key with a unique column, and compare with a row constructor, not with a hand-written AND.

presets.label: Previous page (seek backwards)
presets.sql:
-- page before the cursor row (2026-01-12 13:50:00+00, 50011): flip the comparison and the order, then flip back
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT id, created_at, title FROM events
  WHERE (created_at, id) > ('2026-01-12 13:50:00+00', 50011)
  ORDER BY created_at, id
  LIMIT 10) p
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC;

SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT id, created_at, title FROM events
  WHERE (created_at, id) > ('2026-01-12 13:50:00+00', 50011)
  ORDER BY created_at, id
  LIMIT 10) p
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC;
presets.note: The inner query walks the same index **backward** (`Index Scan Backward`), so one index serves both directions. The outer sort only reorders 10 rows.

presets.label: Page drift with OFFSET
presets.note: The first row of page 2 has `already_seen = true`: the insert pushed every row one position down. With deletes the opposite happens and a row is skipped. Keyset pages cannot drift.

presets.label: Totals: exact vs estimate
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM events;

SELECT reltuples::bigint AS estimated_rows FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'events';

-- "is there a next page?" without counting: ask for one extra row
SELECT
  (SELECT count(*) > 10 FROM (SELECT 1 FROM events
     WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-01-12 13:50:00+00', 50011)
     ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 11) s) AS has_next_mid,
  (SELECT count(*) > 10 FROM (SELECT 1 FROM events
     WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-01-01 00:03:00+00', 11)
     ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 11) s) AS has_next_last_page;
presets.note: An exact `count(*)` reads the whole table or index on every request. `reltuples` is free and maintained by VACUUM and ANALYZE. Fetching `LIMIT n + 1` answers "has next" exactly: true in the middle of the feed, false on the last page (only ids 1 to 10 remain).

presets.label: Cursor (inside one transaction)
presets.note: A cursor keeps its position on the server, so the second FETCH continues where the first stopped. Unless declared `WITH HOLD`, it lives only inside the transaction: good for exports and batch jobs, not for stateless web pages.

production.title: An activity feed API that timed out on deep pages
production.context: A collaboration app serves `GET /feed?page=N` with `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50 OFFSET (N-1)*50` over a 40 M row events table. Most users read page 1. Crawlers and export scripts walk to the end.
production.problem: Each deep page re-reads every row before it, so walking the feed is quadratic: a client fetching all 800 000 pages makes the server produce about 50 × 800 000² / 2 ≈ 16 trillion rows to deliver 40 million. Users also report duplicated and missing items, because new events shift OFFSET positions while they scroll.
production.solution: Replace the page number with an opaque **cursor** holding the last `(created_at, id)`. Make the sort key unique by adding `id`. Back it with one index in the same column order. Return `next_cursor` from the API and fetch `LIMIT 51` to know whether there is a next page.
production.outcome: Every page costs one index descent plus 51 rows, whatever its depth. On the playground table page 10 000 drops from 1 210 shared buffers to 4, and duplicated or skipped items disappear because the cursor names a row rather than a position.

pitfalls.title: A sort key that is not unique
pitfalls.symptom: Rows appear twice or never when paging, even with keyset pagination.
pitfalls.cause: Rows that tie on the sort key have no defined order. With `WHERE created_at < $last`, every row sharing the last timestamp is skipped.
pitfalls.fix: Append a unique column (the primary key) to both the ORDER BY and the cursor, and index the same columns in the same order.
pitfalls.sql:
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
WHERE (created_at, id) < ($last_ts, $last_id)

pitfalls.title: Hand-expanding the row comparison
pitfalls.symptom: Pages silently lose rows after the first one.
pitfalls.cause: `a < $1 AND b < $2` is not the same as `(a, b) < ($1, $2)`. The row form compares left to right and stops at the first unequal pair, so it is `a < $1 OR (a = $1 AND b < $2)`.
pitfalls.fix: Use the row constructor. It is also what lets the planner use the multicolumn index as a single range.

pitfalls.title: Mixed sort directions
pitfalls.symptom: `ORDER BY score DESC, id ASC` cannot be expressed as one row comparison, and the query falls back to a sort.
pitfalls.cause: A row comparison applies one operator to every column. A mixed-direction order needs `<` on one column and `>` on another.
pitfalls.fix: Pick one direction for all keyset columns when you can. Otherwise write the expanded `OR` form and index `(score DESC, id ASC)` to match.

pitfalls.title: An exact total on every request
pitfalls.symptom: The first page is slow even though it returns only 50 rows.
pitfalls.cause: `SELECT count(*)` has to visit every row (or every index entry) on each request.
pitfalls.fix: Show "more results" with `LIMIT n + 1`, or an estimate from `pg_class.reltuples` or `EXPLAIN`. Compute exact totals asynchronously if the product really needs them.

pointers: `OFFSET n` still **computes and discards** n rows. The cost grows with page depth.
Keyset = **unique sort key** + **row comparison** `(a, b) < ($1, $2)` + an **index in the same order**.
Offsets drift when rows are inserted or deleted between requests. A keyset cursor names a row and cannot drift.
Use `LIMIT n + 1` for "has next page", and `reltuples` for an approximate total.
Going deeper: [Index design](/m4/index-design) covers multicolumn order and why the index must match the ORDER BY.

lessons.title: Upserts and de-duplication
tldr: An **upsert** (`INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`) inserts a row or, if a unique index already holds its key, updates the existing row instead, atomically and in one statement.
It needs a **unique index** to act as the arbiter, so cleaning existing duplicates (rank with `row_number()`, delete every rank above 1) and adding that index is usually the first step.

visualizer.title: One batch through ON CONFLICT, and a duplicate clean-up
visualizer.caption: Step through a batch: each proposed row probes the unique index, then inserts, updates or is skipped. Switch to **Clean duplicates** to rank, delete and lock the door with an index.

presets.label: 1. Find duplicates
presets.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS rows,
       count(DISTINCT email) AS distinct_raw,
       count(DISTINCT lower(btrim(email))) AS distinct_people
FROM contacts;

SELECT lower(btrim(email)) AS person, count(*) AS copies, array_agg(id ORDER BY id) AS ids
FROM contacts
GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1
ORDER BY copies DESC, person
LIMIT 5;
presets.note: 2 240 rows but only 2 000 people. Raw `DISTINCT email` sees 2 200 values because case and spaces hide 200 of the 240 duplicates; the other 40 are exact copies.

presets.label: 2. Rank: who survives?
presets.sql:
SELECT id, email, plan, updated_at,
       row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY lower(btrim(email))
                          ORDER BY updated_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn
FROM contacts
WHERE lower(btrim(email)) IN ('user1@example.com', 'user50@example.com', 'user51@example.com')
ORDER BY lower(btrim(email)), rn;
presets.note: The newest row per person gets **rn = 1**. The `id DESC` tiebreaker makes the choice deterministic when timestamps tie. Change the ORDER BY to keep the oldest or the most complete row instead.

presets.label: 3. Delete the losers
presets.note: `DELETE 240` leaves 2 000 rows for 2 000 people. On a table with no key, `ctid` (the physical row address) does the same job inside one statement. Never store a ctid: UPDATE and VACUUM FULL change it.

presets.label: 4. Lock the door
presets.note: The unique **expression index** makes case-insensitive duplicates impossible: the insert fails with `23505 duplicate key value`. It is also the arbiter the next preset uses.

presets.label: 5. Upsert with RETURNING old/new
presets.sql:
SELECT last_value FROM contacts_id_seq;

INSERT INTO contacts AS c (email, name, plan, updated_at)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (lower(email)) email, split_part(email, '@', 1), plan, received_at
FROM staging
ORDER BY lower(email), received_at DESC
ON CONFLICT ((lower(email))) DO UPDATE
  SET plan = excluded.plan, updated_at = excluded.updated_at
  WHERE c.plan IS DISTINCT FROM excluded.plan
RETURNING c.id, c.email, old.plan AS old_plan, new.plan AS new_plan,
          old.id IS NULL AS inserted;

SELECT last_value FROM contacts_id_seq;
presets.note: user1 is updated (`old_plan` pro, `new_plan` team), New.Person is inserted (`inserted` = true) and user2 returns nothing because its plan did not change. The sequence advanced by 3 for 3 proposed rows, although only one was inserted.

presets.label: 6. Same key twice in one statement
presets.sql:
SELECT try_sql($$
  INSERT INTO contacts (email, name, plan, updated_at)
  SELECT email, 'x', plan, received_at FROM staging WHERE email ILIKE 'new.person%'
  ON CONFLICT ((lower(email))) DO UPDATE SET plan = excluded.plan
$$) AS without_dedup;

SELECT try_sql($$
  INSERT INTO contacts (email, name, plan, updated_at)
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (lower(email)) email, 'x', plan, received_at FROM staging
  WHERE email ILIKE 'new.person%' ORDER BY lower(email), received_at DESC
  ON CONFLICT ((lower(email))) DO UPDATE SET plan = excluded.plan
$$) AS with_dedup;
presets.note: Two staging rows map to one key, so the first form fails with `21000: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time`. `DISTINCT ON` keeps the newest row per key and the statement succeeds.

presets.label: 7. MERGE: sync with delete
presets.sql:
CREATE TEMP TABLE crm_export AS
SELECT email, CASE WHEN id % 2 = 0 THEN 'team' ELSE plan END AS plan
FROM contacts WHERE id <= 6;

MERGE INTO contacts c
USING crm_export s ON lower(c.email) = lower(s.email)
WHEN MATCHED AND c.plan <> s.plan THEN UPDATE SET plan = s.plan
WHEN MATCHED THEN DO NOTHING
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND c.id <= 10 THEN DELETE
RETURNING merge_action() AS action, c.id, old.plan AS old_plan, new.plan AS new_plan;
presets.note: MERGE runs the **first** WHEN clause that matches for each row and can also delete target rows missing from the source (`NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE`). It does not have ON CONFLICT's guarantee against concurrent inserts, so prefer ON CONFLICT for plain upserts.

production.title: A nightly CRM import that kept creating duplicate customers
production.context: A B2B SaaS team imports leads from three marketing tools every night with `INSERT … SELECT FROM staging`, after checking `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM contacts WHERE email = s.email)`.
production.problem: Duplicates kept appearing: the check is case-sensitive, two tools send the same lead in one batch, and two import workers running in parallel both pass `NOT EXISTS` before either commits. Sales saw the same company twice, with split activity history.
production.solution: Pick a canonical key, merge the existing duplicates once, add a **unique expression index**, then switch the import to an upsert over a batch de-duplicated with `DISTINCT ON`. Use `RETURNING old/new` to log what changed.
production.sql:
-- one-off clean-up
DELETE FROM contacts c USING (
  SELECT id, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY lower(btrim(email))
                                ORDER BY updated_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn
  FROM contacts) d
WHERE c.id = d.id AND d.rn > 1;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY contacts_email_key ON contacts (lower(email));

-- nightly import
INSERT INTO contacts AS c (email, name, plan, updated_at)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (lower(email)) email, name, plan, received_at
FROM staging ORDER BY lower(email), received_at DESC
ON CONFLICT ((lower(email))) DO UPDATE
  SET plan = excluded.plan, updated_at = excluded.updated_at
  WHERE c.updated_at < excluded.updated_at;
production.outcome: The unique index makes a duplicate impossible, even with parallel workers: one worker inserts, the other takes the update path. On the playground data the clean-up removes 240 of 2 240 rows (11%), and later imports never add them back.

pitfalls.title: Check-then-insert races
pitfalls.symptom: Occasional duplicates (or unique violations) under load, although the code checks first.
pitfalls.cause: Two sessions both run `SELECT … WHERE NOT EXISTS` before either commits, so both see no row and both insert. Plain MERGE has the same race.
pitfalls.fix: Use `INSERT … ON CONFLICT`, which turns a concurrent insert of the same key into the update (or no-op) path, backed by a unique index.

pitfalls.title: No arbiter index
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification`.
pitfalls.cause: The conflict target must exactly match the columns or expression of a unique index. `ON CONFLICT (email)` does not match an index on `lower(email)`.
pitfalls.fix: Write the same expression: `ON CONFLICT ((lower(email)))`, or create the matching unique index. Prefer inference over `ON CONSTRAINT name`, so the index can be swapped later.

pitfalls.title: Updating rows that did not change
pitfalls.symptom: Upserts are slow, WAL volume is high and tables bloat although the data rarely changes.
pitfalls.cause: Every `DO UPDATE` writes a new row version even when the values are identical.
pitfalls.fix: Add a WHERE to the update so unchanged rows are skipped. They are still locked, but no new version is written.
pitfalls.sql:
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET price = excluded.price
WHERE products.price IS DISTINCT FROM excluded.price

pitfalls.title: Gaps in ids after upserts
pitfalls.symptom: Identity values jump by hundreds after each import.
pitfalls.cause: Every proposed row takes a sequence value before the conflict check, and sequence values are never handed back.
pitfalls.fix: This is harmless: ids are identifiers, not counters. If gaps really matter, filter known keys out of the batch first, and do not use ids for numbering visible to users.

pointers: `ON CONFLICT` needs a **unique index** whose columns or expression match the conflict target exactly.
`excluded` is the proposed row. A `DO UPDATE … WHERE` that is false skips the update but still locks the row.
A batch with the same key twice fails with **cannot affect row a second time**. De-duplicate with `DISTINCT ON` first.
Clean duplicates with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY keep_first)` and delete `rn > 1` by primary key (or `ctid` within one statement).
Going deeper: [INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE: what really happens](/m3/dml-lifecycle) shows the row versions each of these writes.

lessons.title: Pivots and reports
tldr: A **pivot** turns rows into columns: `sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE channel = 'web')` per output column, over a **date spine** from `generate_series`, gives one report row per period with zeros where nothing happened.
Reports go wrong in the gaps, so the spine, `coalesce`, window shares and `lag` over a complete series are what keep the totals, percentages and month-over-month changes honest.

visualizer.title: Build a monthly report, one SQL idea at a time
visualizer.caption: Step from long GROUP BY rows to a pivot, then add the date spine, totals, shares and month-over-month change. The last step shows what `lag` does when the spine is missing. Click a cell to see what feeds it.

playground.setup:
SET TimeZone = 'UTC';
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id int PRIMARY KEY,
  ordered_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  channel text NOT NULL,
  amount numeric(10,2) NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO orders
SELECT g,
       timestamptz '2026-01-01 00:00+00' + g * interval '87 minutes',
       (ARRAY['web', 'web', 'app', 'store'])[1 + g % 4],
       10 + (g * 37) % 190
FROM generate_series(1, 2990) g;
-- the store was closed for renovation in April
DELETE FROM orders WHERE channel = 'store' AND ordered_at >= '2026-04-01' AND ordered_at < '2026-05-01';
-- the spine every report below builds on
CREATE VIEW monthly_sales AS
SELECT m.month, c.channel, coalesce(sum(o.amount), 0) AS sales, count(o.id) AS orders
FROM generate_series(timestamptz '2026-01-01', '2026-06-01', interval '1 month') AS m(month)
CROSS JOIN (VALUES ('web'), ('app'), ('store')) AS c(channel)
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.channel = c.channel
                  AND o.ordered_at >= m.month AND o.ordered_at < m.month + interval '1 month'
GROUP BY m.month, c.channel;

presets.label: 1. Pivot with FILTER
presets.sql:
SELECT to_char(date_trunc('month', ordered_at), 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE channel = 'web')   AS web,
       sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE channel = 'app')   AS app,
       sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE channel = 'store') AS store,
       count(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
presets.note: Six rows, one per month. April `store` is **NULL**: `sum` over zero rows is NULL. `count` is the only aggregate that returns 0 for no rows.

presets.label: 2. Missing rows vs the spine
presets.note: Plain GROUP BY yields 17 groups, the spine 18. April store is there with `sales = 0` and `orders = 0`, so charts and averages see the closure instead of skipping it.

presets.label: 3. crosstab (tablefunc)
presets.note: The two-argument form maps each value to its category column, so order within a month does not matter. Columns must still be declared by hand: crosstab cannot invent columns at run time.

presets.label: 4. Subtotals with ROLLUP
presets.sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN grouping(month) = 1 THEN 'Total' ELSE to_char(month, 'YYYY-MM') END AS month,
       sum(sales) FILTER (WHERE channel = 'web')   AS web,
       sum(sales) FILTER (WHERE channel = 'app')   AS app,
       sum(sales) FILTER (WHERE channel = 'store') AS store,
       sum(sales) AS total
FROM monthly_sales
GROUP BY ROLLUP (month)
ORDER BY grouping(month), month;
presets.note: The extra row has `grouping(month) = 1`: it is the grand total, computed in the same pass. Labelling it with `grouping()` rather than `coalesce` keeps it apart from real NULL keys.

presets.label: 5. Percent of the month
presets.sql:
SELECT to_char(month, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, channel, sales,
       round(100.0 * sales / sum(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY month), 1) AS pct_of_month,
       round(100.0 * sales / sum(sales) OVER (), 2) AS pct_of_half_year
FROM monthly_sales
ORDER BY month, channel
LIMIT 9;
presets.note: Window aggregates compute the denominators without collapsing rows: `PARTITION BY month` for the month share, an empty `OVER ()` for the share of everything. Web is about 50% each month.

presets.label: 6. Month over month: the lag trap
presets.sql:
-- with the spine: May store is compared with April (0)
SELECT to_char(month, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, sales,
       sales - lag(sales) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS delta
FROM monthly_sales WHERE channel = 'store' ORDER BY month;

-- without the spine: May is compared with March
SELECT to_char(month, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, sales,
       sales - lag(sales) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS delta
FROM (SELECT date_trunc('month', ordered_at) AS month, sum(amount) AS sales
      FROM orders WHERE channel = 'store' GROUP BY 1) s
ORDER BY month;
presets.note: With the spine, April shows `-13468` and May `+13739`. Without it there are only five rows and May shows **+271**: `lag` returned March, the previous *row*, and the closure vanished from the report.

production.title: A revenue dashboard that hid a lost channel
production.context: A retail analytics team feeds a weekly dashboard from `GROUP BY week, region` and a month-over-month column computed with `lag()`.
production.problem: One region stopped selling for two weeks after a payment outage. Those weeks produced no rows, so the chart joined the points on either side, the average per week went *up*, and `lag` compared the recovery week with the week before the outage, showing healthy growth.
production.solution: Generate the expected periods (and dimension members) first, LEFT JOIN the facts and `coalesce` empty cells to 0. Compute `lag`, shares and averages only over that complete grid.
production.sql:
WITH spine AS (
  SELECT w.week, r.region
  FROM generate_series(date_trunc('week', now()) - interval '12 weeks',
                       date_trunc('week', now()), interval '1 week') AS w(week)
  CROSS JOIN regions r)
SELECT s.week, s.region, coalesce(sum(o.amount), 0) AS sales,
       coalesce(sum(o.amount), 0)
         - lag(coalesce(sum(o.amount), 0)) OVER (PARTITION BY s.region ORDER BY s.week) AS wow
FROM spine s
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.region = s.region
                  AND o.ordered_at >= s.week AND o.ordered_at < s.week + interval '1 week'
GROUP BY s.week, s.region;
production.outcome: The outage weeks show as zeros and the recovery week as a jump from 0. In the playground, the same mistake turns the store's real -13 468 / +13 739 swing into a quiet +271.

pitfalls.title: Missing periods silently disappear
pitfalls.symptom: Charts skip periods, averages per period are too high, and `lag` compares the wrong periods.
pitfalls.cause: GROUP BY only returns groups that have rows. A period with no data produces no row at all.
pitfalls.fix: Build a spine with `generate_series` (cross joined with the dimension values) and LEFT JOIN the facts to it.

pitfalls.title: NULL where the report needs 0
pitfalls.symptom: Totals or percentages come out NULL, or a cell shows blank.
pitfalls.cause: Every aggregate except `count` returns NULL over zero rows, and NULL plus anything is NULL.
pitfalls.fix: Wrap the aggregate: `coalesce(sum(amount), 0)`. Use `NULLIF(denominator, 0)` when dividing.

pitfalls.title: crosstab with the one-argument form
pitfalls.symptom: Values land in the wrong column when a category is missing for some row.
pitfalls.cause: The one-argument form fills columns left to right and ignores the category value, so a missing category shifts the rest left.
pitfalls.fix: Use the two-argument form `crosstab(source_sql, category_sql)`, or plain `FILTER` aggregates, which never shift.

pitfalls.title: Time-zone boundaries
pitfalls.symptom: Monthly totals differ between the report and the finance export by a few orders.
pitfalls.cause: `date_trunc` on a `timestamptz` uses the session `TimeZone`, so months start at different instants for different clients.
pitfalls.fix: Set the reporting zone explicitly: `date_trunc('month', ordered_at, 'Europe/Berlin')`, or `SET TimeZone` in the reporting session.

pointers: Pivot with one `agg(...) FILTER (WHERE key = …)` per output column: one scan, no shifting columns.
Build a **date spine** with `generate_series`, cross join the dimensions, LEFT JOIN the facts, `coalesce` to 0.
`lag()` means the previous **row**. It is only "the previous period" over a complete spine.
Shares come from window aggregates: `x / sum(x) OVER (PARTITION BY period)`. Subtotals come from `ROLLUP` in the same pass.
Going deeper: [Aggregates, FILTER and GROUPING SETS](/m3/aggregates-grouping) and [Window functions and frames](/m3/window-functions).

lessons.title: Gaps and islands
tldr: **Gaps and islands** problems ask for runs of consecutive values (streaks, sessions, busy periods) and the holes between them, and window functions solve them in one pass.
The tricks are `value − row_number()` (constant inside a run), `lag()` plus a running `sum` (a new group starts at every large gap), and `range_agg` for overlapping intervals.

visualizer.title: Streaks, sessions and merged ranges
visualizer.caption: Step through the **row_number difference** trick on one user's login days. Then drag the session timeout and watch sessions split and merge, and toggle bookings to see `range_agg` fuse them.

presets.label: 1. Streaks: day − row_number
presets.sql:
SELECT day,
       row_number() OVER (ORDER BY day) AS rn,
       day - (row_number() OVER (ORDER BY day))::int AS grp
FROM logins WHERE user_id = 7 ORDER BY day;

SELECT min(day) AS first_day, max(day) AS last_day, count(*) AS days
FROM (SELECT day, day - (row_number() OVER (ORDER BY day))::int AS grp
      FROM logins WHERE user_id = 7) s
GROUP BY grp ORDER BY first_day;
presets.note: `grp` stays constant inside a run. Four streaks come out: 3, 2, 4 and 1 days, exactly the visualizer's islands. `date − integer` is a date, so the anchor is a date too.

presets.label: 2. Longest streak per user
presets.sql:
WITH runs AS (
  SELECT user_id, min(day) AS first_day, count(*) AS days
  FROM (SELECT user_id, day,
               day - (row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day))::int AS grp
        FROM logins) s
  GROUP BY user_id, grp)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (user_id) user_id, first_day, days AS longest_streak
FROM runs
ORDER BY user_id, days DESC, first_day
LIMIT 8;
presets.note: `PARTITION BY user_id` restarts the numbering per user. `DISTINCT ON` keeps the longest run per user. One sort and one window pass over all 18 872 login rows; streak lengths vary from user to user.

presets.label: 3. Gaps: the days in between
presets.sql:
SELECT day + 1 AS gap_start, next_day - 1 AS gap_end, next_day - day - 1 AS missing_days
FROM (SELECT day, lead(day) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS next_day
      FROM logins WHERE user_id = 7) s
WHERE next_day > day + 1;

-- or list every missing value against a series
SELECT d::date AS missing
FROM generate_series(date '2026-03-01', date '2026-03-15', interval '1 day') d
EXCEPT SELECT day FROM logins WHERE user_id = 7
ORDER BY 1;
presets.note: `lead()` pairs each day with the next one, so a gap is any step larger than 1: 03-04, 03-07..08 and 03-13..14. The `EXCEPT` form lists the five missing days one by one.

presets.label: 4. Sessionize clicks (30 min)
presets.sql:
SELECT ts, gap, is_new,
       sum(is_new) OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS session_id
FROM (SELECT ts, ts - lag(ts) OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS gap,
             CASE WHEN ts - lag(ts) OVER (ORDER BY ts) <= interval '30 minutes' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS is_new
      FROM clicks WHERE user_id = 1 AND ts < '2026-03-03') s
ORDER BY ts;
presets.note: The first click has a NULL gap, so the CASE falls through to 1. Five sessions, the same as the visualizer at 30 minutes. Try 10 or 60 minutes and compare with the slider.

presets.label: 5. Sessions per user, all users
presets.sql:
WITH flagged AS (
  SELECT user_id, ts,
         CASE WHEN ts - lag(ts) OVER w <= interval '30 minutes' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS is_new
  FROM clicks WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts)),
numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, ts, sum(is_new) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) AS session_id
  FROM flagged)
SELECT count(DISTINCT (user_id, session_id)) AS sessions,
       round(avg(clicks), 1) AS avg_clicks,
       max(len) AS longest_session
FROM (SELECT user_id, session_id, count(*) AS clicks, max(ts) - min(ts) AS len
      FROM numbered GROUP BY 1, 2) s;
presets.note: The same two-step pattern over 5 014 clicks: flag with `lag`, number with a running `sum`, then aggregate per (user, session). Result: 655 sessions of 7.7 clicks on average, the longest 28 minutes. A named `WINDOW` keeps the two window calls consistent.

presets.label: 6. Merge overlapping bookings
presets.note: Room A collapses to three busy blocks, as in the visualizer: 09:00 to 12:00 (booking 3 is only adjacent, yet merges), 13:00 to 14:00 and 15:30 to 16:30. The `&&` self-join finds the two overlapping pairs, `*` gives the overlap.

presets.label: 7. Forbid overlaps with EXCLUDE
presets.note: With the overlaps removed, an **exclusion constraint** rejects any new booking that overlaps one in the same room (`23P01`). The adjacent slot is fine, because `[)` ranges that touch do not overlap. `btree_gist` provides `=` for the GiST index.

production.title: Streak badges and session analytics for a learning app
production.context: A language-learning app awards badges for daily streaks and reports average session length. The first version ran a loop in application code over each user's activity, fetched row by row.
production.problem: The nightly job pulled 60 M activity rows over the network and took hours. A second job counted sessions with a fixed 30-minute window per hour bucket, which split sessions that crossed the hour and disagreed with the product definition.
production.solution: Compute both inside the database with window functions: the `day − row_number()` trick for streaks, and `lag` plus a running `sum` for sessions with a true inactivity timeout. Only the per-user results leave the database.
production.sql:
-- streaks that ended yesterday (users not yet active today)
SELECT user_id, count(*) AS streak_days
FROM (SELECT user_id, day,
             day - (row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day))::int AS grp
      FROM daily_activity) s
GROUP BY user_id, grp
HAVING max(day) = current_date - 1;
production.outcome: Both jobs become one sort and one window pass per table, and only one row per user is transferred. Sessions now match the product rule exactly, because a session boundary is defined by the gap between events, not by the clock.

pitfalls.title: Duplicate values break the difference trick
pitfalls.symptom: A streak is split, or a run appears shorter than it is.
pitfalls.cause: If a day appears twice, `row_number()` advances twice while the day does not, so the difference changes in the middle of a run.
pitfalls.fix: De-duplicate first (`SELECT DISTINCT user_id, day`), or use `dense_rank()` instead of `row_number()`.

pitfalls.title: Timestamps instead of days
pitfalls.symptom: Every login becomes its own island.
pitfalls.cause: The trick needs a step of exactly 1 between consecutive values. Timestamps are never exactly one unit apart.
pitfalls.fix: Reduce to the unit first: `ts::date` (or `date_trunc` in the user's time zone) and de-duplicate. For irregular events use the `lag` + running-sum pattern with a threshold.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting PARTITION BY
pitfalls.symptom: Sessions or streaks run across users.
pitfalls.cause: `lag` and `row_number` without `PARTITION BY user_id` treat the whole table as one sequence.
pitfalls.fix: Partition every window by the entity, and order by the time column plus a tiebreaker. A named `WINDOW w AS (…)` keeps them identical.

pitfalls.title: Merging ranges in application code
pitfalls.symptom: Calendars show double bookings, or free-slot searches are slow and buggy at boundaries.
pitfalls.cause: Hand-written interval merging gets inclusive and exclusive bounds wrong, and cannot prevent concurrent overlaps.
pitfalls.fix: Store `tstzrange` with `[)` bounds, merge with `range_agg`, and enforce "no overlap" with `EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&)`.

pointers: Streaks: `value − row_number() OVER (ORDER BY value)` is constant inside a run. GROUP BY it.
Sessions: flag rows where `lag()` is NULL or too far back, then a running `sum(flag)` numbers the groups.
Gaps: `lead(value)` minus value > 1, or a `generate_series` EXCEPT the values present.
Intervals: `range_agg` fuses overlapping and adjacent ranges, and `EXCLUDE … WITH &&` forbids overlaps.
Going deeper: [Window functions and frames](/m3/window-functions) explains partitions, ordering and the running-sum frame.

lessons.title: Trees and graphs
tldr: A tree can be stored as an **adjacency list** (each row points to its parent), a **materialized path** (`ltree`: each row stores its whole path) or a **closure table** (one row per ancestor and descendant pair).

They trade read cost against write cost: the adjacency list is trivial to change but needs a recursive query per level, while paths and closure rows answer "the whole subtree" with one index scan and must be rewritten when a subtree moves.

visualizer.title: One org chart, three storage models
visualizer.caption: Click any node to fetch its subtree. In **Adjacency list** press Next iteration to watch the recursive CTE descend one level at a time. Switch models to compare one index scan, and the rows each model must rewrite to move the subtree.

presets.label: 1. Subtree with a recursive CTE
presets.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, name, 0 AS depth FROM staff WHERE id = 6
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.id, s.parent_id, s.name, sub.depth + 1
  FROM staff s JOIN sub ON s.parent_id = sub.id)
SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY id SET ord
SELECT repeat('  ', depth) || name AS tree, depth
FROM sub ORDER BY ord LIMIT 12;

WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
  SELECT id, 0 AS depth FROM staff WHERE id = 6
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.id, sub.depth + 1 FROM staff s JOIN sub ON s.parent_id = sub.id)
SELECT depth, count(*) FROM sub GROUP BY depth ORDER BY depth;
presets.note: `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST` adds an ordering column so the output reads like an outline. The second query shows the levels: 1, 4, 16, 64, 256 = 341 people under n6.

presets.label: 2. What the recursion costs
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
  SELECT id FROM staff WHERE id = 6
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.id FROM staff s JOIN sub ON s.parent_id = sub.id)
SELECT count(*) FROM sub;
presets.note: A **Recursive Union** over a **WorkTable Scan**: the join runs `loops=5` (one per level) and probes `staff_parent` once per row, `Index Searches: 341`, about 770 buffers in total. Without the `parent_id` index every level would be a full scan.

presets.label: 3. Subtree with ltree
presets.note: `<@` means "is a descendant of (or equal to)". One **Bitmap Index Scan** on the GiST index returns all 341 rows for about 16 buffers. ltree comparison sorts in tree order, so `ORDER BY path` is depth-first.

presets.label: 4. Ancestors and patterns (ltree)
presets.note: `@>` finds ancestors, `~` matches an **lquery** pattern (`*{1}` = exactly one more label). Seven levels from 1 person to 4 096.

presets.label: 5. Closure table reads
presets.note: 36 409 pairs for 5 461 people: about 6.7 rows per person, growing with depth. Both directions are one B-tree lookup (about 10 buffers), and `depth` comes for free.

presets.label: 6. Graphs: stop cycles with CYCLE
presets.note: `a → b → c → a` is a loop. The **CYCLE** clause tracks visited `dst` values in `path` and marks the row that revisits one with `is_cycle = true`, so recursion stops instead of running forever.

presets.label: 7. Move a subtree in each model
presets.note: Watch the row counts: `UPDATE 1` for the adjacency list, `UPDATE 341` for paths, and `DELETE 682` plus `INSERT 682` (2 ancestors × 341) for the closure table.

production.title: A product catalogue with deep category trees
production.context: An e-commerce site stores 40 000 categories as `parent_id` rows. Every listing page needs "all products in this category and its subcategories" and a breadcrumb.
production.problem: Each request ran a recursive CTE to collect descendant categories, then joined products. Top-level pages walked thousands of categories level by level, and the breadcrumb needed a second recursive query, together the slowest queries on the site.
production.solution: Keep `parent_id` as the source of truth (cheap to edit) and add a materialized **ltree path** maintained by a trigger, indexed with GiST. Subtree and breadcrumb queries become single index scans. Category moves are rare and rewrite one subtree in a transaction.
production.outcome: On the playground tree the subtree read drops from about 770 buffers and 341 index probes to about 16 buffers in one scan. The cost moves to writes: a move rewrites every path in the moved subtree, which is acceptable for data that changes a few times a day.

pitfalls.title: No index on parent_id
pitfalls.symptom: Recursive queries get slower with table size, not with subtree size.
pitfalls.cause: Each iteration joins the working table to the whole table on `parent_id`. Without an index every level is a full scan.
pitfalls.fix: `CREATE INDEX ON staff (parent_id);` Foreign keys do not create this index for you.

pitfalls.title: Cycles in graph data
pitfalls.symptom: A recursive query never finishes, or fails when it runs out of memory or disk.
pitfalls.cause: A recursive CTE stops only when an iteration returns no rows. A loop in the data keeps producing rows forever, and `UNION` only helps if whole rows repeat.
pitfalls.fix: Add `CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path`, or carry an array of visited ids and stop on `id = ANY(path)`. Add a depth limit as a safety net.

pitfalls.title: Paths and closure rows drift from the truth
pitfalls.symptom: A node appears under two parents, or a subtree query misses nodes after a move.
pitfalls.cause: Paths and closure tables are derived data. A move that updates `parent_id` but not the derived rows leaves them inconsistent.
pitfalls.fix: Change the parent and the derived rows in **one transaction**, ideally inside a trigger or a single function, and add a periodic consistency check.

pitfalls.title: ltree label rules
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: ltree syntax error` when building paths from names.
pitfalls.cause: Labels may contain only letters, digits, underscores and hyphens, and each label is limited to 1 000 characters.
pitfalls.fix: Build paths from ids or slugs (`n42`, `garden_tools`), never from free-text names.

pointers: **Adjacency list**: one `parent_id` column, cheap writes, a recursive CTE per read (index `parent_id`).
**ltree**: `path <@ x` = subtree, `path @> x` = ancestors, GiST index, rewrite the subtree on a move.
**Closure table**: every ancestor/descendant pair with depth, B-tree lookups both ways, the most rows and the costliest moves.
For graphs with loops use the **CYCLE** clause, and `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST` for outline order.
Going deeper: [Recursive CTEs](/m3/recursive-ctes) shows the working table and termination rules step by step.

lessons.title: Searching text
tldr: Text search in PostgreSQL comes in three shapes: **prefix** matching (`LIKE 'abc%'`, a B-tree range), **substring and typo** matching (trigrams from `pg_trgm`, GIN or GiST), and **word** matching (full-text search with `tsvector` and `tsquery`).
Each needs a different index, and the wrong pairing silently falls back to reading the whole table, so choosing the pattern first and the index second is the whole game.

visualizer.title: Trigrams, similarity, and which index serves which query
visualizer.caption: Type a misspelled product name (or press **Next typo**) to see its trigrams and the similarity of each candidate. Then click cells in the matrix: every number is a measured buffer count with only that index present.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id int PRIMARY KEY,
  name text COLLATE "en_US" NOT NULL,
  description text NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO products
SELECT g,
  (ARRAY['Bosch','Makita','DeWalt','Ryobi','Stanley','Festool','Milwaukee','Einhell'])[1 + g % 8] || ' ' ||
  (ARRAY['cordless','compact','heavy-duty','brushless','corded','mini','pro','classic'])[1 + (g / 8) % 8] || ' ' ||
  (ARRAY['drill','hammer drill','impact driver','angle grinder','jigsaw','circular saw','sander','router',
         'screwdriver','multitool','planer','nail gun'])[1 + (g / 64) % 12] || ' ' ||
  (ARRAY['18V','12V','230V','kit','set','XR','plus','2.0'])[1 + (g / 768) % 8] || ' #' || g,
  'Model ' || g || ': a ' || (ARRAY['lightweight','powerful','quiet','robust'])[1 + g % 4] || ' tool for ' ||
  (ARRAY['wood','metal','masonry','drywall','tiles'])[1 + g % 5] || ' with ' ||
  (ARRAY['two batteries','a carrying case','an LED light','variable speed','a quick-change chuck'])[1 + g % 5]
FROM generate_series(1, 20000) g;
-- an ordinary index on the en_US column
CREATE INDEX products_name ON products (name);
ANALYZE products;

presets.label: 1. Prefix search and the collation trap
presets.note: The column uses the **en_US** collation, whose sort order is not plain character order, so the ordinary B-tree cannot turn a prefix into a range: Seq Scan. The `text_pattern_ops` index compares character by character, and the plan shows `Index Cond: (name ~>=~ … AND name ~<~ …)`.

presets.label: 2. Substring search with trigrams
presets.note: No B-tree can serve a leading `%`. The **GIN trigram** index looks up the trigrams of `impact driver` and intersects their posting lists: the scan drops from 323 to about 91 buffers, and the gap widens with selective terms.

presets.label: 3. ILIKE and regex reuse it
presets.note: The same index serves `ILIKE` and POSIX regexes (trigrams are extracted from the pattern). A selective substring like `#1234` (11 rows) costs about 16 buffers instead of 323.

presets.label: 4. Typos: similarity and "did you mean"
presets.note: `%` keeps words above `pg_trgm.similarity_threshold` (0.3); `<->` (1 − similarity) orders them nearest first. Ordering by distance with an index needs **GiST**: GIN cannot return rows in distance order.

presets.label: 5. Patterns an index cannot help
presets.note: Inside `%xr%` the two letters never form a complete trigram, so the index has nothing selective to look up and the planner reads the table (about 320 buffers). With three letters (`gun`) the trigram index is usable again. Ask for at least three characters in search boxes.

presets.label: 6. Full-text search with ranking
presets.note: Full-text search matches **words** after stemming, so `drills` would match `drill`. `websearch_to_tsquery` accepts search-box syntax (`-hammer` excludes). The GIN index on the stored `tsvector` serves `@@`.

production.title: A product search box that read the whole catalogue
production.context: A hardware shop searches 2 M products with `WHERE name ILIKE '%' || $1 || '%'`. It worked in development on a few thousand rows.
production.problem: In production every keystroke of the type-ahead ran a full sequential scan. An ordinary B-tree on `name` was never used, because leading wildcards cannot use a B-tree. Users also got nothing back for small typos such as "drivr".
production.solution: Split the box into the patterns it really needs: a **GIN trigram** index for substring matching, a small word dictionary with a **GiST trigram** index for "did you mean", and full-text search with a stored `tsvector` for multi-word queries. Require at least three characters before searching.
production.outcome: Substring searches stop scanning the table: on the playground a selective substring drops from 323 buffers to about 16, and the saving scales with the catalogue. Typos now return suggestions instead of an empty page.

pitfalls.title: LIKE prefix ignores the B-tree
pitfalls.symptom: `WHERE name LIKE 'abc%'` does a Seq Scan although `name` is indexed.
pitfalls.cause: In a non-C collation, sort order is not character order, so the planner cannot turn a prefix into an index range.
pitfalls.fix: Add `CREATE INDEX … (name text_pattern_ops)` for pattern queries (keep the ordinary index for `<`, `>` and ORDER BY), or declare the column `COLLATE "C"` if linguistic sorting is not needed.

pitfalls.title: GIN where you need distance order
pitfalls.symptom: `ORDER BY name <-> $1 LIMIT 10` sorts the whole table.
pitfalls.cause: GIN can find matching rows but cannot return them nearest first. Only GiST supports ordering by `<->`.
pitfalls.fix: Use `gist_trgm_ops` for nearest-neighbour queries, or filter with `%` on a GIN index and sort the (small) result.

pitfalls.title: Very short search terms
pitfalls.symptom: Searches for one or two letters are as slow as without an index.
pitfalls.cause: A pattern with no complete trigram gives the index nothing to look up, so the scan degenerates to reading everything.
pitfalls.fix: Require a minimum of three characters, or use a prefix search on a `text_pattern_ops` B-tree for very short input.

pitfalls.title: Using LIKE for word search
pitfalls.symptom: `%drill%` also matches "drilling" and "screwdriller", and "drills" misses "drill".
pitfalls.cause: LIKE and trigrams match characters, not words. They know nothing about stemming or stop words.
pitfalls.fix: Use full-text search for natural-language queries: `to_tsvector('english', …) @@ websearch_to_tsquery(…)`, ranked with `ts_rank`.

pointers: **Prefix**: B-tree, with `text_pattern_ops` unless the column collation is C.
**Substring, ILIKE, regex**: `gin_trgm_ops`. Patterns need at least one full trigram to be selective.
**Typos**: `similarity()`, `%` (threshold 0.3) and `<->`. Distance ordering needs **GiST**.
**Words**: a stored `tsvector` with a GIN index, `@@ websearch_to_tsquery`, ranked by `ts_rank`.
Going deeper: [Full-text search](/m6/full-text-search) covers parsers, dictionaries and ranking.

lessons.title: Job queues and concurrency patterns
tldr: A **job queue** in PostgreSQL is a table plus one claim statement, `UPDATE … WHERE id = (SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1)`, that lets many workers take different rows without waiting for each other.

Around it sit the patterns that make concurrent writes safe: **leases** for crashed workers, **idempotency keys** for retries, **version columns** against lost updates, and **advisory locks** for work that has no row.

visualizer.title: Workers, leases and conflicts on a timeline
visualizer.caption: Step through three workers claiming jobs with SKIP LOCKED, one crashing mid-job, and the retry that cannot double-charge. Switch to **Optimistic update** and **Singleton job** for the other two patterns.

presets.label: 1. Claim one job
presets.sql:
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', attempts = attempts + 1,
       locked_until = now() + interval '30 seconds'
WHERE id = (SELECT id FROM jobs
            WHERE status = 'ready'
               OR (status = 'running' AND locked_until < now())
            ORDER BY id
            LIMIT 1
            FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING id, kind, payload, attempts;
presets.note: The subquery picks and row-locks the oldest open job; the UPDATE turns it into a lease and the statement commits on its own. A second worker running the same statement at the same moment would skip this row and get the next one.

presets.label: 2. What the claim costs
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
SELECT id FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'ready' OR (status = 'running' AND locked_until < now())
ORDER BY id LIMIT 1
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
presets.note: The plan uses the small **partial index** `jobs_open`, which contains only the 100 open jobs, not the 49 900 finished ones. A **LockRows** node sits above the scan: that is where locked rows are skipped.

presets.label: 3. Claim a batch
presets.sql:
WITH batch AS (
  SELECT id FROM jobs
  WHERE status = 'ready'
  ORDER BY id LIMIT 10
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
UPDATE jobs j SET status = 'running', attempts = attempts + 1,
       locked_until = now() + interval '5 minutes'
FROM batch WHERE j.id = batch.id
RETURNING j.id;
presets.note: Ten jobs per round trip. The locking clause goes **inside** the CTE: a `FOR UPDATE` on the outer query does not reach into WITH queries.

presets.label: 4. Idempotent side effects
presets.note: The first insert returns an id, the retry returns **no row**: the unique key turned a double charge into a no-op the worker can detect. One payment exists.

presets.label: 5. Optimistic concurrency
presets.note: Watch the command tags: `UPDATE 1`, then **`UPDATE 0`** for the stale version. The application must check the row count and retry. The final row is 110, version 9.

presets.label: 6. Advisory locks
presets.note: The same session can take a lock it already holds; session locks **stack**, so two unlocks are needed. Another session would get `false`. The `xact` variant needs no unlock at all.

presets.label: 7. Wake workers with NOTIFY
presets.note: A notification is delivered only when its transaction **commits**, so a worker can never be woken for a job it cannot see yet. Workers still poll occasionally: notifications are not stored for sessions that were not listening.

production.title: An email queue that stalled under load
production.context: A SaaS app sends transactional email from a `jobs` table. Each worker ran `BEGIN; SELECT … FOR UPDATE LIMIT 1;`, sent the email, then marked the row done and committed.
production.problem: With 20 workers, all of them queued on the same first row: `FOR UPDATE` waits for the lock holder, so throughput was one email at a time. Every worker held a transaction open for the whole SMTP call, which also held back VACUUM, and a worker killed mid-send left an email that was sent twice after restart.
production.solution: Claim with **SKIP LOCKED** and commit immediately, recording a lease instead of holding a lock. Index only the open jobs. Make the side effect idempotent with a unique key, and wake idle workers with NOTIFY.
production.sql:
CREATE INDEX jobs_open ON jobs (id) WHERE status IN ('ready', 'running');

UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', attempts = attempts + 1,
       locked_until = now() + interval '2 minutes'
WHERE id = (SELECT id FROM jobs
            WHERE status = 'ready' OR (status = 'running' AND locked_until < now())
            ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING id, payload;

INSERT INTO sent_emails (idempotency_key) VALUES ('job-' || $1)
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING id;   -- no row: already sent
