pitfalls.symptom: A nightly `TRUNCATE staging` stalls every query on the table, and a report running at the same time sees the table as empty.
pitfalls.cause: A common claim is that TRUNCATE is fast because it locks lightly. It takes **ACCESS EXCLUSIVE**, the strongest lock, and swaps in a new file. It is not MVCC-safe: a REPEATABLE READ snapshot taken before it sees no rows afterwards.
pitfalls.fix: Use TRUNCATE for tables nobody else is reading at that moment. Keep its transaction short, and set `lock_timeout` so it gives up instead of queueing everyone behind it.
pitfalls.sql:
SET lock_timeout = '2s';
TRUNCATE staging;

pointers: Plain VACUUM: **SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE**, runs online, space is **reused**, only the empty tail goes back to the OS.
Phases: **scan heap (prune, collect dead TIDs) → vacuum indexes → vacuum heap → clean up indexes → truncate → final cleanup**.
Dead TIDs must fit in **`maintenance_work_mem`**, or indexes are scanned more than once.
VACUUM sets **all-visible / all-frozen** bits and fills the **FSM**; DELETE does neither.
VACUUM FULL: **ACCESS EXCLUSIVE**, new relfilenode, rebuilt indexes, needs disk for a full copy.

lessons.title: Tuning autovacuum
tldr: **Autovacuum** is a launcher plus a few worker processes that vacuum and analyze each table once its counts of dead, inserted or changed rows cross a threshold computed from the table size.
The defaults suit small tables, so big or hot tables need per-table thresholds and a larger I/O budget, or dead rows pile up faster than the throttled workers can remove them.

visualizer.title: When autovacuum fires, and how fast it can work
visualizer.caption: Pick a scenario or drag the sliders: the trigger formulas update, and a 24-hour simulation shows dead rows and runs. Switch to **How fast can it go?** for the cost-based throttle.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE sessions (id int PRIMARY KEY, user_id int NOT NULL, last_seen timestamptz NOT NULL, data text);
INSERT INTO sessions SELECT g, g % 5000, timestamptz '2026-11-01' + g * interval '1 second', md5(g::text)
FROM generate_series(1, 20000) g;
ANALYZE sessions;

CREATE FUNCTION av_opt(opts text[], name text) RETURNS float LANGUAGE sql STABLE AS $$
  SELECT coalesce((SELECT option_value FROM pg_options_to_table(opts) WHERE option_name = name),
                  current_setting(name))::float $$;

CREATE VIEW av_status AS
SELECT c.relname,
       greatest(c.reltuples, 0)::bigint AS reltuples,
       s.n_dead_tup,
       CASE WHEN o.vmax < 0 THEN o.vthr + o.vsf * greatest(c.reltuples, 0)
            ELSE least(o.vmax, o.vthr + o.vsf * greatest(c.reltuples, 0)) END::bigint AS vacuum_trigger,
       s.n_ins_since_vacuum,
       (o.ithr + o.isf * greatest(c.reltuples, 0)
          * (1 - CASE WHEN c.relpages > 0 THEN c.relallfrozen::float / c.relpages ELSE 0 END))::bigint AS insert_trigger,
       s.n_mod_since_analyze,
       (o.athr + o.asf * greatest(c.reltuples, 0))::bigint AS analyze_trigger
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_stat_user_tables s ON s.relid = c.oid
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT
  av_opt(c.reloptions, 'autovacuum_vacuum_threshold')           AS vthr,
  av_opt(c.reloptions, 'autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor')        AS vsf,
  av_opt(c.reloptions, 'autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold')       AS vmax,
  av_opt(c.reloptions, 'autovacuum_vacuum_insert_threshold')    AS ithr,
  av_opt(c.reloptions, 'autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor') AS isf,
  av_opt(c.reloptions, 'autovacuum_analyze_threshold')          AS athr,
  av_opt(c.reloptions, 'autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor')       AS asf) o;

presets.label: The global knobs
presets.sql:
SELECT name, setting, unit FROM pg_settings
WHERE name LIKE 'autovacuum%' OR name IN ('vacuum_cost_limit', 'vacuum_cost_page_miss',
      'vacuum_cost_page_dirty', 'vacuum_cost_page_hit', 'track_counts', 'track_cost_delay_timing')
ORDER BY name;
presets.note: New in 18: `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold` (100 M), and `autovacuum_worker_slots` (16) next to `autovacuum_max_workers` (3). Slots reserve shared memory and need a restart; `max_workers` is reloadable up to the slot count. `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = -1` means "use `vacuum_cost_limit`" (200).

presets.label: When will this table be vacuumed?
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_stat_force_next_flush();
SELECT * FROM av_status WHERE relname = 'sessions';
presets.note: With 20,000 rows the dead-row trigger is 50 + 0.2 × 20,000 = **4,050**. The `av_status` view in the setup applies the trigger formulas, including per-table overrides.

presets.label: Churn rows past the trigger
presets.note: 3,000 dead rows: not yet. 5,000: due. On a server the launcher would start a worker within `autovacuum_naptime` (1 min). This playground runs no autovacuum, so nothing happens by itself here.

presets.label: Per-table override
presets.note: Now 1000 + 0.01 × 20,000 = **1,200**. Storage parameters beat the global settings for this table only.

presets.label: Insert-only tables and freezing
presets.note: The insert trigger scales with the **unfrozen** share of the table. After VACUUM FREEZE every page is all-frozen, so the trigger falls to the base **1,000** instead of 1000 + 0.2 × 30,000 = 7,000. (`relpages` and `relallfrozen` refresh only at the next VACUUM or ANALYZE.)

presets.label: Throttle arithmetic
presets.sql:
SELECT current_setting('autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay') AS delay,
       current_setting('vacuum_cost_limit')::int AS cost_limit,
       round(current_setting('vacuum_cost_limit')::int / current_setting('vacuum_cost_page_miss')::numeric
             / 0.002 * 8192 / 1048576, 1) AS max_mb_per_s_reading,
       round(current_setting('vacuum_cost_limit')::int
             / (current_setting('vacuum_cost_page_miss')::numeric + current_setting('vacuum_cost_page_dirty')::int)
             / 0.002 * 8192 / 1048576, 1) AS max_mb_per_s_read_and_dirty;
presets.note: At defaults one worker can read about 390 MB/s from disk but only about 35 MB/s when it also dirties every page. That budget is shared by all running workers.

presets.label: Health check and 18's timing columns
presets.note: The dead-row share uses `NULLIF` so an empty table does not divide by zero. The `total_*_time` columns (milliseconds, new in 18) show where vacuum time goes; `autovacuum_ms` stays 0 here because nothing runs automatically. A per-table `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold = 500` caps the trigger at **500** dead rows.

production.title: A 200 M-row orders table that bloated between vacuums
production.context: An e-commerce team runs a 200 M-row `orders` table. Each order is updated several times during fulfilment, about 40,000 updates a minute at peak.
production.problem: With the default scale factor, autovacuum waited for 50 + 0.2 × 200 M = **40 M** dead rows. That took about 17 hours of updates to reach, so heap and indexes carried up to 20% dead rows between runs, and every run had 40 M index entries to remove. Queries slowed as scans read through dead rows.
production.solution: Set per-table thresholds so the table is vacuumed after about 2 M dead rows, give autovacuum a bigger I/O budget, and monitor dead rows against the trigger.
production.outcome: The trigger drops from 40 M to about 2 M dead rows: roughly one run every 50 minutes at peak instead of one every 17 hours, and each run has 20× less to clean. Dead rows stay near 1% of the table.

pitfalls.title: Big tables wait for 20% of their rows to die
pitfalls.symptom: A large table shows millions of `n_dead_tup` and `last_autovacuum` days ago, while small tables are vacuumed constantly.
pitfalls.cause: The trigger is `50 + 0.2 × reltuples`. PostgreSQL 18 caps it at `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold` (100 M), which still allows huge backlogs.
pitfalls.fix: Lower `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` per table (0.01 to 0.05 for big, hot tables), or lower `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold`.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER TABLE orders SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01);

pitfalls.title: Autovacuum keeps getting cancelled
pitfalls.symptom: The log shows `canceling autovacuum task` again and again and the table is never fully vacuumed.
pitfalls.cause: Autovacuum yields to any conflicting lock request, such as frequent `ALTER TABLE`, `LOCK`, or manual ANALYZE on the same table. Only anti-wraparound runs refuse to yield.
pitfalls.fix: Stop the frequent conflicting command, or run a manual `VACUUM` in a quiet window. Check `pg_stat_user_tables.autovacuum_count` to confirm runs complete.

pitfalls.title: Adding workers does not make vacuum faster
pitfalls.symptom: After raising `autovacuum_max_workers` from 3 to 10, each table takes longer to vacuum.
pitfalls.cause: The cost limit is shared: total I/O stays at `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` per `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay`, split among busy workers.
pitfalls.fix: Raise `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` (or lower the delay) together with the worker count, within what the disks can sustain.

pitfalls.title: Partitioned parents are never auto-analyzed
pitfalls.symptom: Queries on a partitioned table get poor plans even though every partition has fresh statistics.
pitfalls.cause: Autovacuum processes partitions, but a partitioned table stores no rows, so it never triggers ANALYZE on the parent.
pitfalls.fix: Run `ANALYZE parent_table` after large loads and on a schedule.

pitfalls.title: Hunting autovacuum workers by query text
pitfalls.symptom: A script meant to cancel the autovacuum that blocks a migration kills the wrong session, or finds nothing, and the migration keeps waiting.
pitfalls.cause: Matching `query LIKE '%autovacuum%'` also matches the monitoring query itself. A worker's `query` reads `autovacuum: VACUUM public.orders`, and only `backend_type` identifies it reliably. Signalling it needs superuser unless the role has `pg_signal_autovacuum_worker` (new in 18).
pitfalls.fix: Filter on `backend_type`, grant the predefined role to the migration user, and remember that an anti-wraparound run will simply restart.

pointers: Vacuum when dead rows > **min(max_threshold, 50 + 0.2 × reltuples)**; max_threshold (100 M) is **new in 18**.
Insert-only tables: **1000 + 0.2 × reltuples × unfrozen share**; analyze: **50 + 0.1 × reltuples**.
Override per table with **storage parameters** (`ALTER TABLE … SET (autovacuum_…)`).
Throttle: **cost_limit 200** per **2 ms** delay, page hit 1 / miss 2 / dirty 20, **shared by all workers**.
Watch **`pg_stat_user_tables`**: `n_dead_tup`, `n_ins_since_vacuum`, `last_autovacuum`, `autovacuum_count`.

lessons.title: XID wraparound, freezing and MultiXacts
tldr: Transaction IDs are 32-bit counters compared modulo 2^32, so any row whose `xmin` falls more than about 2 billion transactions behind would suddenly look like it came from the future.

VACUUM prevents that by **freezing** old rows, marking them older than every XID, and PostgreSQL escalates from aggressive vacuums to forced autovacuums to refusing new XIDs as a table approaches the limit.

visualizer.title: The XID circle
visualizer.caption: Advance through each threshold and watch what the server does. Run VACUUM to freeze and pull `relfrozenxid` forward, then switch to **What if nothing froze?** and push past 2^31.

presets.label: How old is everything?
presets.note: The three ages to monitor: per table, including its TOAST table, and per database. `pg_current_xact_id()` returns a 64-bit `xid8` (epoch + xid); the on-disk xmin is the low 32 bits.

presets.label: Which statements use an XID?
presets.note: A transaction gets an XID only when it first **writes**: reads alone leave it NULL, so read traffic never ages the cluster. `txid_current()` and `pg_current_xact_id()` force one, so each probe call burns an XID (they differ by 1).

presets.label: Burn 100,000 XIDs
presets.note: Each loop commits once, so each consumes one XID. `relfrozenxid` stays put and its age grows. Busy servers burn this many in seconds to minutes.

presets.label: Not frozen yet
presets.note: Rows still carry their original xmin and no `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN` flag. No page is all-frozen.

presets.label: VACUUM (FREEZE)
presets.note: `relfrozenxid` jumps forward and its age drops to almost 0. Each tuple shows `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN`, yet `t_xmin` keeps its original value: freezing sets flag bits, it no longer overwrites xmin.

presets.label: The freeze settings
presets.sql:
SELECT name, to_char(setting::bigint, 'FM9,999,999,999') AS value
FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('vacuum_freeze_min_age', 'vacuum_freeze_table_age', 'autovacuum_freeze_max_age',
               'vacuum_failsafe_age', 'vacuum_multixact_freeze_min_age',
               'vacuum_multixact_freeze_table_age', 'autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age')
ORDER BY setting::bigint;
presets.note: 50 M, 150 M, 200 M and 1.6 B for XIDs; multixacts have their own, larger limits (5 M, 150 M, 400 M).

presets.label: Make a MultiXact
presets.note: Two lockers on one row do not fit in `xmax`, so `xmax` holds a **MultiXact ID** (`HEAP_XMAX_IS_MULTI`) and its members live in `pg_multixact`. MultiXact IDs wrap around too.

production.title: A forgotten replication slot and the wraparound countdown
production.context: A logistics company runs about 3,000 write transactions per second on its primary. Months ago a team created a logical replication slot for a CDC pilot and abandoned it.
production.problem: Monitoring showed `age(datfrozenxid)` climbing past 1 billion although autovacuum ran constantly. The slot's `catalog_xmin` pinned the oldest XID that VACUUM could freeze past. At 3,000 XIDs/s, about 1.1 billion remaining XIDs is roughly 4 days until the 40 M warning zone.
production.solution: Follow the recovery order: find what holds the horizon back (prepared transactions, long sessions, slots), remove it, then plain VACUUM the oldest tables. No single-user mode, no VACUUM FULL, no FREEZE.
production.outcome: Once the slot was dropped, the next aggressive vacuums advanced `relfrozenxid`, and `age(datfrozenxid)` fell back to around the 200 M `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` range. An alert on `age(datfrozenxid) > 500 M` and on inactive slots now catches this weeks earlier.

pitfalls.title: Panicking into single-user mode
pitfalls.symptom: The server refuses new XIDs with "database is not accepting commands that assign new transaction IDs".
pitfalls.cause: A common belief is that you must stop the server and vacuum in single-user mode. In PostgreSQL 18 that is neither necessary nor desirable, and single-user mode disables the wraparound safeguards.
pitfalls.fix: Stay online. Clear prepared transactions, long transactions and stale slots, then run a plain database-wide `VACUUM` as superuser. Do not use VACUUM FULL (it needs an XID) or VACUUM FREEZE (more work than needed).

pitfalls.title: An idle-in-transaction session blocks freezing
pitfalls.symptom: `age(datfrozenxid)` keeps growing even though aggressive autovacuums finish.
pitfalls.cause: VACUUM cannot freeze past the oldest snapshot still running anywhere in the cluster. One forgotten `BEGIN` in a pooled connection holds it back.
pitfalls.fix: Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` and alert on old `backend_xmin`.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS open_for, age(backend_xmin)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_xmin IS NOT NULL ORDER BY 3 DESC;

pitfalls.title: Insert-only tables surprise you with a huge vacuum
pitfalls.symptom: An append-only table that never had dead rows suddenly gets a long, unstoppable `(to prevent wraparound)` autovacuum that reads every page.
pitfalls.cause: Without dead rows, normal vacuums skipped its all-visible pages, so nothing was frozen until `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` forced a full aggressive scan.
pitfalls.fix: Let insert-triggered autovacuum freeze as you go (keep `autovacuum_vacuum_insert_threshold` enabled, consider a lower per-table `autovacuum_freeze_min_age`), or run `VACUUM (FREEZE)` after bulk loads.

pitfalls.title: A health check that burns XIDs
pitfalls.symptom: `age(datfrozenxid)` grows quickly on a database that is mostly read, and the XID rate tracks the monitoring interval.
pitfalls.cause: A probe such as `SELECT txid_current()` assigns a new XID on every call, even though it writes nothing. Thousands of probes per minute from load balancers add up to millions of XIDs a day.
pitfalls.fix: Probe with `SELECT 1`, or read the current value without assigning one: `pg_current_snapshot()` or `pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned()`.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT pg_snapshot_xmax(pg_current_snapshot()) AS next_xid;  -- assigns nothing

pointers: XIDs are **32-bit, compared modulo 2^32**: 2 billion in the past, 2 billion in the future.
**Freezing** marks a row older than every XID; `relfrozenxid` / `datfrozenxid` track the oldest unfrozen XID.
Ladder: **150 M** aggressive · **200 M** forced autovacuum · **1.6 B** failsafe · **40 M before wrap** warnings · **3 M before wrap** no new XIDs.
Recovery: end prepared/long transactions, drop stale slots, plain **VACUUM** as superuser; never single-user mode, FULL or FREEZE.
**MultiXacts** (several lockers in one `xmax`) age and wrap the same way: watch `mxid_age(relminmxid)`.

lessons.title: Physical streaming replication
tldr: A **standby** is a copy of the primary that stays in permanent recovery, receiving the primary's WAL over a replication connection and replaying it byte for byte.
Streaming gives a second server for failover and read queries, and **synchronous replication** lets a COMMIT wait until a standby has written, flushed or replayed its WAL.

visualizer.title: A primary streaming to a hot standby
visualizer.caption: Press **COMMIT** and watch WAL travel out and replies come back. Change the `synchronous_commit` level, the latency, cut the network, or start a long standby query. The standby is simulated: the playground database is a single process.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE orders (id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, total numeric(10,2) NOT NULL, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now());
INSERT INTO orders (total) SELECT (random() * 100)::numeric(10,2) FROM generate_series(1, 1000);

presets.label: Replication settings
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() AS is_standby;

SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('wal_level', 'max_wal_senders', 'max_replication_slots', 'wal_keep_size',
               'max_slot_wal_keep_size', 'synchronous_standby_names', 'synchronous_commit',
               'hot_standby', 'hot_standby_feedback', 'max_standby_streaming_delay',
               'wal_receiver_status_interval')
ORDER BY name;
presets.note: `wal_level = replica` is enough for physical standbys. `max_slot_wal_keep_size = -1` means a slot may retain unlimited WAL. The standby-side settings are listed too; they only matter on a standby.

presets.label: Create a physical slot
presets.sql:
SELECT * FROM pg_create_physical_replication_slot('standby_a', true);

SELECT slot_name, slot_type, active, restart_lsn, wal_status FROM pg_replication_slots;
presets.note: The second argument reserves WAL immediately. A standby would use it with `primary_slot_name = 'standby_a'`.

presets.label: Write WAL nobody consumes
presets.note: With no standby attached, `restart_lsn` never moves, so every byte written since is pinned in `pg_wal`. `safe_wal_size` is NULL because `max_slot_wal_keep_size` is unlimited.

presets.label: What a lag query computes
presets.sql:
-- the shape of pg_stat_replication on a real primary (one row per walsender):
SELECT column_name FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_name = 'pg_stat_replication' AND column_name ~ '(lsn|lag|state)$' ORDER BY ordinal_position;

-- the standard lag query, applied to a sample row
WITH r(application_name, sent_lsn, write_lsn, flush_lsn, replay_lsn) AS (
  VALUES ('standby_a', '0/3A00148'::pg_lsn, '0/3A00148'::pg_lsn, '0/3A00060'::pg_lsn, '0/39F2000'::pg_lsn))
SELECT application_name,
       sent_lsn - write_lsn   AS network_or_write_bytes,
       write_lsn - flush_lsn  AS awaiting_fsync_bytes,
       flush_lsn - replay_lsn AS replay_backlog_bytes
FROM r;
presets.note: Each gap points at a different bottleneck: network, standby disk, or replay (often a query conflict). `write_lag`, `flush_lag` and `replay_lag` give the same stages as time.

presets.label: Recovery functions on a primary
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_is_in_recovery()          AS in_recovery,
       pg_last_wal_receive_lsn()     AS last_received,
       pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()      AS last_replayed,
       pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS last_replay_time,
       pg_current_wal_lsn()          AS current_lsn;
presets.note: On a primary the standby-side functions return NULL. On a standby, `now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()` is a common lag-in-time check.

presets.label: Drop the slot
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('standby_a');
SELECT count(*) AS slots_left FROM pg_replication_slots;
presets.note: Dropping an unused slot releases the retained WAL at the next checkpoint. Forgotten slots are the classic cause of a full `pg_wal`.

production.title: Synchronous replication without single-standby hangs
production.context: A payments team runs a primary and two standbys in different zones and must not lose an acknowledged payment if the primary's zone fails.
production.problem: They started with `synchronous_standby_names = 's1'`. During a routine restart of s1, every write transaction on the primary hung at COMMIT for the whole maintenance window, because the only synchronous standby was gone.
production.solution: Use a quorum: any one of two standbys must confirm. Keep `synchronous_commit = on` for payments and let bulk jobs opt out per transaction. Monitor `sync_state` and lag.
production.outcome: Either standby can now confirm a commit, so restarting one no longer blocks writes, and an acknowledged payment is still on durable storage in a second zone. Commit latency is one round trip to the nearest healthy standby plus its fsync.

pitfalls.title: An inactive slot fills pg_wal
pitfalls.symptom: Disk usage of `pg_wal` grows for days; eventually the primary hits a full disk and PANICs.
pitfalls.cause: A replication slot whose standby is gone keeps `restart_lsn` in place, so no WAL after it can be recycled. `max_slot_wal_keep_size` defaults to -1 (unlimited).
pitfalls.fix: Alert on inactive slots and retained bytes, drop slots you no longer need, and set `max_slot_wal_keep_size` so a dead standby is invalidated instead of taking the primary down.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_current_wal_lsn() - restart_lsn) AS retained
FROM pg_replication_slots ORDER BY pg_current_wal_lsn() - restart_lsn DESC;

pitfalls.title: Standby queries cancelled with "conflict with recovery"
pitfalls.symptom: Reports on the standby fail with `canceling statement due to conflict with recovery`.
pitfalls.cause: Replay must apply a VACUUM cleanup record that removes rows a standby query still needs. Replay waits at most `max_standby_streaming_delay` (30 s), then cancels the query.
pitfalls.fix: Enable `hot_standby_feedback` (costs some bloat on the primary), raise `max_standby_streaming_delay` on reporting standbys, or move long reports to a dedicated delayed replica.

pitfalls.title: Both nodes think they are primary
pitfalls.symptom: After a failover, the old primary comes back and accepts writes; the two histories diverge.
pitfalls.cause: PostgreSQL does not detect failures or fence nodes. Promotion of the standby does not stop the old primary.
pitfalls.fix: Fence the old primary (STONITH) before promoting, and use a cluster manager. Rejoin the old primary as a standby with `pg_rewind` instead of a full re-clone.

pointers: **walsender** (primary) streams WAL to the **walreceiver** (standby); the **startup process** replays it.
Positions: **sent → write → flush → replay**; `pg_stat_replication` shows each LSN and the matching **lag**.
Slots keep WAL (and with feedback, old rows) until the standby has it; cap with **`max_slot_wal_keep_size`**.
`synchronous_standby_names` = `FIRST n (…)` or `ANY n (…)`; `synchronous_commit` picks **remote_write / on / remote_apply**.
Hot standby is read-only; conflicts are resolved by **delaying replay** up to `max_standby_streaming_delay`, then cancelling.

lessons.title: Logical replication
tldr: **Logical replication** decodes the WAL back into row-level INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE messages and streams them, per table, from a **publication** to a **subscription** on another server.
Unlike physical streaming it can replicate a subset of tables, rows and columns, across major versions and platforms, into a database that stays writable.

visualizer.title: From WAL records to filtered row changes
visualizer.caption: Step through four interleaved transactions: decoding, the reorder buffer, commit order, an abort, and a publication with a row filter and column list. Then flip old and new values below.

presets.label: Publication with a row filter and column list
presets.note: An INSERT-only publication may filter on any column. `total` and `card_last4` are not in the column list, so they never leave the publisher (but a column list is not a security boundary).

presets.label: Replica identity
presets.sql:
SELECT relname, relreplident,
       CASE relreplident WHEN 'd' THEN 'default: primary key, if any' WHEN 'f' THEN 'full row'
                         WHEN 'n' THEN 'nothing' WHEN 'i' THEN 'index' END AS meaning
FROM pg_class WHERE relname IN ('orders', 'products', 'clicks');
presets.note: UPDATE and DELETE messages identify the old row by its replica identity. `clicks` has no primary key, so its default identity is empty.

presets.label: Publishing UPDATEs needs an identity
presets.note: The error is raised **on the publisher**, even with no subscriber attached. `FULL` fixes it, at the cost of logging whole old rows and slow row lookups on the subscriber.

presets.label: Row filters must use identity columns
presets.note: A publication that sends UPDATEs must evaluate the filter on the old row, so it may only reference replica identity columns. Filtering on the primary key works.

presets.label: Generated columns (new in 18)
presets.note: With `publish_generated_columns = stored` the stored `price_with_vat` is sent; the **virtual** `label` never is, because it has no stored value. Listing a stored generated column in a column list publishes it even with the default `none`. On the subscriber the target column must be an ordinary column.

presets.label: DDL is not replicated
presets.sql:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN coupon text;
SELECT pubname, attnames FROM pg_publication_tables WHERE tablename = 'orders' ORDER BY pubname;
presets.note: The new column joins publications without a column list automatically, but the ALTER itself is not sent: the subscriber must add `coupon` first, or apply errors start.

presets.label: The WAL is the source
presets.note: Logical decoding reads the same WAL as everything else; `pg_logical_emit_message` writes a record decoders pass through. Creating a logical slot needs `wal_level = logical`, which this playground runs without (it reports `replica`).

production.title: Upgrading a major version with near-zero downtime
production.context: A marketplace runs PostgreSQL 16 with a 2 TB database and wants to move to 18. `pg_upgrade --link` would need a maintenance window it cannot get.
production.problem: Physical replication cannot cross major versions, and a dump and restore of 2 TB takes many hours of read-only time.
production.solution: Stand up an 18 cluster, copy the schema, and replicate logically. After the initial sync and catch-up, freeze writes for a minute, sync sequences (they are not replicated), and switch the application.
production.outcome: The write freeze lasts as long as the final catch-up and the sequence sync, typically seconds to minutes instead of hours. Tables without a primary key were given one (or `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`) beforehand, because their UPDATEs would otherwise fail on the publisher.

pitfalls.title: UPDATE fails: "does not have a replica identity"
pitfalls.symptom: After adding a table to a publication, application UPDATEs and DELETEs on it fail on the **publisher**.
pitfalls.cause: The table has no primary key, so its default replica identity is empty, and a publication that publishes UPDATE/DELETE needs one.
pitfalls.fix: Add a primary key, or `REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX` on a unique non-null index, or as a last resort `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER TABLE clicks ADD COLUMN id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY;

pitfalls.title: Replication stops on a conflict
pitfalls.symptom: The subscriber log repeats `conflict detected on relation ...: conflict=insert_exists` and lag grows.
pitfalls.cause: Incoming changes apply like normal DML. A row written locally on the subscriber violates a unique constraint, so the apply worker errors and retries forever.
pitfalls.fix: Fix the local data, or skip the remote transaction with `ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... SKIP (lsn = ...)` using the finish LSN from the log (with the default `streaming = parallel` it can be missing; set streaming to `on` and let the error repeat). Skipping drops the whole transaction. In 18, per-type conflict counters show what keeps happening; the `*_origin_differs` ones need `track_commit_timestamp = on` on the subscriber.

pitfalls.title: A dropped subscription leaves its slot behind
pitfalls.symptom: The publisher's `pg_wal` keeps growing after a subscriber was decommissioned.
pitfalls.cause: If the publisher was unreachable during `DROP SUBSCRIPTION`, or the slot was disassociated, the logical slot stays and retains WAL and catalog rows.
pitfalls.fix: Check `pg_replication_slots` on the publisher and drop orphaned slots; cap retention with `max_slot_wal_keep_size`.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT slot_name, plugin, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_current_wal_lsn() - restart_lsn)
FROM pg_replication_slots WHERE slot_type = 'logical';

pitfalls.title: Sequences and DDL silently drift
pitfalls.symptom: After failing over to the subscriber, inserts fail with duplicate keys, or apply breaks after a schema change.
pitfalls.cause: Logical replication does not replicate DDL or sequence state.
pitfalls.fix: Apply schema changes to the subscriber first (additive changes), and run `setval` for every sequence before a switchover.

pitfalls.title: Publishing a generated column into a generated column
pitfalls.symptom: After enabling `publish_generated_columns = stored`, the subscriber's apply worker errors on every change to the table.
pitfalls.cause: The publisher now sends a value for `price_with_vat`, but on the subscriber that column is also `GENERATED`, and a generated column cannot accept a supplied value.
pitfalls.fix: Either leave the option at `none` and let the subscriber compute the column itself, or make the subscriber column an ordinary column. Virtual generated columns are never published.

pointers: **Publication** (what to send) on the publisher, **subscription** (where from) on the subscriber, one logical **slot** per subscription.
Decoding is in **commit order**; rolled-back transactions are **never sent**.
**Replica identity** (default: primary key) identifies old rows; without one, published UPDATE/DELETE fail on the publisher.
**Row filters** turn UPDATEs into INSERT/DELETE when rows cross the filter; **column lists** limit columns but are not security.
Not replicated: **DDL, sequences, large objects**. Initial data is copied by table-sync workers, then changes stream.

lessons.title: Declarative partitioning and pruning
tldr: A **partitioned table** has no storage of its own: each row is routed by its partition key to one partition, an ordinary table with its own heap, indexes and statistics.
Queries that constrain the key touch only the relevant partitions through **partition pruning**, and old data leaves by dropping a whole partition instead of deleting rows.

visualizer.title: Which partitions does a query touch?
visualizer.caption: Pick a query and see where pruning happens (plan time, executor start, or run time), next to its EXPLAIN output. Then route a few rows and compare DELETE with DROP for retention.

presets.label: Partitions and routing
presets.note: The parent stores nothing (0 bytes). `tableoid` shows which partition each row was routed to.

presets.label: Plan-time pruning
presets.note: With pruning only `events_2026_10` appears. Turn it off and the plan becomes an Append over all five partitions.

presets.label: Pruning at executor start
presets.note: Look for **Subplans Removed: 4**: the generic plan kept every partition, and pruning ran when the parameter became known.

presets.label: Pruning during execution
presets.note: Four subplans say **(never executed)**: the value came from an InitPlan, so the Append pruned at run time.

presets.label: Unique keys must include the partition key
presets.note: Each partition enforces uniqueness only inside itself, so a primary key on `id` alone is rejected. With `created_at` added it works, and the parent's key creates one index per partition.

presets.label: Retention: DELETE vs DROP
presets.note: DELETE logged every row (about 1.2 MB) and left 22,320 dead rows for VACUUM. DROP removed a month in a few kB of WAL and left nothing to clean.

presets.label: Add next month with ATTACH
presets.note: ATTACH takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE on the parent. The matching CHECK constraint lets it skip the validation scan; the DEFAULT partition is still checked for December rows.

presets.label: DEFAULT partition traps
presets.note: A late row lands in the DEFAULT partition, and then creating January **fails**: the new bounds would make that row belong elsewhere. Moving the rows out and attaching in one transaction fixes it. As long as `partdefid` is set, `DETACH … CONCURRENTLY` is refused too.

production.title: Monthly partitions for a 3-year event log
production.context: An analytics product keeps 36 months of click events, about 1.5 billion rows, and deletes the oldest month every month. Most queries look at the last 7 days.
production.problem: The monthly `DELETE` produced tens of GB of WAL, saturated the replica link, and left a month of dead rows that autovacuum took days to clear. Recent-data queries still walked indexes covering three years.
production.solution: Range-partition by `created_at` per month. Create next month's partition ahead of time, and retire the oldest month with `DETACH PARTITION … CONCURRENTLY` and `DROP TABLE`. Queries filter on `created_at`, so they prune to one or two partitions.
production.outcome: Retention became a metadata operation of a few kB of WAL (dropping a 22,000-row month writes about 6 kB, deleting it about 1.2 MB), with no dead rows. Recent-data queries touch one month instead of 36, so their indexes are 36 times smaller and stay in cache.

pitfalls.title: Queries that do not mention the partition key
pitfalls.symptom: A lookup by `user_id` on a partitioned table is slower than before partitioning; EXPLAIN shows an Append over every partition.
pitfalls.cause: Pruning uses only conditions on the partition key. Without one, every partition and every partition index is searched.
pitfalls.fix: Partition by the column most queries filter on, add the key to hot queries, or accept the fan-out for rare queries.

pitfalls.title: DETACH CONCURRENTLY refused
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: cannot detach partitions concurrently when a default partition exists`.
pitfalls.cause: A popular rotation recipe adds a DEFAULT partition as a safety net and later detaches old partitions with CONCURRENTLY. The two do not mix: concurrent detach is refused while a DEFAULT partition exists, and it cannot run inside a transaction block either.
pitfalls.fix: Avoid a DEFAULT partition on tables you rotate (create future partitions ahead of time instead), or use a plain DETACH in a short maintenance window.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_2026_08;  -- takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the parent

pitfalls.title: Too many partitions
pitfalls.symptom: Planning time and backend memory grow; simple queries that cannot prune become slow to plan.
pitfalls.cause: Every partition a session touches loads metadata into its local memory, and planning considers each one that is not pruned.
pitfalls.fix: Keep partition counts in the hundreds to low thousands, choose coarser ranges, and make sure common queries prune.

pitfalls.title: A DEFAULT partition that quietly fills up
pitfalls.symptom: `CREATE TABLE … PARTITION OF` for next month fails with `updated partition constraint for default partition would be violated by some row`, and every new partition takes longer to add.
pitfalls.cause: Rows with no matching range were routed to the DEFAULT partition. Adding a range scans the default for rows that would now belong to it, and refuses if any exist.
pitfalls.fix: Create partitions ahead of time and alert when the default holds any rows. To add a range, move its rows out of the default and ATTACH in one transaction (the last playground preset).
pitfalls.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM events_default;  -- should stay 0

pointers: RANGE / LIST / HASH; range bounds are **inclusive below, exclusive above**; the parent has **no storage**.
Pruning at **plan time** (constants), **executor start** (`Subplans Removed`), and **run time** (`(never executed)`).
PRIMARY KEY / UNIQUE must **include the partition key**; an index on the parent is created on every partition.
Retention: **DROP / DETACH a partition**, not DELETE; ATTACH with a matching CHECK to skip validation.
Autovacuum handles partitions, but **ANALYZE the parent** yourself.

lessons.title: Backups and point-in-time recovery
tldr: PostgreSQL backs up either **logically** with `pg_dump` (SQL or an archive of one database) or **physically** with a base backup of the whole cluster plus the continuous stream of archived WAL.
Physical backups enable **point-in-time recovery**: restore the base backup and replay archived WAL up to any moment after it, such as one second before a destructive mistake.

visualizer.title: Recover to one minute before the mistake
visualizer.caption: Step through a day with a base backup, archived WAL and a bad DROP, then recovery. Drag `recovery_target_time` to before 01:20, before 14:05, or after it and step again.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE invoices (id int PRIMARY KEY, customer text NOT NULL, amount numeric(10,2) NOT NULL, paid boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false);
INSERT INTO invoices SELECT g, 'cust_' || (g % 40), (g % 300) + 0.5, g % 3 = 0 FROM generate_series(1, 2000) g;

presets.label: What pg_dump does inside the server
presets.note: A dump is one **REPEATABLE READ** transaction: every table is read in the same snapshot, so the output is consistent. It holds **AccessShareLock** on each table it dumps until the end, and no XID. `pg_export_snapshot()` is how `pg_dump -j` workers share that one snapshot.

presets.label: Archiving settings
presets.note: This playground runs with archiving off. A PITR-ready server needs `wal_level` replica or higher, `archive_mode = on` and a working `archive_command` or `archive_library`.

presets.label: A low-level base backup
presets.note: `labelfile` is the `backup_label` you must save with the copy: START WAL LOCATION and CHECKPOINT LOCATION tell recovery where to begin.

presets.label: Segment files and switches
presets.note: `pg_switch_wal` closes the current segment so it can be archived now (what `archive_timeout` does on a timer). Every file is a full 16 MB.

presets.label: A named restore point
presets.note: A `RESTORE_POINT` record sits in the WAL before the purge. Recovery could stop exactly there with `recovery_target_name = 'before_invoice_purge'`.

presets.label: Write the recovery settings
presets.sql:
SELECT format($f$restore_command = 'cp /mnt/archive/%%f "%%p"'
recovery_target_time = %L
recovery_target_inclusive = off
recovery_target_action = 'pause'
-- then: touch $PGDATA/recovery.signal and start the server$f$,
  now() - interval '1 minute') AS postgresql_conf_lines;

SELECT now() AS time, pg_current_wal_lsn() AS lsn, pg_current_xact_id() AS xid;
presets.note: Targets can be a time, a restore point name, an LSN or an XID (one at a time). `pause` lets you check the data before ending recovery.

presets.label: Incremental backups need WAL summaries
presets.note: `pg_basebackup --incremental` (17+) copies only blocks changed since a previous backup, using summaries written by the WAL summarizer. With `summarize_wal = off` there are none.

production.title: Undoing a bad migration with PITR
production.context: A billing service takes a nightly `pg_basebackup` at 01:00 and archives WAL to object storage. At 14:05 a migration meant for staging dropped the `invoices` table in production.
production.problem: A nightly `pg_dump` would restore last night's state and lose 13 hours of invoices. Restoring the base backup alone would do the same.
production.solution: Restore the 01:00 base backup on a new host, replay archived WAL to 14:04, inspect, then copy the table back to production (or promote the recovered host). The old timeline stays intact in the archive.
production.sql:
# postgresql.conf on the recovery host
restore_command = 'aws s3 cp s3://wal-archive/%f %p'
recovery_target_time = '2026-11-10 14:04:00+00'
recovery_target_action = 'pause'
# touch $PGDATA/recovery.signal ; pg_ctl start
# once paused at the target:
#   psql -c "SELECT count(*) FROM invoices"
#   pg_dump -t invoices | psql -h prod billing
production.outcome: Data loss is bounded by the recovery target, one minute here, instead of 13 hours. Recovery time is dominated by replaying 13 hours of WAL; newer incremental backups (`pg_basebackup --incremental` + `pg_combinebackup`) or a more recent base backup shorten it.

pitfalls.title: An archive_command that lies
pitfalls.symptom: Recovery stops early with `could not open file` for a segment that the archiver reported as done.
pitfalls.cause: The command returned 0 without storing the file (for example `cp -i` or a script that ignores errors), so PostgreSQL recycled the segment.
pitfalls.fix: Return 0 only after the file is durably stored, refuse to overwrite existing files, and test restores regularly. `pg_stat_archiver.failed_count` must stay flat.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT archived_count, failed_count, last_failed_wal, last_failed_time FROM pg_stat_archiver;

pitfalls.title: Archiving silently stopped and pg_wal filled
pitfalls.symptom: Disk usage of `pg_wal` grows until the server PANICs with a full disk.
pitfalls.cause: If `archive_command` keeps failing, segments cannot be recycled. PostgreSQL keeps retrying forever.
pitfalls.fix: Alert on `failed_count` and on `pg_wal` size; fix the archive target. Never delete files from `pg_wal` by hand.

pitfalls.title: Treating pg_dump as the only backup
pitfalls.symptom: After an incident the newest recoverable state is last night's dump.
pitfalls.cause: `pg_dump` is a logical snapshot of one database at one moment; it cannot be combined with WAL for PITR.
pitfalls.fix: Use base backups plus WAL archiving for recovery, and keep `pg_dump` for migrations, partial restores and cross-version moves. Verify base backups with `pg_verifybackup`.

pitfalls.title: pg_restore refuses the dump file
pitfalls.symptom: `pg_restore: error: input file appears to be a text format dump. Please use psql.`
pitfalls.cause: Plain format (the `pg_dump` default) and all `pg_dumpall` output are SQL scripts for `psql`. Only the custom, directory and tar archives are read by `pg_restore`, which is also what enables `-j` parallel restore and `-l` / `-L` to restore selected objects.
pitfalls.fix: Dump with `-Fc` or `-Fd` for anything you may restore selectively. Repeat `-t` / `-n` once per object (they do not take comma lists), use `-O` (`--no-owner`) when roles differ, and dump roles and tablespaces separately with `pg_dumpall --globals-only`, because `pg_dump` never includes them.
pitfalls.sql:
pg_dump -Fd -j 4 -t invoices -t customers -f /backups/billing.dir billing
pg_dumpall --globals-only > /backups/globals.sql
psql -f /backups/globals.sql postgres
pg_restore -j 4 -O -d billing_copy /backups/billing.dir

pitfalls.title: A long pg_dump blocks a migration and VACUUM
pitfalls.symptom: During the nightly dump an `ALTER TABLE` hangs, every query behind it queues, and dead rows pile up across the cluster.
pitfalls.cause: The dump holds ACCESS SHARE on every table until it finishes, which conflicts with the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE an ALTER needs. Its snapshot also stops VACUUM from removing rows deleted after the dump began.
pitfalls.fix: Schedule DDL outside dump windows and set `lock_timeout` on migrations. Take large dumps from a standby, or rely on base backups and use `pg_dump` for smaller, targeted exports.

pointers: **pg_dump**: one database in one snapshot; plain SQL goes to **psql**, custom/directory archives to **pg_restore** (`-j`, `-L`); roles need **pg_dumpall --globals-only**.
**Base backup + archived WAL** = PITR; replay must start at the backup's `START WAL LOCATION`.
`restore_command` + `recovery.signal` + one **recovery_target_*** (time, name, lsn, xid, immediate).
Ending recovery starts a **new timeline**; `.history` files record branch points.
Incremental backups (17+) need **`summarize_wal`** and are rebuilt with **`pg_combinebackup`**.

lessons.title: Connection pooling
tldr: Every PostgreSQL connection is a separate backend process with its own memory and session state, so thousands of mostly idle connections waste RAM and slots up to `max_connections`.

A **pooler** such as PgBouncer lets many clients share a few server connections, and its pooling mode decides which session features, such as `SET`, prepared statements, advisory locks and `LISTEN`, still behave correctly.

visualizer.title: Four clients, two server connections
visualizer.caption: Step through the same client script in **transaction**, **session** and **statement** mode and watch where session state lands and what breaks.

presets.label: Session state a pooler can leak
presets.note: All five live in **this backend**, not in the client. Under transaction pooling the next client on this server connection would inherit them, including the tenant_a search_path.

presets.label: DISCARD ALL wipes it
presets.note: `DISCARD ALL` resets settings to their defaults, drops prepared statements and temp tables, releases session advisory locks and stops listening: every count is back to 0. Session-mode poolers run it between clients.

presets.label: Transaction-scoped alternatives
presets.note: `SET LOCAL` and `pg_advisory_xact_lock` end with the transaction, so nothing survives COMMIT. This is what is safe under transaction pooling.

presets.label: Per-request context: set_config(…, true)
presets.note: The third argument `true` makes the value transaction-local, like `SET LOCAL`, so a tenant id used by row-level security policies cannot leak to the next client on the connection. Afterwards the value is an **empty string**, not NULL. Without `missing_ok = true`, reading a name that was never set raises an error.

presets.label: What one connection costs
presets.note: Even this idle backend holds about 2 MB in memory contexts (caches, plans), before any query runs, and each query can add `work_mem` per sort or hash node. The playground has one standalone backend; a server forks one process per connection.

presets.label: Timeouts that protect a pool
presets.note: All are off (0) by default. `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` kills sessions that sit in an open transaction holding locks and an old snapshot; `idle_session_timeout` is dangerous behind a pooler, which keeps idle server connections on purpose.

presets.label: Idle in transaction holds an XID
presets.note: While a transaction stays open its `backend_xid` and snapshot hold back VACUUM cluster-wide. A pooled client that forgets COMMIT pins a server connection and the cleanup horizon.

presets.label: Find the sessions that hog the pool
presets.sql:
SELECT pid, usename, application_name, state,
       now() - xact_start  AS xact_open_for,
       now() - state_change AS in_state_for,
       left(query, 40)     AS last_query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend' OR backend_type = 'standalone backend'
ORDER BY xact_start NULLS LAST;

SELECT pg_get_function_arguments('pg_terminate_backend'::regproc) AS terminate_signature;
presets.note: On a server, sort `idle in transaction` sessions by `xact_open_for` to find the ones holding connections and snapshots. `pg_terminate_backend(pid)` returns true once the signal is **sent**; with a `timeout` in ms it returns true only if the backend actually exited.

production.title: From 4,000 connections to 60
production.context: A Kubernetes deployment runs 200 pods, each with a client-side pool of 20 connections, against one primary: 4,000 connections, almost all idle.
production.problem: The server needed `max_connections = 5000`; each backend kept its own caches and memory even when idle, connection storms during deploys forked hundreds of processes at once, and snapshot work grows with the number of backends.
production.solution: Put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of the primary with a small server pool, shrink the per-pod pools, and remove session state from the application: `SET LOCAL` instead of `SET`, transaction-level advisory locks, schema-qualified names, protocol-level prepared statements with `max_prepared_statements` enabled.
production.sql:
; pgbouncer.ini
[databases]
app = host=10.0.0.5 dbname=app
[pgbouncer]
pool_mode = transaction
default_pool_size = 60
max_client_conn = 5000
max_prepared_statements = 200

-- server side
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_connections = 200;
ALTER ROLE app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';
production.outcome: The primary serves the same traffic with about 60 busy backends instead of 4,000 mostly idle ones, deploys no longer cause fork storms, and memory goes to `shared_buffers` and `work_mem` instead of idle processes. A sensible pool size is a small multiple of CPU cores, measured under load.

pitfalls.title: Session SET under transaction pooling
pitfalls.symptom: Requests intermittently see another tenant's data, the wrong time zone, or a stray `statement_timeout`.
pitfalls.cause: A plain `SET` sticks to the server connection, which the pooler hands to the next client.
pitfalls.fix: Use `SET LOCAL` inside a transaction, or pass settings per role/database (`ALTER ROLE … SET`). Schema-qualify names instead of relying on `search_path`.
pitfalls.sql: BEGIN; SET LOCAL search_path = tenant_b; SELECT …; COMMIT;

pitfalls.title: Session advisory locks that never unlock
pitfalls.symptom: A job scheduler using `pg_advisory_lock` stops running jobs; `pg_locks` shows advisory locks held by idle connections.
pitfalls.cause: Lock and unlock ran on different server connections, so the unlock returned false and the lock stayed with the first backend.
pitfalls.fix: Use `pg_advisory_xact_lock` (released at COMMIT) or route lock holders through a session-mode pool.

pitfalls.title: Prepared statements "do not exist"
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: prepared statement "S_1" does not exist` after enabling transaction pooling.
pitfalls.cause: The driver prepared on one server connection and executed on another.
pitfalls.fix: Enable the pooler's prepared-statement support (PgBouncer 1.21+ `max_prepared_statements`) for protocol-level statements, or disable server-side prepares in the driver. SQL-level `PREPARE` is never safe in transaction mode.

pitfalls.title: A new connection for every query
pitfalls.symptom: Latency is dominated by connection setup, CPU shows constant process creation, and with `log_connections` on the log records one new connection per request.
pitfalls.cause: Helper functions open and close their own connection on every call. Each one is a fork of a new backend plus authentication and cache warm-up, often several milliseconds before the first query runs.
pitfalls.fix: Create one pool per application process (the driver's built-in pool or a pool library) and borrow from it per request; add a server-side pooler when many processes connect.

pitfalls.title: Drivers that leave transactions open
pitfalls.symptom: `pg_stat_activity` shows many `idle in transaction` sessions whose last query is a plain SELECT, and VACUUM stops removing dead rows.
pitfalls.cause: With autocommit off, many drivers send BEGIN before the first statement. A read-only request that never commits keeps its transaction, snapshot and server connection open.
pitfalls.fix: Use autocommit for read paths, always end transactions (commit or rollback in a `finally`), and set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` as a backstop.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER ROLE app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';

pointers: One connection = **one backend process** with private memory; `max_connections` (100) sizes shared memory and slots.
**Session** mode: safe but no multiplexing. **Transaction** mode: multiplexes, breaks session state. **Statement** mode: autocommit only.
Session state lives in the backend: **SET, PREPARE, session advisory locks, LISTEN, temp tables**; `DISCARD ALL` resets it.
Transaction-safe forms: **`SET LOCAL`**, **`pg_advisory_xact_lock`**, schema-qualified names.
Guard the pool with **`idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`**; avoid `idle_session_timeout` behind a pooler.

lessons.title: Embeddings and the vector type
tldr: An **embedding** is a fixed-length list of numbers that a model produces for a piece of text or an image, and pgvector stores it in a `vector(n)` column.
Similar meanings land close together in that space, so storing embeddings next to your rows turns "find related things" into a plain SQL query.

visualizer.title: An embedding, from meaning to bytes
visualizer.caption: Click a word (or **Next word**) to see its 8 numbers and its nearest neighbours. Switch the storage type to see the exact byte layout, then compare sizes at real model dimensions.

playground.setup:
CREATE FUNCTION try_sql(stmt text) RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $fn$
BEGIN
  EXECUTE stmt;
  RETURN 'OK';
EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN
  RETURN 'ERROR: ' || SQLERRM;
END $fn$;
CREATE TABLE words (
  id        int PRIMARY KEY,
  word      text NOT NULL,
  kind      text NOT NULL,
  embedding vector(8) NOT NULL   -- alive, tame, wild, edible, sweet, machine, speed, size
);
INSERT INTO words VALUES
 (1, 'cat',    'animal',  '[0.9,0.8,-0.3,-0.6,0,-0.9,0.3,-0.5]'),
 (2, 'dog',    'animal',  '[0.9,0.9,-0.2,-0.6,0,-0.9,0.4,-0.2]'),
 (3, 'wolf',   'animal',  '[0.9,-0.7,0.9,-0.6,0,-0.9,0.6,0.1]'),
 (4, 'lion',   'animal',  '[0.9,-0.8,0.9,-0.6,0,-0.9,0.6,0.6]'),
 (5, 'apple',  'food',    '[0.2,0,0,0.9,0.6,-0.8,-0.8,-0.7]'),
 (6, 'cake',   'food',    '[-0.6,0,0,0.9,0.95,-0.8,-0.8,-0.4]'),
 (7, 'honey',  'food',    '[-0.4,0,0.2,0.8,0.9,-0.8,-0.9,-0.8]'),
 (8, 'bread',  'food',    '[-0.6,0,0,0.95,0.1,-0.8,-0.8,-0.3]'),
 (9, 'car',    'vehicle', '[-0.9,0,0,-0.9,0,0.95,0.7,0.3]'),
 (10,'bike',   'vehicle', '[-0.9,0,0,-0.9,0,0.8,0.3,-0.4]'),
 (11,'train',  'vehicle', '[-0.9,0,0,-0.9,0,0.9,0.8,0.95]'),
 (12,'rocket', 'vehicle', '[-0.9,0,0,-0.9,0,0.7,1,0.9]');

presets.label: Read vectors
presets.note: The extension is called `vector` (version 0.8.7). A vector literal is a bracketed list. `vector_dims` gives the length of the list, `vector_norm` its geometric length.

presets.label: Nearest words
presets.sql:
SELECT w.word, round((w.embedding <-> c.embedding)::numeric, 3) AS distance
FROM words w, words c
WHERE c.word = 'wolf' AND w.word <> 'wolf'
ORDER BY w.embedding <-> c.embedding
LIMIT 4;
presets.note: `<->` is the straight-line distance between two vectors. Lion and dog come first because their numbers are closest to wolf's. [Distance metrics](/e1/distance-and-exact-search) covers every operator.

presets.label: Bytes per type
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_column_size('[1,2,3]'::vector)  AS vector_3d,
       pg_column_size('[1,2,3]'::halfvec) AS halfvec_3d,
       pg_column_size(array_fill(0.5::real, ARRAY[1536])::vector)  AS vector_1536,
       pg_column_size(array_fill(0.5::real, ARRAY[1536])::halfvec) AS halfvec_1536,
       pg_column_size(repeat('1', 1536)::bit(1536))                AS bit_1536,
       pg_column_size('{1:0.9,3:0.5}/8'::sparsevec)                AS sparse_2nnz;

presets.label: Errors you will meet
presets.sql:
SELECT stmt, try_sql(stmt) AS result FROM (VALUES
  ($$SELECT '[1,2]'::vector(3)$$),
  ($$SELECT '[1,2]'::vector <-> '[1,2,3]'$$),
  ($$SELECT '[1,NaN]'::vector$$),
  ($$SELECT '[65520]'::halfvec$$),
  ($$SELECT array_fill(1, ARRAY[16001])::vector$$),
  ($$INSERT INTO words VALUES (13, 'x', 'x', '[1,2,3]')$$)
) t(stmt);
presets.note: The type checks the dimension count on every value, rejects NaN and infinity, and caps storage at 16 000 dimensions. halfvec overflows above 65504.

presets.label: halfvec, sparsevec, bit
presets.sql:
SELECT '[0.1,0.2,0.3333333]'::vector  AS as_vector,
       '[0.1,0.2,0.3333333]'::halfvec AS as_halfvec;

SELECT word,
       embedding::halfvec(8)       AS half,
       embedding::sparsevec(8)     AS sparse,
       binary_quantize(embedding)  AS bits
FROM words WHERE kind = 'vehicle';
presets.note: halfvec keeps about 3 significant digits: 0.1 becomes 0.099975586. The sparse form lists only non-zero positions (1-based). `binary_quantize` keeps only the sign of each element.

presets.label: Normalise and average
presets.note: `l2_normalize` scales a vector to length 1 without changing its direction. `avg()` works on vectors element by element, which gives the centre of each group.

presets.label: Big vectors live in TOAST
presets.note: Storage `e` (EXTERNAL) means out-of-line and uncompressed. A 6 KB vector is above the 2 KB TOAST threshold, so the main heap holds only small pointers (8 kB for 100 rows) and the vectors sit in the TOAST table.

production.title: Sizing an embeddings column before the first insert
production.context: A support team wants "similar tickets" next to every new ticket. Their model returns 1536 numbers per ticket, and they expect 2 million tickets.
production.problem: Nobody had sized the column. Stored as `vector(1536)`, each embedding is 6152 bytes, so the vectors alone are about 12.3 GB, more than the RAM of the instance they planned.
production.solution: Declare the column with the exact model dimension so wrong-sized inserts fail loudly. Keep full precision in the table, and plan a half-precision index ([HNSW](/e1/hnsw), [pgvector in production](/e1/pgvector-production)). Store the model name, because vectors from different models cannot be compared.
production.outcome: The arithmetic (2 M × 6152 B) settled the hardware question before launch. As `halfvec(1536)` the same data would be 2 M × 3080 B, about 6.2 GB.

pitfalls.title: Dimension does not match the model
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: expected 1536 dimensions, not 3072` after someone switches to a bigger embedding model.
pitfalls.cause: A `vector(n)` column checks the count on every insert. A new model has a different size, and its vectors are not comparable with the old ones anyway.
pitfalls.fix: Treat a model change as a migration: add a new column (or a `model` key), re-embed every row, build its index, then switch reads over.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER TABLE items ADD COLUMN embedding_v2 vector(3072);

pitfalls.title: Expecting the database to make embeddings
pitfalls.symptom: Searching for `CREATE EMBEDDING` or a function that turns text into a vector.
pitfalls.cause: pgvector stores, compares and indexes vectors. It does not run models.
pitfalls.fix: Call the model in your application or a job, then `INSERT` (or `COPY … FORMAT BINARY` for bulk loads) the resulting numbers.

pitfalls.title: Indexing vectors wider than 2000 dimensions
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: column cannot have more than 2000 dimensions for hnsw index` on a 3072-d column.
pitfalls.cause: An index entry must fit on one 8 KB page. 2000 × 4 bytes is the ceiling for `vector`.
pitfalls.fix: Index a half-precision expression (up to 4000 dims) or binary-quantized bits (up to 64 000), as shown in [pgvector in production](/e1/pgvector-production).
pitfalls.sql: CREATE INDEX ON items USING hnsw ((embedding::halfvec(3072)) halfvec_cosine_ops);

pointers: `CREATE EXTENSION vector;` adds `vector`, `halfvec`, `sparsevec`, distance operators and two index types.
`vector(n)`: 4-byte floats, **4·n + 8** bytes, up to 16 000 dims stored and 2000 dims indexed.
`halfvec(n)`: **2·n + 8** bytes, about 3 significant digits, max value 65504, indexable to 4000 dims.
`sparsevec`: `{index:value,…}/dims`, 1-based, **8·nnz + 16** bytes. `bit(n)`: **n/8 + 8** bytes, from `binary_quantize()`.
Large vectors are stored out of line in TOAST without compression; random floats do not compress anyway.

lessons.title: Distance metrics and exact search
tldr: pgvector compares vectors with six distance operators: `<->` (L2), `<#>` (negative inner product), `<=>` (cosine), `<+>` (L1) for real-valued vectors, and `<~>` (Hamming) and `<%>` (Jaccard) for bits.
Without an index, `ORDER BY embedding <-> $1 LIMIT k` is an **exact** search that computes every distance and keeps the best k, which is always correct but costs a full table scan.

visualizer.title: Rank 20 vectors four different ways
visualizer.caption: Drag the query ✕ and switch operators: the same points rank differently. **Compare next row** steps the exact scan one row at a time, keeping a top-5 heap.

playground.setup:
SELECT setseed(0.42);
-- 40 topic centres in 32 dimensions
CREATE TABLE topics AS
  SELECT t AS topic, array_agg(random() * 2 - 1 ORDER BY j)::real[] AS center
  FROM generate_series(0, 39) t, generate_series(1, 32) j
  GROUP BY t;
-- 10 000 items: each one is its topic centre plus noise
CREATE TABLE items (
  id        int PRIMARY KEY,
  topic     int NOT NULL,
  region    int NOT NULL,
  category  int NOT NULL,
  embedding vector(32)
);
INSERT INTO items
  SELECT i, t.topic, t.topic % 4, floor(random() * 10)::int,
         array_agg(t.center[j] + random() - 0.5 ORDER BY j)::vector(32)
  FROM generate_series(1, 10000) i
  JOIN topics t ON t.topic = i % 40
  CROSS JOIN generate_series(1, 32) j
  GROUP BY i, t.topic;
-- 20 query vectors, drawn the same way
CREATE TABLE queries AS
  SELECT q AS qid, t.topic, array_agg(t.center[j] + random() - 0.5 ORDER BY j)::vector(32) AS v
  FROM generate_series(1, 20) q
  JOIN topics t ON t.topic = (q * 7) % 40
  CROSS JOIN generate_series(1, 32) j
  GROUP BY q, t.topic;
-- exact top-10 for every query, computed before any vector index exists
CREATE TABLE truth AS
  SELECT q.qid, n.id
  FROM queries q, LATERAL (SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> q.v LIMIT 10) n;
-- recall@10 of whatever plan the planner picks right now
CREATE VIEW recall AS
  SELECT round(avg(hit) / 10.0, 3) AS recall_at_10, round(avg(n), 1) AS avg_rows
  FROM queries q, LATERAL (
    SELECT count(*) AS n,
           count(*) FILTER (WHERE a.id IN (SELECT id FROM truth t WHERE t.qid = q.qid)) AS hit
    FROM (SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> q.v LIMIT 10) a) x;
ANALYZE;
-- the 20 two-dimensional points from the visualizer
CREATE TABLE pts (id int PRIMARY KEY, v vector(2));
INSERT INTO pts VALUES (1, '[0.25,0.17]'), (2, '[0.5,0.38]'), (3, '[0.8,0.55]'), (4, '[0.95,0.7]'), (5, '[0.42,0.22]'), (6, '[-0.3,0.25]'), (7, '[-0.6,0.5]'), (8, '[-0.85,0.62]'), (9, '[-0.45,0.48]'), (10, '[-0.2,-0.5]'), (11, '[-0.3,-0.85]'), (12, '[-0.12,-0.3]'), (13, '[-0.4,-0.65]'), (14, '[0.7,-0.2]'), (15, '[0.3,-0.6]'), (16, '[0.1,0.6]'), (17, '[0.9,0.1]'), (18, '[-0.9,-0.1]'), (19, '[0.55,-0.75]'), (20, '[0.05,0.05]');

presets.label: Six operators
presets.sql:
SELECT '[1,2,3]'::vector <-> '[3,1,2]' AS l2,
       '[1,2,3]'::vector <#> '[3,1,2]' AS neg_inner_product,
       '[1,2,3]'::vector <=> '[3,1,2]' AS cosine_distance,
       '[1,2,3]'::vector <+> '[3,1,2]' AS l1,
       '101'::bit(3) <~> '111' AS hamming,
       '101'::bit(3) <%> '111' AS jaccard;
presets.note: L2 = 2.449, the negative inner product = **−11** (the dot product is 11), cosine distance = 0.214, L1 = 4. Hamming counts differing bits (1). Jaccard = 1 − shared ones / all ones = 0.333.

presets.label: Similarity and edge cases
presets.sql:
SELECT inner_product('[1,2,3]'::vector, '[3,1,2]') AS inner_product,
       1 - ('[1,2,3]'::vector <=> '[3,1,2]')         AS cosine_similarity,
       '[1,1]'::vector <=> '[2,2]'                    AS same_direction,
       '[1,0]'::vector <=> '[-1,0]'                   AS opposite,
       '[0,0]'::vector <=> '[1,1]'                    AS zero_vector;
presets.note: Cosine distance runs from 0 (same direction, any length) to 2 (opposite). A zero vector has no direction, so its cosine distance is **NaN**.

presets.label: Same query, four rankings
presets.sql:
SELECT 'L2 <->' AS operator, string_agg(id::text, ', ' ORDER BY v <-> '[0.45,0.3]') AS top5
FROM (SELECT id, v FROM pts ORDER BY v <-> '[0.45,0.3]' LIMIT 5) a
UNION ALL
SELECT 'cosine <=>', string_agg(id::text, ', ' ORDER BY v <=> '[0.45,0.3]')
FROM (SELECT id, v FROM pts ORDER BY v <=> '[0.45,0.3]' LIMIT 5) a
UNION ALL
SELECT 'inner product <#>', string_agg(id::text, ', ' ORDER BY v <#> '[0.45,0.3]')
FROM (SELECT id, v FROM pts ORDER BY v <#> '[0.45,0.3]' LIMIT 5) a
UNION ALL
SELECT 'L1 <+>', string_agg(id::text, ', ' ORDER BY v <+> '[0.45,0.3]')
FROM (SELECT id, v FROM pts ORDER BY v <+> '[0.45,0.3]' LIMIT 5) a;
presets.note: These are the visualizer's points and its starting query. L2 picks the nearby points, inner product prefers the long vectors 4 and 3, and cosine ranks by angle only.

presets.label: Exact k-NN plan
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF)
SELECT id, embedding <-> (SELECT v FROM queries WHERE qid = 1) AS distance
FROM items
ORDER BY embedding <-> (SELECT v FROM queries WHERE qid = 1)
LIMIT 10;
presets.note: No index yet: **Seq Scan** reads all 10 000 rows, then **top-N heapsort** keeps only the best 10 in 17 kB of memory. This is exact search, with perfect recall.

presets.label: Neighbours of a row
presets.sql:
SELECT i.id, i.topic, round((i.embedding <-> s.embedding)::numeric, 4) AS distance
FROM items i, items s
WHERE s.id = 1 AND i.id <> s.id
ORDER BY i.embedding <-> s.embedding
LIMIT 5;
presets.note: "More like this" for an existing row: join to the row, exclude it, order by distance. All five neighbours share item 1's topic, because the data is clustered.

presets.label: Normalised: same order
presets.sql:
WITH q AS (SELECT l2_normalize(v) AS v FROM queries WHERE qid = 1),
n AS (SELECT id, l2_normalize(embedding) AS e FROM items)
SELECT (SELECT array_agg(id) FROM (SELECT id FROM n, q ORDER BY e <-> q.v LIMIT 5) a) AS by_l2,
       (SELECT array_agg(id) FROM (SELECT id FROM n, q ORDER BY e <=> q.v LIMIT 5) a) AS by_cosine,
       (SELECT array_agg(id) FROM (SELECT id FROM n, q ORDER BY e <#> q.v LIMIT 5) a) AS by_inner_product;
presets.note: For unit-length vectors the three metrics give the **same ranking**. Many embedding models return normalised vectors, so inner product (the cheapest) is a safe choice for them.

production.title: Picking the operator for a semantic search API
production.context: A documentation site stores 384-d sentence embeddings. The model card says the vectors are normalised to length 1 and recommends cosine similarity.
production.problem: The first version ranked with `ORDER BY 1 - (embedding <=> $1) DESC`, reading "highest similarity first". It returned correct rows, but it can never use a vector index, so every query scanned the whole table.
production.solution: Order by the raw operator, ascending, with a LIMIT. Because the vectors are unit length, inner product gives the same order as cosine and skips the normalisation work. Compute the similarity only in the select list.
production.outcome: Rankings were unchanged (the "Normalised: same order" preset shows why). The query shape is now index-friendly, which [HNSW indexes](/e1/hnsw) turn into a speed-up.

pitfalls.title: Sorting by similarity instead of distance
pitfalls.symptom: An HNSW index exists but `EXPLAIN` shows `Seq Scan` + `Sort`.
pitfalls.cause: Indexes serve only `ORDER BY column <op> constant` **ascending** with a `LIMIT`. `1 - (a <=> b) DESC` is a different expression.
pitfalls.fix: Order by the operator itself and compute similarity in the select list.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT id, 1 - (embedding <=> $1) AS similarity FROM items ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 10;

pitfalls.title: Reading <#> as a similarity
pitfalls.symptom: The "best" match has the most negative score, and code that keeps scores above a threshold keeps the worst rows.
pitfalls.cause: `<#>` returns the **negative** inner product, because index scans only run in ascending order.
pitfalls.fix: Multiply by −1 for the real inner product, or call `inner_product(a, b)`.

pitfalls.title: Zero vectors in a cosine search
pitfalls.symptom: Some rows come back with distance `NaN`, sorted after every real distance.
pitfalls.cause: A vector of all zeros has no direction. Failed embedding calls often store one.
pitfalls.fix: Reject them at insert time with a check constraint.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER TABLE items ADD CONSTRAINT nonzero CHECK (vector_norm(embedding) > 0);

pointers: `<->` L2, `<#>` **negative** inner product, `<=>` cosine distance (0 to 2), `<+>` L1, `<~>` Hamming and `<%>` Jaccard on `bit`.
Similarity: `1 - (a <=> b)` for cosine, `(a <#> b) * -1` for inner product.
Unit-length vectors rank identically under L2, cosine and inner product; prefer `<#>` for them.
Exact search = Seq Scan + top-N heapsort: perfect recall, cost linear in rows × dimensions.
Use the distance your embedding model was trained for; the model card says which.

lessons.title: HNSW indexes
tldr: An **HNSW** index is a layered proximity graph: a search drops in at a sparse top layer, walks greedily toward the query, and finishes with a beam search of width `hnsw.ef_search` on the bottom layer.
It visits a small fraction of the rows, so k-NN queries get much faster in exchange for **approximate** results whose recall you tune with `m`, `ef_construction` and `ef_search`.

visualizer.title: Search a real HNSW graph, layer by layer
visualizer.caption: Step through one query from the entry point down to layer 0. Then drag **ef_search** below **LIMIT** and watch the result count drop. The second tab shows which query shapes can use the index at all.

playground.setup:
SELECT setseed(0.42);
-- 40 topic centres in 32 dimensions
CREATE TABLE topics AS
  SELECT t AS topic, array_agg(random() * 2 - 1 ORDER BY j)::real[] AS center
  FROM generate_series(0, 39) t, generate_series(1, 32) j
  GROUP BY t;
-- 10 000 items: each one is its topic centre plus noise
CREATE TABLE items (

  category  int NOT NULL,

);
INSERT INTO items
  SELECT i, t.topic, t.topic % 4, floor(random() * 10)::int,
         array_agg(t.center[j] + random() - 0.5 ORDER BY j)::vector(32)
  FROM generate_series(1, 10000) i
  JOIN topics t ON t.topic = i % 40
  CROSS JOIN generate_series(1, 32) j
  GROUP BY i, t.topic;
-- 20 query vectors, drawn the same way
CREATE TABLE queries AS
  SELECT q AS qid, t.topic, array_agg(t.center[j] + random() - 0.5 ORDER BY j)::vector(32) AS v
  FROM generate_series(1, 20) q
  JOIN topics t ON t.topic = (q * 7) % 40
  CROSS JOIN generate_series(1, 32) j
  GROUP BY q, t.topic;
-- exact top-10 for every query, computed before any vector index exists
CREATE TABLE truth AS
  SELECT q.qid, n.id
  FROM queries q, LATERAL (SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> q.v LIMIT 10) n;
-- recall@10 of whatever plan the planner picks right now
CREATE VIEW recall AS
  SELECT round(avg(hit) / 10.0, 3) AS recall_at_10, round(avg(n), 1) AS avg_rows
  FROM queries q, LATERAL (
    SELECT count(*) AS n,
           count(*) FILTER (WHERE a.id IN (SELECT id FROM truth t WHERE t.qid = q.qid)) AS hit
    FROM (SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> q.v LIMIT 10) a) x;
ANALYZE;

presets.label: Build the index
presets.note: The build takes a second or two here (m = 16, ef_construction = 64). The plan is now an **Index Scan … Order By**, under a millisecond, versus about 6 ms for the exact scan. The index is larger than the table: it stores every vector plus its links.

presets.label: Recall vs ef_search
presets.note: The `recall` view runs 20 queries with `LIMIT 10` and compares each with the exact answers stored in `truth`. At ef_search 5 you get only 5 rows, so recall is at most 0.5. At 10 it is about 0.98 and from 20 up it reaches 1.0 on this clustered data. The graph is built with random levels, so the third decimal varies between builds.

presets.label: ef_search caps LIMIT
presets.note: `LIMIT 100` returns only **40 rows** at the default ef_search of 40, with no error or warning. `SET LOCAL` inside a transaction raises it for one query: now all 100 rows arrive.

presets.label: A thinner graph: m = 4
presets.note: Fewer links and a narrow build beam make a smaller, faster-to-build index, but recall drops to about 0.4–0.5 at ef_search 10 and stays near 0.6 even at 100: a larger ef_search cannot fix it. The links are fixed at build time; ef_search only widens the walk over them.

presets.label: When the index is NOT used
presets.note: Five shapes, five sequential scans: DESC, an expression around the operator, no LIMIT, the wrong operator for `vector_l2_ops`, and a distance predicate in WHERE.

presets.label: Zero vectors and NULLs
presets.note: Through the cosine index only rows 2 and 4 come back: the zero vector cannot be normalised and NULLs are not indexed. The sequential scan returns all four, with NaN and NULL last.

production.title: A RAG pipeline that silently got 40 chunks
production.context: A question-answering service retrieves the 50 nearest document chunks with `ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 50`, then re-ranks them with a cross-encoder. It ran on exact search until an HNSW index was added.
production.problem: After the index went in, answer quality dipped. The retrieval step was returning **40 rows**, never 50: the default `hnsw.ef_search` of 40 caps how many rows one HNSW scan can produce, and the re-ranker never saw chunks 41–50.
production.solution: Set ef_search above the LIMIT for this query only, and measure recall against exact search on a sample of real questions.
production.outcome: Every request now gets 50 candidates. On the playground data the same fix takes `LIMIT 100` from 40 rows to 100, and recall@10 is about 0.98 at ef_search 10 versus 0.5 at ef_search 5.

pitfalls.title: LIMIT larger than ef_search
pitfalls.symptom: Queries return fewer rows than their LIMIT, with no error.
pitfalls.cause: An HNSW scan returns at most `hnsw.ef_search` rows (default 40), fewer if some are dead tuples or filtered out.
pitfalls.fix: Keep ef_search ≥ LIMIT, per query with `SET LOCAL`, or enable iterative scans ([Filtering and hybrid search](/e1/filtering-and-hybrid)).
pitfalls.sql: SET LOCAL hnsw.ef_search = 200;

pitfalls.title: One index, several distance functions
pitfalls.symptom: Cosine queries scan the whole table although an HNSW index exists.
pitfalls.cause: There is no default operator class. An index built with `vector_l2_ops` only serves `<->`.
pitfalls.fix: Create the index with the opclass that matches the operator the application uses (`vector_cosine_ops` for `<=>`, `vector_ip_ops` for `<#>`).

pitfalls.title: Slow builds on big tables
pitfalls.symptom: An HNSW build runs for hours and logs `NOTICE: hnsw graph no longer fits into maintenance_work_mem after … tuples`.
pitfalls.cause: Once the graph outgrows `maintenance_work_mem` the build continues on disk, which is much slower. The finished index is an ordinary on-disk index of 8 kB pages, not an in-memory structure: memory decides how fast it builds, and caching decides how fast it is queried.
pitfalls.fix: Load the data first, raise `maintenance_work_mem` for the session (keep it well below RAM), add parallel workers, and build with `CONCURRENTLY` in production. Watch progress from a second session.

pitfalls.title: Turning m and ef_construction down to save time
pitfalls.symptom: Recall is poor and raising ef_search barely helps.
pitfalls.cause: Links are fixed at build time. A sparse graph (small `m`) or a narrow build beam (small `ef_construction`) leaves good neighbours unreachable.
pitfalls.fix: Start from the defaults (m = 16, ef_construction = 64, which must be at least 2·m) and raise them only when measured recall is too low.

pointers: Layers: every row on layer 0; each node is promoted with probability 1/m; one entry point on top.
Build: `WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64)`; no training step, so it can be created on an empty table.
Query: `hnsw.ef_search` (default 40, 1–1000) is the beam width and also the **maximum rows returned**.
Index use needs `ORDER BY embedding <op> $1 LIMIT n`, ascending, with the matching opclass.
Measure recall against exact search with `SET LOCAL enable_indexscan = off`.

lessons.title: IVFFlat indexes
tldr: An **IVFFlat** index runs k-means on the existing rows to find `lists` centroids, files every vector under its nearest centroid, and at query time scans only the `ivfflat.probes` closest lists.
It builds far faster and smaller than HNSW, but its centroids are frozen at build time, so it needs data before it is created and periodic rebuilds as the data drifts.

visualizer.title: Voronoi cells, probes and recall
visualizer.caption: Click to move the query and raise **probes** one list at a time: recall climbs as more cells are scanned. Then switch to **Built too early** to see what stale centroids do.

presets.label: Build with 100 lists
presets.note: The build is roughly five to ten times faster than HNSW on the same table, and the index is about the size of the table. With the default `ivfflat.probes = 1` the scan touches about 15 buffers instead of the 224 of a sequential scan.

presets.label: Recall vs probes
presets.note: probes = 1 misses neighbours that sit in an adjacent list (recall 0.6–0.7; k-means starts from a random sample, so it varies by build). Three probes bring it near 0.98. A starting point is **probes ≈ √lists** (10 here).

presets.label: Cost of more probes
presets.note: Each probe reads one more list. Compare `Buffers: shared hit` between the two plans: about 15 at probes = 1 and about 40 at probes = 10. Every probed list adds its rows to the distance computations, so the work grows with probes.

presets.label: probes = lists
presets.note: Probing every list would read the whole index, so the planner prefers an exact **Seq Scan + Sort**. At 50 probes it still uses the index.

presets.label: Built too early
presets.note: Centroids trained on 4 topics cannot separate the other 36, so recall drops to about 0.6–0.7. `REINDEX` re-runs k-means on all rows and recall returns to about 0.99–1.0 (k-means starts from a random sample, so the exact figures vary by build).

presets.label: Empty table warning
presets.note: Watch the messages: `ivfflat index created with little data`. It still builds, but its lists are meaningless. IVFFlat also rejects L1 and strict-order iterative scans. IVFFlat has 7 operator classes (L2, inner product, cosine for vector and halfvec, Hamming for bit); HNSW has 14.

production.title: An IVFFlat index created by the first migration
production.context: A product-search team added `CREATE INDEX … USING ivfflat … WITH (lists = 1000)` to the migration that created the table, before any data was loaded. A year later the table held 3 million products.
production.problem: Recall was poor and some queries returned fewer rows than their LIMIT. The centroids had been computed from an empty table, so millions of rows were filed under arbitrary lists, and a single probe often hit a nearly empty one.
