production.solution: Drop the index from the migration. Build it after the bulk load, size it with the rule of thumb (rows/1000 up to 1M rows, √rows above), set probes to about √lists, and schedule a rebuild when the data distribution changes.
production.outcome: The playground reproduces the effect at small scale: an index trained on 4 of 40 topics gives recall@10 of about 0.6–0.7; after `REINDEX` it is about 0.99–1.0.

pitfalls.title: Creating the index on an empty table
pitfalls.symptom: `NOTICE: ivfflat index created with little data` at migration time, poor recall later.
pitfalls.cause: IVFFlat has a training step: centroids come from rows that exist at build time.
pitfalls.fix: Load data first, then build. If the table starts empty, use HNSW (no training step) or rebuild IVFFlat once data exists.

pitfalls.title: probes left at 1
pitfalls.symptom: Recall is noticeably worse than with exact search, especially for queries near cluster borders.
pitfalls.cause: The default `ivfflat.probes` is 1: only the single nearest list is scanned.
pitfalls.fix: Start at probes ≈ √lists and measure. Set it per query with `SET LOCAL`, or per database.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER DATABASE app SET ivfflat.probes = 10;

pitfalls.title: Expecting IVFFlat to track new data
pitfalls.symptom: Recall slowly degrades as the catalogue grows or shifts to new topics.
pitfalls.cause: Centroids never move after the build. New rows are filed into the nearest existing list, even if it is a poor fit.
pitfalls.fix: Rebuild after big changes with `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, or prefer HNSW, whose graph is updated on every insert.

pointers: Build: k-means picks `lists` centroids (default 100); each row goes to its nearest list.
Sizing: lists ≈ rows/1000 up to 1M rows, √rows above; probes ≈ √lists to start.
`ivfflat.probes` (default 1) trades speed for recall; probes = lists makes the planner fall back to exact search.
Versus HNSW: faster, smaller build; worse speed/recall trade-off; needs data first; goes stale.
IVFFlat supports L2, inner product, cosine and Hamming, for `vector`, `halfvec` and `bit` (no `sparsevec`, no L1).

lessons.title: Filtering and hybrid search
tldr: An approximate index applies `WHERE` filters **after** it finds candidates, so a filtered k-NN query can return fewer rows than its LIMIT unless you use iterative scans, a B-tree path, partial indexes or partitions.
**Hybrid search** runs a vector search and a full-text search side by side and merges them with **Reciprocal Rank Fusion**, so exact keywords and fuzzy meaning both count.

visualizer.title: Where filtered rows go, and how two rankings merge
visualizer.caption: Pick a filter and an `ef_search`, then turn iterative scans on: watch rows returned and the measured recall. The second tab merges a semantic and a keyword ranking; drag **k** to see how RRF weighs ranks.

playground.setup:
SELECT setseed(0.42);
-- 40 topic centres in 32 dimensions
CREATE TABLE topics AS
  SELECT t AS topic, array_agg(random() * 2 - 1 ORDER BY j)::real[] AS center
  FROM generate_series(0, 39) t, generate_series(1, 32) j
  GROUP BY t;
-- 10 000 items: each one is its topic centre plus noise
CREATE TABLE items (
  id        int PRIMARY KEY,
  topic     int NOT NULL,
  region    int NOT NULL,
  category  int NOT NULL,
  embedding vector(32)
);
INSERT INTO items
  SELECT i, t.topic, t.topic % 4, floor(random() * 10)::int,
         array_agg(t.center[j] + random() - 0.5 ORDER BY j)::vector(32)
  FROM generate_series(1, 10000) i
  JOIN topics t ON t.topic = i % 40
  CROSS JOIN generate_series(1, 32) j
  GROUP BY i, t.topic;
-- 20 query vectors, drawn the same way
CREATE TABLE queries AS
  SELECT q AS qid, t.topic, array_agg(t.center[j] + random() - 0.5 ORDER BY j)::vector(32) AS v
  FROM generate_series(1, 20) q
  JOIN topics t ON t.topic = (q * 7) % 40
  CROSS JOIN generate_series(1, 32) j
  GROUP BY q, t.topic;
-- exact top-10 for every query, computed before any vector index exists
CREATE TABLE truth AS
  SELECT q.qid, n.id
  FROM queries q, LATERAL (SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> q.v LIMIT 10) n;
-- recall@10 of whatever plan the planner picks right now
CREATE VIEW recall AS
  SELECT round(avg(hit) / 10.0, 3) AS recall_at_10, round(avg(n), 1) AS avg_rows
  FROM queries q, LATERAL (
    SELECT count(*) AS n,
           count(*) FILTER (WHERE a.id IN (SELECT id FROM truth t WHERE t.qid = q.qid)) AS hit
    FROM (SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> q.v LIMIT 10) a) x;
ANALYZE;
-- exact answers for two filtered searches (computed before any vector index exists)

CREATE TABLE truth_cat AS
  SELECT q.qid, n.id
  FROM queries q, LATERAL (SELECT id FROM items WHERE category = 3 ORDER BY embedding <-> q.v LIMIT 10) n;
CREATE VIEW recall_cat AS
  SELECT round(avg(hit) / 10.0, 3) AS recall_at_10, round(avg(n), 1) AS avg_rows
  FROM queries q, LATERAL (
    SELECT count(*) AS n,
           count(*) FILTER (WHERE a.id IN (SELECT id FROM truth_cat t WHERE t.qid = q.qid)) AS hit
    FROM (SELECT id FROM items WHERE category = 3 ORDER BY embedding <-> q.v LIMIT 10) a) x;

CREATE TABLE truth_region AS
  SELECT q.qid, n.id
  FROM queries q, LATERAL (SELECT id FROM items WHERE region = (q.topic + 2) % 4 ORDER BY embedding <-> q.v LIMIT 10) n;
CREATE VIEW recall_region AS
  SELECT round(avg(hit) / 10.0, 3) AS recall_at_10, round(avg(n), 1) AS avg_rows
  FROM queries q, LATERAL (
    SELECT count(*) AS n,
           count(*) FILTER (WHERE a.id IN (SELECT id FROM truth_region t WHERE t.qid = q.qid)) AS hit
    FROM (SELECT id FROM items WHERE region = (q.topic + 2) % 4 ORDER BY embedding <-> q.v LIMIT 10) a) x;
-- a tiny help-centre corpus for hybrid search (4-d "meaning" vectors: account, security, billing, network)
CREATE TABLE articles (
  id int PRIMARY KEY, title text NOT NULL, body text NOT NULL, embedding vector(4) NOT NULL,
  tsv tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (setweight(to_tsvector('english', title), 'A') || setweight(to_tsvector('english', body), 'B')) STORED
);
INSERT INTO articles VALUES
 (1, 'Reset your password', 'Open the reset link we email you and choose a new password.', '[0.92,0.30,0.02,0.05]'),
 (2, 'Recover a locked account', 'After five failed sign-ins we lock the account for an hour.', '[0.88,0.42,0.05,0.02]'),
 (3, 'Password rules', 'A strong password has at least twelve characters.', '[0.55,0.80,0.02,0.03]'),
 (4, 'Turn on two-factor sign-in', 'Add an authenticator app as a second step.', '[0.60,0.78,0.05,0.04]'),
 (5, 'Reset the router', 'Hold the button for ten seconds to restore factory settings.', '[0.05,0.10,0.02,0.99]'),
 (6, 'Update your card', 'Change the card we charge for your invoice.', '[0.10,0.05,0.98,0.05]'),
 (7, 'Forgot your username', 'We email your username and a link to reset your password.', '[0.90,0.35,0.03,0.02]'),
 (8, 'Cannot log in after changing email', 'Sign in with the new address; the old one stops working.', '[0.85,0.20,0.10,0.05]'),
 (9, 'Change your billing date', 'Support can reset the day your billing cycle starts.', '[0.05,0.05,0.95,0.20]'),
 (10,'Wi-Fi keeps dropping', 'Move the router away from walls and microwaves.', '[0.05,0.05,0.02,0.99]');
CREATE INDEX ON articles USING gin (tsv);

presets.label: Filter after the index
presets.note: Look at the Index Scan node: `Filter: (category = 3)` and `Rows Removed by Filter: 39`. The scan produced its 40 candidates (ef_search) and only 1 matched, so `rows=1` for a LIMIT 10 query.

presets.label: Lost rows, lost recall
presets.note: With a 10% filter, 40 candidates leave about **4 rows** on average (recall about 0.37). A larger ef_search helps, but only because it reads more candidates for every query.

presets.label: Iterative scans
presets.note: The index now keeps scanning until 10 rows pass: `rows=10` with well over 100 rows removed by the filter. Recall returns to 1.0, at the default ef_search of 40.

presets.label: A filter against the clusters
presets.note: Each query asks for rows from a region its own topic is not in. Off: **0 rows**. Iterative scans return 10 rows, but recall is only about 0.8 (strict) and just under 0.9 (relaxed), varying a little between builds, because the walk starts in the wrong place.

presets.label: Re-sort relaxed results
presets.note: Relaxed order can be slightly out of order. Materialise the scan, then sort the 10 rows again. The `+ 0` stops PostgreSQL 17+ from assuming the CTE is already sorted.

presets.label: Selective filters: go exact
presets.note: For a handful of matching rows the planner picks the B-tree (**Bitmap Index Scan**) and sorts them exactly: perfect recall, tiny cost. The partial HNSW index holds only category 3, so every candidate passes the filter and recall is about 1.0 without iterative scans.

presets.label: Hybrid search (RRF)
presets.sql:
WITH semantic AS (
  SELECT id, rank() OVER (ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.95,0.30,0.05,0.03]') AS rank
  FROM articles ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.95,0.30,0.05,0.03]' LIMIT 5
), keyword AS (
  SELECT id, rank() OVER (ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(tsv, q) DESC) AS rank
  FROM articles, websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'reset or password') q
  WHERE tsv @@ q ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(tsv, q) DESC LIMIT 5
)
SELECT coalesce(s.id, k.id) AS id, a.title,
       s.rank AS semantic_rank, k.rank AS keyword_rank,
       round(coalesce(1.0 / (60 + s.rank), 0) + coalesce(1.0 / (60 + k.rank), 0), 5) AS rrf_score
FROM semantic s
FULL OUTER JOIN keyword k ON s.id = k.id
JOIN articles a ON a.id = coalesce(s.id, k.id)
ORDER BY rrf_score DESC, id;
presets.note: Rows found by both searches lead (1 and 7). "Recover a locked account" comes only from the vector side, "Reset the router" only from keywords. The FULL OUTER JOIN keeps both; `coalesce(…, 0)` scores a missing side as zero.

presets.label: Sparse vectors for exact codes
presets.note: The parser turns `RTX-4090` into `rtx` and `-4090`, so the query "RTX 4090" misses it, while stemming makes "organization" match "organic". In the sparse vector the code is its own weighted dimension: the 4090 card scores **4.55**, the 3090 only **0.75** from the shared "gaming" term. Note the scales: an unbounded dot product next to a cosine distance between 0 and 2. `sparsevec` supports L2, inner product, cosine and L1 with HNSW only; Jaccard `<%>` exists only for `bit`.

production.title: Per-tenant search in a shared embeddings table
production.context: A B2B knowledge-base product keeps every customer's document chunks in one table with a `tenant_id` column and one HNSW index. Each query filters on the tenant.
production.problem: Large tenants were fine, but small tenants (under 1% of rows) got 0–3 results for `LIMIT 10`: the 40 nearest candidates almost never belonged to them. Their vectors also shared one graph with everyone else's.
production.solution: Turn on iterative scans as a safety net, and give the index a per-tenant layout: list partitions for the big tenants, and a B-tree on `tenant_id` so the planner can take the exact path for tiny ones.
production.outcome: Every tenant gets full result lists. In the playground the same mechanisms take a 10% filter from about 4 rows (recall 0.37) to 10 rows (recall 1.0), and a 0.1% filter is answered exactly from the B-tree.

pitfalls.title: Filtered vector query returns too few rows
pitfalls.symptom: `WHERE tenant_id = $1 ORDER BY embedding <=> $2 LIMIT 10` returns 2 rows although the tenant has thousands.
pitfalls.cause: The filter runs after the index scan. With ef_search 40 and a 10% filter, about 4 rows survive on average.
pitfalls.fix: Enable iterative scans (0.8.0+), or raise ef_search for that query.
pitfalls.sql: SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order;

pitfalls.title: Iterative scan over a very selective filter
pitfalls.symptom: A filtered query takes many milliseconds and reads tens of thousands of buffers, or returns 0 rows.
pitfalls.cause: The scan walks the graph until `hnsw.max_scan_tuples` (20 000) is hit, filtering almost everything out.
pitfalls.fix: Add a B-tree on the filter column so the planner can choose an exact scan of the few matching rows, or use a partial index or partition for that value.

pitfalls.title: Adding vector distance and text rank directly
pitfalls.symptom: Hybrid results are dominated by one side, and changing the text query wording flips the whole ranking.
pitfalls.cause: Cosine distance and `ts_rank_cd` have unrelated scales. So do a sparse dot product and a dense cosine distance: both are plain floats, but one is unbounded and the other lies between 0 and 2.
pitfalls.fix: Fuse by rank, not by score: Reciprocal Rank Fusion with k = 60, or re-rank the union with a cross-encoder. To trust one list more, multiply its `1/(k + rank)` term by a weight.

pitfalls.title: Ordering by the rank instead of the distance
pitfalls.symptom: The semantic half of a hybrid query takes milliseconds per call and `EXPLAIN` shows `Seq Scan` → `Sort` → `WindowAgg` over every row.
pitfalls.cause: With `ORDER BY rank LIMIT 20`, where `rank` is the `rank() OVER (…)` output, the window must number all rows before the sort can pick 20. On 10 000 rows that is 10 000 rows through the window instead of 20.
pitfalls.fix: Order the branch by the distance operator itself (`ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 20`), or take the top 20 in a subquery and number them outside. Then the index scan feeds the window and stops after 20 rows.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY d) AS rank
FROM (SELECT id, embedding <=> $1 AS d FROM documents ORDER BY d LIMIT 20) top;

pointers: Approximate indexes filter **after** the scan; with HNSW the result count is at most ef_search before filtering.
`hnsw.iterative_scan = strict_order | relaxed_order` (HNSW) and `ivfflat.iterative_scan = relaxed_order` keep scanning until LIMIT is met.
Selective filter: B-tree exact path. Few hot values: partial index. Many tenants: `PARTITION BY LIST`.
Re-sort relaxed results with a `MATERIALIZED` CTE and `ORDER BY distance + 0`.

RRF: score = Σ 1/(60 + rank) across lists, joined with `FULL OUTER JOIN`. For exact codes, a learned **sparsevec** gives each term its own weighted dimension, scored with `<#>` (HNSW indexes at most 1000 non-zeros per row).

lessons.title: pgvector in production
tldr: In production the questions are memory, build time and recall: keep full vectors in the table, index a smaller form (`halfvec` or binary bits), and re-rank with exact distances.
Sizing `maintenance_work_mem` for builds, checking recall against exact search, and knowing when a dedicated vector database is worth it keep a pgvector deployment fast as it grows.

visualizer.title: Smaller indexes, measured
visualizer.caption: Step through the four index strategies and compare bytes, index size and recall, all measured on the playground table. For **bit + re-rank**, change the candidate count. The second tab sizes a real deployment.

presets.label: Bytes per row
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_column_size(embedding)                  AS vector_bytes,
       pg_column_size(embedding::halfvec(256))         AS halfvec_bytes,
       pg_column_size(binary_quantize(embedding))      AS bit_bytes,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_table_size('docs'))           AS table_size
FROM docs LIMIT 1;
presets.note: A 256-d vector takes 4·256 + 8 = **1032 bytes**, half precision 520, and the bit form 40. The vectors are small enough to stay inline in the heap.

presets.label: Full-precision HNSW
presets.note: The baseline: an index somewhat larger than the table, with recall 1.0 on this data.

presets.label: Half-precision index
presets.note: The table keeps full precision; only the index is float16. The query must repeat the **same expression** (`::halfvec(256)`) or the index is ignored. Recall is unchanged at about 60% of the index size. (Building the float16 index is slower than the full-precision one in this in-browser database; build speed on a native server can differ, so measure on your own hardware.)

presets.label: Binary quantization
presets.note: A quarter of the size, but sign bits alone are a blunt instrument: recall is below 0.5.

presets.label: Re-rank the bits
presets.sql:
SET hnsw.ef_search = 40;
SELECT 20 AS candidates, * FROM (SELECT round(avg(hit) / 10.0, 3) AS recall_at_10
FROM queries q, LATERAL (
  SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE a.id IN (SELECT id FROM truth t WHERE t.qid = q.qid)) AS hit
  FROM (SELECT id FROM (
    SELECT id, embedding FROM docs
    ORDER BY binary_quantize(embedding)::bit(256) <~> binary_quantize(q.v) LIMIT 20) c
  ORDER BY embedding <-> q.v LIMIT 10) a) x) r;
SET hnsw.ef_search = 40;
SELECT 40 AS candidates, * FROM (SELECT round(avg(hit) / 10.0, 3) AS recall_at_10
FROM queries q, LATERAL (
  SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE a.id IN (SELECT id FROM truth t WHERE t.qid = q.qid)) AS hit
  FROM (SELECT id FROM (
    SELECT id, embedding FROM docs
    ORDER BY binary_quantize(embedding)::bit(256) <~> binary_quantize(q.v) LIMIT 40) c
  ORDER BY embedding <-> q.v LIMIT 10) a) x) r;
SET hnsw.ef_search = 100;
SELECT 100 AS candidates, * FROM (SELECT round(avg(hit) / 10.0, 3) AS recall_at_10
FROM queries q, LATERAL (
  SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE a.id IN (SELECT id FROM truth t WHERE t.qid = q.qid)) AS hit
  FROM (SELECT id FROM (
    SELECT id, embedding FROM docs
    ORDER BY binary_quantize(embedding)::bit(256) <~> binary_quantize(q.v) LIMIT 100) c
  ORDER BY embedding <-> q.v LIMIT 10) a) x) r;
SET hnsw.ef_search = 200;
SELECT 200 AS candidates, * FROM (SELECT round(avg(hit) / 10.0, 3) AS recall_at_10
FROM queries q, LATERAL (
  SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE a.id IN (SELECT id FROM truth t WHERE t.qid = q.qid)) AS hit
  FROM (SELECT id FROM (
    SELECT id, embedding FROM docs
    ORDER BY binary_quantize(embedding)::bit(256) <~> binary_quantize(q.v) LIMIT 200) c
  ORDER BY embedding <-> q.v LIMIT 10) a) x) r;
RESET hnsw.ef_search;
presets.note: Fetch N candidates by Hamming distance, then sort them by exact `<->` on the full vectors. 100 candidates recover about 0.93, 200 about 0.96. ef_search is raised to match each inner LIMIT.

presets.label: Build memory
presets.note: Watch the messages: `hnsw graph no longer fits into maintenance_work_mem after … tuples`, and compare the run time with the "Full-precision HNSW" preset: roughly three to four times slower. This in-browser server has no parallel workers (0); a real server defaults to 2.

presets.label: Deletes and REINDEX
presets.note: VACUUM repairs the graph and marks space reusable but does not shrink the file. `REINDEX … CONCURRENTLY` rebuilds it at about half the size without blocking writes.

production.title: Fitting 20 million 1536-d chunks on one server
production.context: A document-search product stores 20 M chunks with 1536-d embeddings on a 128 GB server, and wants p95 latency under 50 ms with recall@10 above 0.95.
production.problem: Raw vectors are 20 M × 6152 B ≈ 123 GB. A full-precision HNSW index is larger again, so neither fits in RAM, builds spill out of `maintenance_work_mem`, and queries hit disk.
production.solution: Keep `vector(1536)` in the table for exact re-ranking, and index binary-quantized bits (20 M × 200 B ≈ 4 GB of vectors in the index). Fetch 200 candidates by Hamming distance and re-rank them exactly. Verify recall on a sample of real queries before switching.
production.outcome: The index shrinks by roughly 30× in vector bytes (200 B instead of 6152 B per row) and fits in memory. The playground shows the recall trade on 256-d data: bits alone about 0.44, with 200-candidate re-ranking about 0.96. High-dimensional text embeddings usually quantize well; low-dimensional ones do not, so measure first.

pitfalls.title: Binary quantization without re-ranking
pitfalls.symptom: Results after moving to a `bit` index are noticeably worse.
pitfalls.cause: Sign bits keep only the rough direction of each dimension. Hamming distance cannot separate close candidates.
pitfalls.fix: Always re-rank a larger candidate set by the full vectors, and set `hnsw.ef_search` at least as large as that candidate LIMIT.

pitfalls.title: Expression index never used
pitfalls.symptom: A `halfvec` or `binary_quantize` index exists, but queries still scan the table.
pitfalls.cause: The ORDER BY must contain exactly the indexed expression, including the cast and its dimension.
pitfalls.fix: Write the query with the same expression as the index.
pitfalls.sql: ORDER BY embedding::halfvec(1536) <=> $1::halfvec(1536) LIMIT 10

pitfalls.title: HNSW vacuum taking hours
pitfalls.symptom: Autovacuum on a vector table runs for a very long time after a big delete.
pitfalls.cause: Vacuuming HNSW must repair the graph around every deleted node.
pitfalls.fix: Rebuild first, then vacuum. Run pgvector 0.8.4 or later, which fixed HNSW vacuum bugs.
pitfalls.sql:
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY items_embedding_idx;
VACUUM items;

pitfalls.title: Never measuring recall
pitfalls.symptom: Search quality slowly drifts and nobody notices until users do.
pitfalls.cause: Approximate indexes fail silently: they always return plausible rows.
pitfalls.fix: Periodically replay a sample of real queries with `SET LOCAL enable_indexscan = off` and compare the top-k overlap with the indexed results.

pointers: Store `vector`, index `halfvec` (same recall, about half the size) or bits (with re-ranking).
Re-rank: inner `LIMIT N` by `<~>` on bits, outer `ORDER BY` exact distance; ef_search ≥ N.
Builds: load first, `maintenance_work_mem` big enough for the graph, `max_parallel_maintenance_workers`, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.
Maintenance: `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY` then `VACUUM` after large deletes; stay on 0.8.4+.

Stay in PostgreSQL while vectors share rows, filters, transactions and backups with the rest of your data; consider a dedicated engine only when one node can no longer hold the index in memory and sharding is not an option.

lessons.title: Time-series data on PostgreSQL
tldr: **Time-series data** is a stream of timestamped measurements that arrive roughly in time order, are rarely changed, are read by time range and are deleted when they age out.

Plain PostgreSQL already handles it with **BRIN indexes**, **range partitioning** and `date_bin`, and **TimescaleDB** packages those ideas as an extension that automates partitioning, rollups, compression and retention.

visualizer.title: Why time order makes a 24 kB index work
visualizer.caption: Drag the query window across 200,000 rows and watch which BRIN block ranges match. Switch to **Shuffled** to see the same index read the whole table, then open **What TimescaleDB adds** for the edition split.

presets.label: Physical order
presets.note: `correlation` = **1** for `time`: physical order matches time order exactly, because rows were appended as they arrived. `sensor_id` is near 0.25, so BRIN would be useless on it.

presets.label: BRIN: one hour
presets.note: `Heap Blocks: lossy=32` is one block range. BRIN knows only min and max per range, so it returns whole pages and **Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 1424** are filtered out.

presets.label: B-tree vs BRIN size
presets.note: The B-tree has one entry per row (**4408 kB**). BRIN has one summary per 32 pages (**24 kB**, three pages). The B-tree is dropped again so later presets use BRIN.

presets.label: Bucket by hour
presets.sql:
SELECT date_bin('1 hour', time, timestamptz '2000-01-03') AS hour,
       sensor_id, round(avg(temperature)::numeric, 2) AS avg_temp, count(*) AS n
FROM readings
WHERE time < '2026-01-01 03:00'
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2;
presets.note: `date_bin` is the native `time_bucket`: it maps each timestamp to the start of its bucket. Each sensor reports 900 times per hour. The origin `2000-01-03` matches the TimescaleDB default.

presets.label: Shuffled: BRIN breaks
presets.note: Same rows, random physical order: correlation is near **0**. Every range matches, so the plan reads **lossy=1280** blocks (the whole table) and rechecks away 196,400 rows.

presets.label: Latest reading needs a B-tree
presets.note: BRIN can filter but cannot return rows in order, so "latest row" is a full scan plus a top-N sort. A B-tree on `time DESC` (the index TimescaleDB creates by default) turns it into a one-row index scan.

production.title: Keeping 30 days of 1 Hz sensor data in plain PostgreSQL
production.context: An IoT platform stores one reading per second from 5,000 sensors in a single table: **432 million rows a day**. Dashboards query the last few hours, and data older than 30 days is deleted every night.
production.problem: The B-tree on `time` grew with every row and no longer fit in memory. The nightly `DELETE` rewrote nothing on disk: it left millions of dead tuples, autovacuum ran all day, and the table never shrank.
production.solution: Partition by day, index time ranges with **BRIN** (rows arrive in time order) and keep a B-tree only for "latest per sensor". Retention becomes `DROP TABLE` of a whole partition. A hypertable does the same with less code: chunks are created on demand and `drop_chunks` handles retention. Both of those are in the Apache 2 edition.
production.outcome: On 200,000 time-ordered rows, BRIN is **24 kB against 4408 kB** for the B-tree, about 180 times smaller, and still narrows a one-hour query to one 32-page range. Dropping a daily partition removes its files outright, so there are no dead tuples and no vacuum debt.

pitfalls.title: BRIN on data that is not physically ordered
pitfalls.symptom: A BRIN index exists, yet `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows `Heap Blocks: lossy=` equal to nearly the whole table.
pitfalls.cause: BRIN stores min/max per block range. Backfills, updates and shuffled loads mix old and new timestamps into the same pages, so every range overlaps every query.
pitfalls.fix: Check `pg_stats.correlation` for the column (near 1 or -1 is good). Use BRIN only on append-ordered columns, partition so each partition stays ordered, or use a B-tree.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT attname, correlation FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename = 'readings';

pitfalls.title: Retention with DELETE
pitfalls.symptom: Nightly deletes create WAL spikes and replication lag, autovacuum never finishes, and disk usage stays flat.
pitfalls.cause: `DELETE` marks every row dead and logs every change. The space is reused only after VACUUM, and the file never gets smaller (see [VACUUM](/m7/vacuum)).
pitfalls.fix: Partition by time and drop whole partitions. With TimescaleDB, use `drop_chunks` (Apache 2 edition) or `add_retention_policy` (Community edition).
pitfalls.sql: SELECT drop_chunks('readings', older_than => INTERVAL '30 days');

pitfalls.title: Expecting the full feature set on a managed service
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: functionality not supported under the current "apache" license` when creating a continuous aggregate or enabling compression.
pitfalls.cause: Services that resell PostgreSQL, Neon among them, may ship only the **Apache 2 edition**. Continuous aggregates, the columnstore, gap filling, policies and jobs are **Community edition** features under the Tiger Data License.
pitfalls.fix: Run `SHOW timescaledb.license;` before designing around a feature. Use the Community edition (self-hosted) or Tiger Cloud, or the native equivalents shown in this module.
pitfalls.sql: SHOW timescaledb.license;  -- apache | timescale

pitfalls.title: Monthly buckets with date_bin
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: timestamps cannot be binned into intervals containing months or years`.
pitfalls.cause: `date_bin` only accepts fixed-length strides. Months and years vary in length.
pitfalls.fix: Use `date_trunc('month', time)` natively, or `time_bucket('1 month', time)` with TimescaleDB, which supports month and year widths.

pointers: Time-series = **append-mostly**, read by **time range**, deleted by **age**. Every tool in this module exploits one of those three facts.
**BRIN** stores min/max per block range: tiny, and only useful when physical order follows the column (`correlation` near 1). More in [BRIN indexes](/m4/brin).
Partition by time so queries **prune** to a few partitions and retention is a `DROP`, not a `DELETE`.
**TimescaleDB** is an extension loaded through `shared_preload_libraries`. Version 2.32 supports PostgreSQL 16 to 18.
**Apache 2 edition**: hypertables, `time_bucket`, `drop_chunks`. **Community edition**: continuous aggregates, columnstore, gap filling, policies and jobs. Neon offers only the Apache edition.

lessons.title: Hypertables and chunks
tldr: A **hypertable** is a table that TimescaleDB splits by time into child tables called **chunks**, creating each chunk automatically the first time a row needs it.
Chunks let queries skip every time slice outside their WHERE clause (**chunk exclusion**) and let old data leave by dropping whole chunks, without anyone managing partitions by hand.

visualizer.title: Chunks appear as time advances
visualizer.caption: Ingest data and watch chunks being created on demand, then add a late row and a row from a broken clock. Drag the query window to see chunk exclusion, and switch to **Native partitioning** to see what PostgreSQL does without the extension.

presets.label: List the chunks
presets.sql:
SELECT c.relname AS chunk,
       pg_get_expr(c.relpartbound, c.oid) AS range,
       c.reltuples::bigint AS row_count,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(c.oid)) AS size
FROM pg_inherits i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.inhrelid
WHERE i.inhparent = 'conditions'::regclass
ORDER BY 1;
presets.note: Seven daily partitions of 1440 rows and 216 kB each. This is what `show_chunks()` and `timescaledb_information.chunks` report for a hypertable.

presets.label: Exclusion at plan time
presets.note: Only `conditions_20260303` appears: the planner compared the constants with each partition's range and dropped the other six. TimescaleDB calls this **chunk exclusion**.

presets.label: Exclusion at run time
presets.note: A generic plan cannot know `$1`, so pruning happens when execution starts: **Subplans Removed: 5**, two chunks scanned with 1440 rows each. TimescaleDB's ChunkAppend node does the same for values such as `now()`.

presets.label: No automatic chunks
presets.note: Native PostgreSQL rejects the row: **no partition of relation "conditions" found for row**. After `ensure_chunk()` creates `conditions_20260308` the insert succeeds. A hypertable does that step for you, inside the INSERT.

presets.label: Unique keys need the time column
presets.sql:
SELECT try_sql('ALTER TABLE conditions ADD UNIQUE (device_id)') AS unique_on_device;
SELECT try_sql('ALTER TABLE conditions ADD UNIQUE (device_id, time)') AS unique_on_device_and_time;
presets.note: Uniqueness is enforced inside each partition, so every unique key must include the partition column. Hypertables have the same rule: `cannot create a unique index without the column "time"`.

presets.label: Space partitioning
presets.note: This mirrors `add_dimension('readings', by_hash('device_id', 2))`: each time slice becomes two chunks. A filter on both columns prunes down to one (`readings_d1_h1`). The chunk count doubles, which is why the extra dimension is discouraged.

presets.label: Latest row vs latest per device
presets.note: The first plan is an **ordered Append**: chunks are read newest first and the LIMIT stops after one row. "Latest per device" needs a Merge Append over every chunk. TimescaleDB's SkipScan (Community edition) speeds that up.

production.title: Turning a growing metrics table into a hypertable
production.context: An IoT platform writes 2 GB of new index data per day into a 64 GB database server. Every query asks for one device over a few hours or days.
production.problem: One huge table means one huge B-tree that no longer fits in memory, so inserts read cold index pages from disk. Hand-made partitions helped until a scheduled job that created them failed one weekend, and inserts stopped with "no partition found".
production.solution: Create a hypertable. Chunks are created by the INSERT itself. The interval follows the sizing rule: active chunk indexes within about 25% of memory, 16 GB / 2 GB per day → 7-day chunks. (A rough starting point before you can measure: tables taking 100 M+ rows a day often land on hours to one day, 1–10 M rows a day on about one day, quiet tables on a week or more. The memory rule decides.) Ingest in batches, with multi-row `INSERT` or `COPY`, not one statement per reading. Use the default `time DESC` index plus one per access path, and do not add a hash dimension on a single disk. All of this is in the **Apache 2 edition**. The CREATE TABLE form adds a columnstore policy by default since 2.23, which needs the Community edition.
production.outcome: Inserts touch only the newest chunk's indexes, which stay in memory, and a one-day query reads one or two chunks. With 7-day chunks a year of data is about 52 chunks, far below the 1,000-chunk warning level.

pitfalls.title: Chunks that are far too small
pitfalls.symptom: Planning time grows with history, queries over a month open thousands of chunks, and you see `out of shared memory` with a hint to increase `max_locks_per_transaction`.
pitfalls.cause: Every chunk a query touches is planned and locked. A 1-hour interval on a slow table makes 8,760 chunks a year, each one tiny and hard to compress.
pitfalls.fix: Size by the memory rule, not by query granularity. `set_chunk_time_interval` changes new chunks only, so fix history with a table-swap migration. Raise `max_locks_per_transaction` (restart needed) as a stopgap.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT set_chunk_time_interval('metrics', INTERVAL '7 days');

pitfalls.title: Unique key without the time column
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: cannot create a unique index without the column "time" (used in partitioning)`.
pitfalls.cause: Each chunk has its own indexes, so uniqueness can only be checked inside one chunk.
pitfalls.fix: Include the partition column in every PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraint, for example `(device_id, time)`. Enforce global uniqueness of other ids elsewhere.

pitfalls.title: A bad clock creates future chunks
pitfalls.symptom: `timescaledb_information.chunks` lists chunks years ahead, and "latest" queries return garbage rows.
pitfalls.cause: A device sent a timestamp far in the future, and the INSERT created a chunk for it as designed.
pitfalls.fix: Validate timestamps at ingest (for example a CHECK against `now() + interval '1 day'` in the application), and clean up with `drop_chunks(newer_than => …)`.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT drop_chunks('metrics', newer_than => now() + INTERVAL '3 months');

pitfalls.title: Space partitioning on one disk
pitfalls.symptom: After `add_dimension(…, by_hash(…))`, chunk count multiplies and planning slows, with no speed-up.
pitfalls.cause: Hash dimensions exist to spread I/O across tablespaces on separate disks. On one volume they only multiply chunks, and every unique key must now include the hash column too.
pitfalls.fix: Use time-only partitioning plus a `(device_id, time DESC)` index. On a hypertable that already has data, `add_dimension` only partitions chunks created afterwards, and existing chunks keep covering the whole hash range.

pointers: A hypertable is a parent table, and **chunks** are child tables in `_timescaledb_internal`. Insert and query the parent only.
Chunks are created **on demand** by the INSERT. Ranges are aligned on the epoch; the default `chunk_interval` is **7 days**.
Size chunks so the **indexes of active chunks fit in about 25% of memory**; more than 1,000 chunks is a warning sign.
**Chunk exclusion** = partition pruning: at plan time for constants, at run time for parameters and `now()`. The native mechanism is covered in [partitioning and pruning](/m7/partitioning).
Hypertables, `show_chunks`, `add_dimension` and `set_chunk_time_interval` are **Apache 2 edition**; SkipScan and `reorder_chunk` need the **Community edition**.

lessons.title: time_bucket and gap filling
tldr: `time_bucket` maps every timestamp to the start of a fixed-width bucket, and `time_bucket_gapfill` with `locf` or `interpolate` adds rows for buckets that have no data.
Charts and rollups need one row per interval, while real sensors report irregularly and go silent, so bucketing and gap filling turn raw readings into a regular series.

visualizer.title: Where bucket boundaries fall, and filling the holes
visualizer.caption: In **Bucketing**, change width, origin, offset and time zone and watch readings regroup; pick 1 day in Berlin to see the 23-hour day. In **Gap filling**, step from plain buckets to gapfill, locf and interpolate.

presets.label: time_bucket = date_bin
presets.note: `time_bucket('15 minutes', ts)` equals `date_bin` with origin 2000-01-03, a **Monday**, so weekly buckets start on Monday 2026-11-09. A Sunday origin moves them to 2026-11-08.

presets.label: Month buckets
presets.note: `date_bin` refuses months: **timestamps cannot be binned into intervals containing months or years**. `time_bucket('3 months', t)` counts from origin 2000-01-01; month arithmetic reproduces it (April and October).

presets.label: Time zones and DST
presets.note: 23:30 UTC on 28 March is already the 29th in Berlin. The day of the clock change lasts **23:00:00**. This is what `time_bucket('1 day', time, timezone => 'Europe/Berlin')` produces.

presets.label: Gap filling
presets.sql:
-- plain bucketing: silent hours are missing
SELECT date_bin('1 hour', time, timestamptz '2000-01-03') AS hour, avg(value)
FROM metrics WHERE device_id = 1 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

-- time_bucket_gapfill equivalent: a series of buckets LEFT JOIN the data
SELECT g.hour, avg(m.value) AS avg_value, count(m.*) AS n
FROM generate_series(timestamptz '2026-01-05 00:00', timestamptz '2026-01-05 05:00', interval '1 hour') g(hour)
LEFT JOIN metrics m ON m.device_id = 1 AND m.time >= g.hour AND m.time < g.hour + interval '1 hour'
GROUP BY g.hour ORDER BY g.hour;
presets.note: Three rows become six: 01:00, 03:00 and 04:00 now exist with `NULL` average and `n = 0`. The series supplies the buckets that gapfill takes from the WHERE bounds.

presets.label: locf
presets.note: `count(v)` only counts non-NULL values, so each NULL joins the group of the last real value, and `first_value` copies it forward: **11, 11, 20, 20, 20, 50**.

presets.label: interpolate
presets.sql:
WITH filled AS (
  SELECT g.hour, avg(m.value) AS v
  FROM generate_series(timestamptz '2026-01-05 00:00', timestamptz '2026-01-05 05:00', interval '1 hour') g(hour)
  LEFT JOIN metrics m ON m.device_id = 1 AND m.time >= g.hour AND m.time < g.hour + interval '1 hour'
  GROUP BY g.hour
), marks AS (
  SELECT hour, v, count(v) OVER (ORDER BY hour) AS gp, count(v) OVER (ORDER BY hour DESC) AS gn FROM filled
), pn AS (
  SELECT hour, v,
    first_value(v)    OVER (PARTITION BY gp ORDER BY hour)      AS prev_v,
    first_value(hour) OVER (PARTITION BY gp ORDER BY hour)      AS prev_t,
    first_value(v)    OVER (PARTITION BY gn ORDER BY hour DESC) AS next_v,
    first_value(hour) OVER (PARTITION BY gn ORDER BY hour DESC) AS next_t
  FROM marks
)
SELECT hour, v,
  CASE WHEN v IS NOT NULL THEN v
       WHEN prev_v IS NULL OR next_v IS NULL THEN NULL
       ELSE prev_v + (next_v - prev_v) * extract(epoch FROM hour - prev_t) / extract(epoch FROM next_t - prev_t)
  END AS interpolated
FROM pn ORDER BY hour;
presets.note: Linear interpolation needs the previous **and** the next real value: **15.5** between 11 and 20, then **30** and **40** on the way to 50. One `interpolate()` call replaces this whole query.

presets.label: first / last
presets.note: These match `first(value, time)` and `last(value, time)`. The `array_agg` versions sort the whole group. PostgreSQL 18 has no `IGNORE NULLS`, which is why the locf preset needs the count() trick.

production.title: A dashboard that stopped drawing false lines
production.context: A building-management team charts room temperature from battery sensors that report every 5 minutes, but skip reports when the value has not changed and drop out when the radio is busy.
production.problem: The chart grouped by `time_bucket('15 minutes', time)`. Silent periods produced no rows, so the charting library drew a straight line across a two-hour outage, and "rooms out of range per hour" undercounted because missing hours were not rows at all.
production.solution: Use `time_bucket_gapfill` so every 15-minute bucket exists, and `locf` because a silent sensor means "unchanged". Bucket by local time so daily panels start at local midnight. `time_bucket_gapfill` and `locf` are **Community edition** features; on the Apache 2 edition use the `generate_series` pattern from the playground.
production.sql:
SELECT time_bucket_gapfill('15 minutes', time, timezone => 'Europe/Berlin') AS bucket,
       room_id,
       locf(avg(temperature)) AS temperature,
       avg(temperature) IS NULL AS was_silent
FROM room_readings
WHERE time >= now() - INTERVAL '1 day' AND time < now()   -- both bounds required
GROUP BY bucket, room_id
ORDER BY room_id, bucket;
production.outcome: Every room returns one row for every 15-minute bucket in the window (96 for a full, aligned day), so charts and per-hour counts line up. The `was_silent` flag keeps filled values distinguishable from measured ones.

pitfalls.title: Gapfill without an upper bound
pitfalls.symptom: An error that gapfill needs a start and finish, or no extra rows appear.
pitfalls.cause: `time_bucket_gapfill` infers its range from the WHERE clause on the time column. Without both `time >= …` and `time < …` it cannot know which buckets to create.
pitfalls.fix: Always give both bounds in WHERE, or pass `start` and `finish` arguments explicitly.

pitfalls.title: Wrapping gapfill or filtering with HAVING
pitfalls.symptom: Errors when you write `round(time_bucket_gapfill(…))` or cast it, or filled buckets vanish from the result.
pitfalls.cause: `time_bucket_gapfill` must be a top-level expression, and `HAVING` runs **before** gap filling.
pitfalls.fix: Cast or round in an outer query, and filter filled rows in an outer CTE, not with HAVING.

pitfalls.title: Buckets aligned to UTC, not local midnight
pitfalls.symptom: Daily totals for a European customer are off by one or two hours of data, and shift when clocks change.
pitfalls.cause: `timestamptz` buckets align to 00:00 UTC by default.
pitfalls.fix: Pass the zone: `time_bucket('1 day', time, timezone => 'Europe/Berlin')`, or natively `date_trunc('day', time, 'Europe/Berlin')`. Expect a 23-hour and a 25-hour day each year.

pitfalls.title: Old code using time_bucket_ng
pitfalls.symptom: `function time_bucket_ng(…) does not exist` after an upgrade.
pitfalls.cause: The experimental `time_bucket_ng` was removed in TimescaleDB 2.25.0.
pitfalls.fix: Use `time_bucket`, which supports months, origin, offset and time zone.

pointers: `time_bucket(width, ts)` returns the bucket **start**. Default origin is **2000-01-03, a Monday** (2000-01-01 for month widths), aligned on UTC.

Natively: `date_bin(width, ts, origin)` for fixed widths, `date_trunc(unit, ts, zone)` for calendar units. `date_bin` cannot do months. Filling gaps by hand is a [gaps-and-islands](/f4/gaps-and-islands) pattern.
`time_bucket_gapfill` creates the missing buckets from the WHERE bounds; `locf` carries values forward; `interpolate` draws lines between them.
`time_bucket`, `first`, `last` and `histogram` are **Apache 2 edition**. `time_bucket_gapfill`, `locf` and `interpolate` are **Community edition** only.

lessons.title: Continuous aggregates
tldr: A **continuous aggregate** is a materialized view over a hypertable that TimescaleDB refreshes incrementally, recomputing only new time buckets and buckets whose raw data changed.
Dashboards ask the same rollup questions every few seconds, and recomputing them from billions of raw rows is too slow, while a plain materialized view must be rebuilt in full on every refresh.

visualizer.title: Watermark, invalidation log and refresh window
visualizer.caption: Advance time and watch the hourly policy materialize buckets behind the watermark. Backfill late rows to fill the invalidation log, compare one transaction with two, and switch on **real-time** to see buckets above the watermark computed live.

presets.label: A plain materialized view
presets.note: An unpopulated matview raises **has not been populated**. `REFRESH` recomputes the entire query every time, however little changed.

presets.label: Concurrent refresh and staleness
presets.note: `CONCURRENTLY` needs a unique index and still recomputes everything. The new 05:30 reading is invisible: the matview still says **50, n = 1** until the next full refresh.

presets.label: Build an incremental engine
presets.note: A summary table (the **materialization hypertable**), an invalidation log fed by a statement trigger, and a refresh that handles whole buckets only. The window ends at 05:00, so 5 buckets are computed and the **watermark** moves to 05:00.

presets.label: Real-time view
presets.sql:
CREATE VIEW metrics_hourly_rt AS
SELECT bucket, device_id, sum_v / n AS avg_v, n FROM cagg_hourly
WHERE bucket < (SELECT wm FROM cagg_watermark)
UNION ALL
SELECT date_bin('1 hour', time, timestamptz '2000-01-03'), device_id, avg(value), count(*)
FROM metrics WHERE time >= (SELECT wm FROM cagg_watermark)
GROUP BY 1, 2;

SELECT * FROM metrics_hourly_rt ORDER BY 1, 2;
presets.note: This is `materialized_only = false`: stored buckets below the watermark, plus raw rows above it aggregated on the fly. The 05:00 bucket appears with **55, n = 2** (50 and 60) without a refresh.

presets.label: Backfill below the watermark
presets.note: The late row is logged as **00:50 → 00:50**, but even the real-time view still shows **11** until a refresh. Refresh number 2 recomputes **1 bucket**, and the average becomes 40.67 (10, 12, 100).

presets.label: One transaction vs two
presets.note: Only min and max are logged, so one write spanning 01:20 to 04:20 recomputes **4 buckets**, while two separate writes recompute **2**. TimescaleDB logs per transaction, so batch backfills by bucket.

presets.label: Rolling up without avg of avgs
presets.sql:
SELECT date_trunc('day', bucket) AS day, device_id,
       sum(sum_v) / sum(n) AS correct_avg,
       avg(sum_v / n)      AS avg_of_avgs
FROM cagg_hourly GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2;
presets.note: A daily rollup of the hourly table (a **hierarchical** aggregate) must combine sums and counts: device 1 is **35.5**, while averaging the hourly averages gives a wrong 30.33.

production.title: Hourly dashboards over a year of per-second data
production.context: An energy-monitoring service stores one reading per second for 20,000 meters, 1.7 billion rows per day, and its dashboards show hourly and daily usage per meter.
production.problem: The dashboard query aggregated raw rows on every page load, and a plain materialized view took longer to refresh than the interval between refreshes. Late readings arrive from meters that were offline for hours.
production.solution: An hourly continuous aggregate with a refresh policy that leaves the current hour out, real-time aggregation for the dashboard, and a daily aggregate on top of the hourly one storing sums and counts. Late batches are written per bucket so the invalidation ranges stay small. Continuous aggregates and their policies are **Community edition** features; on the Apache 2 edition (Neon included) use the trigger-and-summary-table pattern from the playground.
production.sql:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW usage_hourly
WITH (timescaledb.continuous, timescaledb.materialized_only = false) AS
SELECT time_bucket('1 hour', time) AS bucket, meter_id,
       sum(kwh) AS kwh, count(*) AS n
FROM readings
GROUP BY bucket, meter_id
WITH NO DATA;

SELECT add_continuous_aggregate_policy('usage_hourly',
  start_offset      => INTERVAL '3 days',    -- late meters catch up within 3 days
  end_offset        => INTERVAL '1 hour',    -- never materialize the open hour
  schedule_interval => INTERVAL '1 hour');

-- hierarchical: daily on top of hourly (24 h is a whole multiple of 1 h)
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW usage_daily WITH (timescaledb.continuous) AS
SELECT time_bucket('1 day', bucket) AS day, meter_id, sum(kwh) AS kwh, sum(n) AS n
FROM usage_hourly GROUP BY day, meter_id;

-- one-off repair of a range older than the policy window
CALL refresh_continuous_aggregate('usage_hourly', '2026-10-01', '2026-10-08');
production.outcome: A daily dashboard for one meter reads 24 hourly rows instead of 86,400 raw rows, 3,600 times fewer. The policy refreshes each window in batches of 10 buckets (the default since 2.25), so each transaction stays small.

pitfalls.title: The last hour is missing
pitfalls.symptom: The aggregate shows nothing for the most recent hour or two, so the dashboard looks delayed.
pitfalls.cause: `end_offset` keeps the open bucket out of the refresh window, and real-time aggregation has been **off by default since 2.13**. With a 1-hour schedule and a 1-hour end_offset, data can be up to 2 hours late.
pitfalls.fix: Enable real-time aggregation if readers need fresh data, or shorten `end_offset` and `schedule_interval`.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW usage_hourly SET (timescaledb.materialized_only = false);

pitfalls.title: Backfill never appears
pitfalls.symptom: Rows inserted for last month are in the hypertable but not in the aggregate, even with real-time on.
pitfalls.cause: Real-time only covers data above the watermark. Changes below it are logged and wait for a refresh whose window covers them, and the policy window (`start_offset`) does not reach back a month.
pitfalls.fix: Run a manual refresh for that range, or add a second policy with a non-overlapping window for old data.
pitfalls.sql: CALL refresh_continuous_aggregate('usage_hourly', '2026-10-01', '2026-11-01');

pitfalls.title: Retention deletes aggregated history
pitfalls.symptom: After adding a retention policy, old buckets vanish from the continuous aggregate too.
pitfalls.cause: A refresh that covers a range whose raw chunks were dropped recomputes those buckets from nothing, which **deletes** them.
pitfalls.fix: Keep the retention interval longer than the refresh policy's `start_offset`, and give the aggregate its own, longer retention policy.

pitfalls.title: Averages of averages in a hierarchy
pitfalls.symptom: A daily aggregate built on an hourly one disagrees with the same query run on raw data.
pitfalls.cause: Hours have different row counts, so the mean of hourly means weighs them all equally.
pitfalls.fix: Store `sum` and `count` in the lower level and divide in the upper one, or use Toolkit aggregates that support `rollup()` (`stats_agg`, `percentile_agg`).

pointers: A cagg stores finished buckets in a **materialization hypertable**. The **watermark** marks where materialized data ends.
Writes behind the invalidation threshold log **min and max time per transaction**. A refresh recomputes only new and invalidated whole buckets in its window.
Policy = `start_offset` / `end_offset` / `schedule_interval`. Leave the open bucket out, and expect data to lag by up to schedule + end_offset.
**Real-time** (`materialized_only = false`) unions live raw data above the watermark. It has been off by default since 2.13.
Continuous aggregates are **Community edition** only. Natively: a summary table, a trigger-fed invalidation log, a refresh procedure and a UNION view.

lessons.title: Compression and the columnstore
tldr: The TimescaleDB **columnstore** (Hypercore, formerly called compression) rewrites older chunks so that each batch of up to 1000 rows becomes one row of compressed per-column arrays with min/max metadata.

Time-series values repeat and change slowly, so storing columns together with delta and XOR encodings shrinks old data by 90% or more and lets analytical scans skip and read only the columns they need.

visualizer.title: From 12 heap rows to a few compressed rows
visualizer.caption: Step through the conversion of one chunk: group, order, batch, encode, then query and update it. Switch **segmentby** to see why a low-cardinality column groups well and a unique id ruins compression.

presets.label: The rowstore
presets.note: 30,000 rows in 192 pages (**1568 kB**), 156 rows per page. Each row carries its own header and repeats the symbol text.

presets.label: Build columnar batches
presets.sql:
CREATE TABLE ticks_columnar AS
SELECT symbol,                                 -- segmentby
       (rn - 1) / 1000          AS batch,      -- up to 1000 rows per batch
       count(*)                 AS n,
       min(time) AS min_time, max(time) AS max_time,   -- batch metadata
       array_agg(time  ORDER BY time) AS times,        -- orderby time
       array_agg(price ORDER BY time) AS prices
FROM (SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY time) AS rn FROM ticks) s
GROUP BY symbol, (rn - 1) / 1000;

SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('ticks'))          AS rowstore,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('ticks_columnar')) AS columnar,
       round(pg_total_relation_size('ticks')::numeric / pg_total_relation_size('ticks_columnar'), 1) AS ratio,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM ticks_columnar) AS batches;

SELECT symbol, batch, n, min_time, max_time,
       pg_column_size(times) AS times_bytes, pg_column_size(prices) AS prices_bytes
FROM ticks_columnar ORDER BY symbol, batch LIMIT 4;
presets.note: 30 rows replace 30,000: **1568 kB → 216 kB** (7.3x) with only TOAST's generic compression. 1000 prices fit in about 282 bytes because they repeat. Real columnstore codecs do far better on timestamps.

presets.label: Skip batches by metadata
presets.sql:
SELECT symbol, batch, min_time, max_time FROM ticks_columnar
WHERE symbol = 'ETH' AND max_time >= '2026-01-05 03:00' AND min_time <= '2026-01-05 03:00:10';

SELECT u.t, u.p
FROM ticks_columnar c, unnest(c.times, c.prices) AS u(t, p)
WHERE c.symbol = 'ETH'
  AND c.max_time >= '2026-01-05 03:00' AND c.min_time <= '2026-01-05 03:00:10'
  AND u.t BETWEEN '2026-01-05 03:00' AND '2026-01-05 03:00:10'
ORDER BY u.t;
presets.note: The segment value and min/max metadata pick **1 batch of 30** before any array is opened. `unnest` plays decompression and returns the 4 matching ticks.

presets.label: Why timestamps compress
presets.sql:
SELECT time,
       extract(epoch FROM time - lag(time) OVER w) AS delta,
       extract(epoch FROM time - lag(time) OVER w)
         - extract(epoch FROM lag(time) OVER w - lag(time, 2) OVER w) AS delta_of_delta,
       price, price - lag(price) OVER w AS price_delta
FROM ticks WHERE symbol = 'BTC'
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY time) ORDER BY time LIMIT 6;
presets.note: Within one segment ticks arrive every 3 seconds, so **delta-of-delta is 0** for every row: a 64-bit timestamp shrinks to about a bit. Prices step by a constant 3, which run-length and delta encodings capture too.

presets.label: Choosing segmentby
presets.note: No segmentby is about as small here, but a query for ETH must open **all 30 batches** instead of 10. A unique segment key makes 30,000 one-value batches: **4104 kB**, bigger than the rowstore.

presets.label: Changing one value
presets.note: Changing one price writes a **new version of the whole batch row** (1000 values). TimescaleDB instead decompresses the affected batch into the rowstore part of the chunk, which is why large UPDATEs on compressed chunks are expensive.

production.title: Keeping a year of market ticks on one server
production.context: A trading-analytics team stores every tick for about 2,000 symbols in a hypertable with 1-day chunks. Analysts query one symbol over weeks or months; only the last day still receives inserts.
production.problem: A year of rowstore chunks filled the disk, and month-long scans read every column of every row even though they used only time and price.
production.solution: Enable the columnstore with `segmentby = symbol` (filtered on, moderate cardinality) and `orderby = time DESC`, and convert chunks once they stop receiving writes. The columnstore is a **Community edition** feature: it is not in the Apache 2 edition, and Neon does not offer it. Old names from before 2.18 still work but are deprecated.
production.outcome: Expect a reduction of around 90% on data like this; a sample crypto-tick hypertable shrinks from 194 MB to 24 MB, about 8 times (88%). Queries on one symbol open only that symbol's batches and only the columns they reference. Measure your own ratio with `hypertable_columnstore_stats`.

pitfalls.title: High-cardinality segmentby
pitfalls.symptom: Compression ratio is poor, sometimes worse than the rowstore, and `chunk_columnstore_stats` shows little gain.
pitfalls.cause: Every distinct segmentby value gets its own batches. With a near-unique column each batch holds a handful of rows, so there is nothing to compress.
pitfalls.fix: Pick the column you filter or group by most, with low-to-moderate cardinality (device, symbol). Settings apply only to chunks converted afterwards.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER TABLE ticks SET (timescaledb.segmentby = 'symbol');

pitfalls.title: Big UPDATE on compressed chunks
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: tuple decompression limit exceeded by operation`.
pitfalls.cause: DML decompresses the batches it touches. `timescaledb.max_tuples_decompressed_per_dml_transaction` (default 100000) stops runaway transactions.
pitfalls.fix: Batch the change, raise the limit for that session, or pause the policy, convert the chunk back with `convert_to_rowstore`, change it, and convert again.
pitfalls.sql: SET timescaledb.max_tuples_decompressed_per_dml_transaction = 0;  -- 0 = unlimited, this session only

pitfalls.title: Enabling the policy on a large existing table
pitfalls.symptom: Memory pressure or `temporary file size exceeds temp_file_limit` right after adding the policy.
pitfalls.cause: The first run tries to convert the whole backlog of eligible chunks, one after another, in a single-threaded job.
pitfalls.fix: Limit chunks per run with the `maxchunks_to_compress` config key, and convert the backlog manually from parallel sessions.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT alter_job(job_id, config => config || '{"maxchunks_to_compress": 10}')
FROM timescaledb_information.jobs WHERE proc_name = 'policy_compression';

pitfalls.title: Assuming one policy schedule
pitfalls.symptom: Chunks convert later (or earlier) than a runbook promised.
pitfalls.cause: There are two defaults: the policy created by `CREATE TABLE … WITH (tsdb.hypertable)` is specified with a 1-day schedule, while `add_columnstore_policy` defaults to 12 hours for chunk intervals of a day or more (half the interval otherwise).
pitfalls.fix: Read the real value instead of assuming it, and set it explicitly if it matters.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT job_id, schedule_interval, config FROM timescaledb_information.jobs
WHERE proc_name = 'policy_compression';

pointers: Columnstore conversion: group by **segmentby**, sort by **orderby**, cut into batches of **up to 1000 rows**, store each batch as one row of arrays with min/max metadata.

Codecs: since 2.32 the **Adaptive Integer Compressor** picks run-length, frame-of-reference or dictionary per block for integers and timestamps (delta-of-delta, simple-8b and run-length before); XOR for floats; dictionaries for text.
Scans skip batches by segment value and metadata, and decompress only the columns they read. DML decompresses only the batches it touches.
Renamed in 2.18: `compress_chunk` → `convert_to_columnstore`, `add_compression_policy` → `add_columnstore_policy`, `timescaledb.compress` → `enable_columnstore`.
The columnstore is **Community edition** only. Neon does not support compression. The playground's arrays rely on [TOAST](/m2/toast) compression instead.

lessons.title: Retention, tiering and jobs
tldr: **Retention** in TimescaleDB drops whole chunks once their entire time range is older than a cutoff, and a built-in **job scheduler** runs that and every other policy on a schedule.
Dropping a chunk removes files instantly with no dead tuples or vacuum work, and policies turn the chunk lifecycle (rowstore, columnstore, tiered, dropped) into configuration instead of cron scripts.

visualizer.title: The life of a chunk
visualizer.caption: Advance day by day and watch chunks move from rowstore to columnstore and finally get dropped. Change `drop_after` and the continuous aggregate's `start_offset` until retention starts deleting aggregates, and try Tiger Cloud tiering.

presets.label: The chunks
presets.sql:
SELECT * FROM chunks();
SELECT count(*) AS row_count, min(time), max(time) FROM conditions;
presets.note: Ten daily chunks of 1440 rows; the newest is half full (720). This is the table the retention job will trim.

presets.label: Retention with DELETE
presets.note: Deleting one day writes **about 79 kB of WAL** for 1440 rows and leaves 1440 dead tuples for VACUUM. Rolled back, so the data is still there.

presets.label: A retention job
presets.note: The cutoff is Nov 7 12:00, so the Nov 5 and Nov 6 chunks go, using a few kB of WAL for two whole days. Nov 7 stays because part of it is newer than the cutoff: the oldest row is **7 days 12:00** old.

presets.label: A tiny job scheduler
presets.note: This mimics TimescaleDB's scheduler and `timescaledb_information.jobs`: job 1001 ran, dropped Nov 7 and Nov 8 (cutoff Nov 9 12:00), and its **next_start** moved one day ahead.

presets.label: A failing job backs off
presets.note: A bad config fails twice. Each failure pushes `next_start` further out (12:05, then 12:15), the pattern TimescaleDB uses: consecutive failures × `retry_period`, capped at 5 × the schedule, plus jitter.

production.title: A 13-month lifecycle for fleet telemetry
production.context: A logistics company keeps GPS and engine telemetry in a hypertable with 1-day chunks. Ops needs raw data for 30 days, finance needs daily summaries for 13 months, and disk is the main cost.
production.problem: A nightly `DELETE … WHERE time < now() - interval '30 days'` ran for hours, generated gigabytes of WAL and left the table bloated. When someone added a retention policy, a continuous aggregate with a long refresh window silently lost its history.
production.solution: Policies, each one a background job: the columnstore after 1 day, raw retention after 30 days, a daily aggregate with a 3-day refresh window and its own 13-month retention. All four policies and `add_job` are **Community edition** features; on the Apache 2 edition call `drop_chunks` from pg_cron. Tiering to object storage (`add_tiering_policy`) exists only on Tiger Cloud.
production.outcome: Retention removes one chunk file per day instead of deleting millions of rows: dropping two daily chunks in the playground takes a few kB of WAL, while deleting one day row by row takes about 79 kB per 1,440 rows. The daily aggregate keeps 13 months of history after the raw data is gone.

pitfalls.title: Retention shorter than the refresh window
pitfalls.symptom: Old days disappear from a continuous aggregate soon after a retention policy is added.
pitfalls.cause: A refresh covering a range whose raw chunks were dropped recomputes those buckets from no rows, and **deletes** them.
pitfalls.fix: Keep `drop_after` on the hypertable longer than the aggregate policy's `start_offset`, and give the aggregate its own, longer retention.

pitfalls.title: Data older than the cutoff is still there
pitfalls.symptom: After `drop_chunks('t', INTERVAL '30 days')` some rows are 36 days old.
pitfalls.cause: Only chunks whose **entire range** is older than the cutoff are dropped. A 7-day chunk that straddles the cutoff stays.
pitfalls.fix: This is by design. Use a smaller chunk interval if the policy must be tighter, or filter in queries.

pitfalls.title: Replacing a job config by accident
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: could not find hypertable_id in config for job` after `alter_job`.
pitfalls.cause: `alter_job(…, config => …)` replaces the **whole** config object, including the `hypertable_id` the policy needs.
pitfalls.fix: Merge instead of replace: `config_merge` (2.29+) or `config || '{…}'`.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT alter_job(1001, config_merge => '{"drop_after": "45 days"}');

pitfalls.title: Jobs that never run
pitfalls.symptom: `job_stats` shows no recent runs, or `add_job` does not exist.
pitfalls.cause: Too few background workers (`timescaledb.max_background_workers`, default 16, must cover one scheduler per database plus concurrent jobs), the Apache edition (no `add_job`), or a serverless compute that was suspended.
pitfalls.fix: Raise `timescaledb.max_background_workers` and `max_worker_processes` (restart needed), check `SHOW timescaledb.license`, and on Neon use pg_cron while the compute is awake.

pointers: `drop_chunks` / `add_retention_policy` drop a chunk only when its **whole range** is older than the cutoff. One retention policy per hypertable.
Every policy is a **job**: see `timescaledb_information.jobs` and `job_stats`; change it with `alter_job`, run it with `CALL run_job(id)`.
Keep raw retention **longer than** any continuous aggregate's `start_offset`, and retain the aggregate separately.
Multi-node was removed in 2.14. Tiering to object storage is Tiger Cloud only; for sharding PostgreSQL see [Citus](/e3/sharding-citus).
`drop_chunks` is **Apache 2 edition**; retention policies, `add_job` and the scheduler are **Community edition**.

lessons.title: Why and how to distribute PostgreSQL
tldr: PostgreSQL is a **single-node** database, and every "distributed PostgreSQL" adds one of three things around it: **replication** (copies), **distribution** (parts of the data on different machines) or **decentralization** (storage and compute on different machines).
Each design buys scale or availability by adding network round trips and new failure modes, so the right choice starts from what one well-tuned node cannot do.

visualizer.title: Five architectures, one write, one read
visualizer.caption: Pick an architecture, send a write and a read, then fail a component and send them again. The latency panel shows what each extra round trip costs.

presets.label: One node, one WAL stream
presets.note: Every change becomes WAL records: a heap insert, a B-tree insert, a commit. A physical replica replays exactly this stream; a shared-storage system ships only this stream to its storage layer.

presets.label: Commit knobs: latency vs safety
presets.note: `synchronous_commit` can change per transaction. With `remote_apply` a commit waits until a synchronous standby has replayed it. Here the standby list is empty, so nothing waits. `synchronous_standby_names` needs a reload, not a `SET`.

presets.label: A slot for a replica
presets.note: A replica connects through a slot, so the primary keeps the WAL the replica still needs. `active = false`: no replica is connected to this single node.

presets.label: Distribution on one machine
presets.note: Hash partitions on one node model shards: each tenant lands in exactly one part. A sharding extension puts those parts on different machines. Note the uneven sizes: 20 tenants do not split evenly 4 ways.

presets.label: Copies of a subset
presets.sql:
CREATE PUBLICATION big_orders FOR TABLE orders (id, tenant_id, amount) WHERE (amount > 90);
SELECT pubname, tablename, attnames, rowfilter FROM pg_publication_tables;
presets.note: Logical replication publishes chosen tables, columns and rows. It is the building block of multi-master systems. The warning says this node is not configured to send logical changes; the catalog entry still shows what would be published.

presets.label: Latency arithmetic
presets.sql:
SELECT rtt_ms, trips,
       round(trips * (rtt_ms + 0.2), 1)            AS txn_ms,
       round(1000 / (trips * (rtt_ms + 0.2)))      AS tx_per_s_per_session,
       round(100 * 1000 / (trips * (rtt_ms + 0.2))) AS tx_per_s_100_sessions
FROM (VALUES (0.1), (1), (5), (70)) r(rtt_ms), (VALUES (1), (5)) t(trips)
ORDER BY rtt_ms, trips;
presets.note: Same numbers as the visualizer: 5 statements at 70 ms round trip allow about 3 transactions per second per session. Distance, not CPU, sets the ceiling.

production.title: Choosing an architecture from measurements, not fashion
production.context: A B2B SaaS on one 16-core PostgreSQL server sees CPU at 70% at peak and plans a move to a "distributed database" before a big customer launch.
production.problem: Nobody knows whether reads, writes or one heavy tenant drive the load. A distributed design chosen blind would add round trips to every request and change uniqueness, sequences and joins for the whole application.
production.solution: Measure where the time goes first. If reads dominate, add replicas for read-only, staleness-tolerant traffic and an HA manager. If one tenant or the data size dominates, shard by tenant. If the requirement is "survive a region outage with no data loss", that is a consensus system or synchronous replication, and it costs latency on every commit.
production.outcome: Reads were most of the load, so the team added two streaming replicas behind an HA manager and moved reporting to them. Each next step is now driven by a measured bottleneck, not by the architecture of the week.

pitfalls.title: Reading your own write from a replica
pitfalls.symptom: A user saves a setting, the page reloads from a replica, and the old value comes back.
pitfalls.cause: Asynchronous replicas lag. The read went to a copy that had not replayed the write yet: no **read-your-writes**. "Synchronous" does not fix it by itself: the default `synchronous_commit = on` waits until the standby has **flushed** the WAL to disk, not replayed it, so a read there can still miss the row.
pitfalls.fix: Send reads that follow a write to the primary for a short window, or make that transaction commit with `remote_apply` to a synchronous standby. Load-balance only staleness-tolerant reads.

pitfalls.title: One synchronous standby blocks every commit
pitfalls.symptom: The only synchronous standby goes down for maintenance and every write on the primary hangs.
pitfalls.cause: With `synchronous_standby_names` naming one server, each commit waits for that server. If it is gone, commits wait forever.
pitfalls.fix: Name at least two candidates and wait for one: `ANY 1 (s1, s2)`. Then one standby may be down without stopping writes.
pitfalls.sql:
ALTER SYSTEM SET synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (s1, s2)';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

pitfalls.title: Distributing a chatty application
pitfalls.symptom: After moving to a multi-node design, a page that ran 40 queries takes ten times longer although every query is fast.
pitfalls.cause: Each statement is now a network round trip, maybe several. Forty statements at 2 ms each is already 80 ms before any work.
pitfalls.fix: Cut round trips first: batch with multi-row `INSERT` or `COPY`, combine reads, move loops into a single statement or a function, and pool connections. Keep each transaction on one node or one shard.

pitfalls.title: Talking past each other about "cluster"
pitfalls.symptom: A runbook says "restart the cluster", and one engineer restarts one server while another restarts every node.
pitfalls.cause: A PostgreSQL **database cluster** is the set of databases one server serves from one data directory. An **HA cluster** is a primary with standbys. `CLUSTER` is also a SQL command that rewrites a table.
pitfalls.fix: Name the thing: "the instance", "the HA group", "the shard group". Write runbooks with host names, not "the cluster".

pointers: Three mechanisms: **replication** (copies), **distribution** (parts), **decentralization** (storage separated from compute). Real systems stack them.
A transaction costs **round trips × latency**: 20 ms per transaction caps one session at 50 transactions per second.

Replicas scale reads but are stale; shared storage gives durable quorum writes with one writer; sharding splits data by a key; distributed SQL runs Raft per tablet; multi-master accepts writes everywhere and resolves conflicts later.
**CAP**: under a partition choose consistency or availability. **PACELC**: otherwise choose latency or consistency, which `synchronous_commit` lets you pick per transaction.
Most workloads fit one large node plus [streaming replicas](/m7/streaming-replication) and an HA manager. Distribute when a measured limit says so.

lessons.title: Sharding with Citus
tldr: **Citus** is a PostgreSQL extension that hash-splits each distributed table by a **distribution column** into shards, ordinary tables spread over worker nodes, and routes or parallelizes queries from a coordinator.
It exists to scale one database past one machine while keeping PostgreSQL itself, as long as the data model is built around a shard key such as the tenant id.

visualizer.title: A shard map: from a key to a worker
visualizer.caption: Type a company_id or press Route next key. Change the worker count, break colocation for ads, or switch to reference and schema-based sharding.

presets.label: The shard map
presets.note: This table models Citus's `pg_dist_shard` on one node: 32 ranges of 134,217,728 hash tokens each, placed round-robin. Citus itself is not installed here.

presets.label: Route a key to its shard
presets.note: Hash the key, find the range that contains the token, read the node. Company 7 hashes to -978793473, which falls in shard 102048 on worker1: the same numbers the visualizer shows with 2 workers.

presets.label: Colocation: one company, one shard index
presets.sql:
SELECT c.id AS company_id,
       c.tableoid::regclass AS companies_part,
       (SELECT DISTINCT tableoid::regclass FROM campaigns WHERE company_id = c.id) AS campaigns_part,
       (SELECT DISTINCT tableoid::regclass FROM ads WHERE company_id = c.id) AS ads_part
FROM companies c WHERE c.id <= 6 ORDER BY 1;
presets.note: All three tables are split by the same key with the same modulus, so a company's rows always land in partitions with the same suffix. Citus colocation makes the same promise across machines.

presets.label: Unique keys must include the shard key
presets.sql:
SELECT try_sql($$CREATE TABLE users_bad (company_id int, email text UNIQUE) PARTITION BY HASH (company_id)$$) AS unique_email;
SELECT try_sql($$CREATE TABLE users_ok (company_id int, email text, UNIQUE (company_id, email)) PARTITION BY HASH (company_id)$$) AS unique_per_company;
presets.note: No single part can check uniqueness across all parts, so the key column is required. Citus applies the same rule to distributed tables: unique per tenant is easy, globally unique is not.

presets.label: Foreign keys inside a colocation group
presets.note: The foreign key includes `company_id`, so the parent row is always in the matching part. In Citus this is the only way a distributed table may reference another one.

presets.label: Schema per tenant
presets.note: Same table name, no tenant column: `search_path` chooses the tenant. Schema-based sharding in Citus distributes whole schemas like this one, each to one node.

production.title: Sharding a multi-tenant ad platform by company
production.context: An ad platform keeps companies, campaigns and ads in one PostgreSQL. A few hundred companies, a few billion ads, and the largest table no longer fits the cache of the biggest server it can buy.
production.problem: Primary keys are plain `id` columns, so nothing in the schema says which rows belong together. Distributing as is would make every join a cross-node join and every unique key unenforceable.
production.solution: Add `company_id` to every table and make it lead every primary and foreign key. Distribute the root table first, colocate the others with it, and turn small shared tables into reference tables. Then every tenant query carries the key and becomes a single-shard query.
production.outcome: Each company's companies, campaigns and ads shards sit on the same worker, so dashboard queries filtered by `company_id` touch one shard, and foreign keys keep working. Adding a worker and rebalancing adds capacity without touching application queries.

pitfalls.title: A unique key without the distribution column
pitfalls.symptom: `create_distributed_table` fails on a table with `UNIQUE (email)`, or a team drops the constraint to get past it and later finds duplicate emails.
pitfalls.cause: Citus does not check uniqueness across workers. A primary key or unique constraint must include the distribution column so that one shard can enforce it.
pitfalls.fix: Make uniqueness per tenant: `UNIQUE (company_id, email)`. If a value must be unique across all tenants, keep it in a reference table or a separate lookup table.
pitfalls.sql:
ALTER TABLE users DROP CONSTRAINT users_email_key,
  ADD CONSTRAINT users_company_email_key UNIQUE (company_id, email);

pitfalls.title: Distributing the child before the parent
pitfalls.symptom: `create_distributed_table` on the referencing table fails with a foreign key error, because the table it points at is still an ordinary local table.
pitfalls.cause: The foreign key target was still a local table when the referencing table was distributed.
pitfalls.fix: Distribute in dependency order: the referenced table first, then the tables that point at it, with `colocate_with`. Foreign keys from a reference table to a distributed table are never allowed.

pitfalls.title: A distribution column with few values
pitfalls.symptom: One worker is at 100% CPU and holds most of the data while the others idle.
pitfalls.cause: The column has few distinct values (a country, a status) or one value dominates (one huge tenant). Hashing cannot spread what is not there.
pitfalls.fix: Pick a high-cardinality key that matches how queries filter, usually the tenant id. Move one very large tenant to its own shard with `isolate_tenant_to_new_shard`.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT isolate_tenant_to_new_shard('companies', 42, cascade_option => 'CASCADE');

pitfalls.title: The coordinator keeps a local copy
pitfalls.symptom: After `create_distributed_table` the coordinator's disk usage does not drop, although the data now lives on the workers.
pitfalls.cause: Distributing copies existing rows into the shards and leaves the original local data on the coordinator.
pitfalls.fix: Run `truncate_local_data_after_distributing_table('table')` once the copy is verified.

pointers: A distributed table is split by `hashint4`-style hashing of the **distribution column** into `citus.shard_count` (default **32**) shards, each an ordinary table named `<table>_<shardid>` on a worker.
`pg_dist_shard` stores each shard's token range, `pg_dist_placement` its node. The coordinator routes a query that pins the key to one shard.
**Colocated** tables share ranges and placements, so joins and foreign keys on the key stay local. **Reference** tables are copied to every worker and written with 2PC.

Primary keys and unique constraints must **include the distribution column**, the same rule as for [partitioned tables](/m7/partitioning). Foreign keys work between colocated tables on the key, or to reference tables.
Schema-based sharding (Citus 12+) distributes whole schemas, one per node, for apps with up to thousands of tenants and no tenant column.

lessons.title: Distributed query execution
tldr: A sharded query is planned twice: the **coordinator** decides which shards it needs and splits the work into **tasks**, and each worker plans and runs its task as an ordinary PostgreSQL query.
How the query uses the distribution column decides its cost, from one round trip to one worker up to a full shuffle of rows between all workers.

visualizer.title: Five queries on four shard groups
visualizer.caption: Pick a query type and step through it. Tasks fly out, partial results fly back with the real numbers of the playground data.

presets.label: Router: the key prunes to one shard
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM ads WHERE company_id = 7;
SELECT tableoid::regclass AS shard, count(*) FROM ads WHERE company_id = 7 GROUP BY 1;
presets.note: Partition pruning plays the role of the Citus router: only `ads_s3` is scanned, and company 7 has 100 ads there. This is a single-node model of the idea, not Citus.
