presets.label: Fan-out: no key, every shard
presets.sql: EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM ads WHERE clicks > 50;
presets.note: An `Append` over all four parts: the single-node shape of a multi-shard query with **Task Count: 4**.

presets.label: Aggregates in two phases
presets.note: `Partial Aggregate` per part and one `Finalize Aggregate` on top: the same split Citus makes between workers and coordinator. Both averages are 42.55.

presets.label: Colocated join, pushed down
presets.note: Each `ads_sN` joins only `campaigns_sN`, and the grouping happens inside each pair. A colocated distributed join runs exactly like this, one pair per worker.

presets.label: Join without the key
presets.note: Without `company_id` in the join, any part may match any part: one big join over two `Append`s. Even with a filter on `ads`, every `campaigns` part is scanned. In Citus the first query needs a repartition join.

presets.label: Move a shard
presets.note: Copy, swap the new copy in, drop the old one, all in one transaction: the table never loses a row. A Citus shard move does the same across machines, with logical replication so that writes can continue.

presets.label: Split a hot shard
presets.note: The largest part (1300 rows) becomes two parts of 900 and 400 by doubling the modulus for that slice. Splitting the hash range is how a sharded system relieves a hot shard.

production.title: A dashboard query that touched every shard
production.context: A multi-tenant analytics product runs on Citus with 32 shards per table. One dashboard tile became slow for every customer at once.
production.problem: The tile joined `ads` to `campaigns` on `campaign_id` only and filtered by `company_id` on one side. Citus could not prove that both sides were on one shard, so with repartition joins enabled for reporting it re-shuffled rows between all workers on each request.
production.solution: Log multi-shard queries in staging to find such statements, then add the tenant key to every join and filter so the query becomes a router query.
production.outcome: The tile now sends one task to one worker instead of shuffling rows between all of them, so its latency no longer grows with the number of shards, and the workers stop running work that returns nothing.

pitfalls.title: Joins that need repartitioning
pitfalls.symptom: A query that worked on single-node PostgreSQL fails on Citus with an error that the join requires repartitioning.
pitfalls.cause: The join does not use the distribution column of colocated tables, and `citus.enable_repartition_joins` is off by default.
pitfalls.fix: Add the distribution column to the join, make the small side a reference table, or, for rare analytics only, enable repartition joins for that session.
pitfalls.sql: SET citus.enable_repartition_joins = on;  -- per session, for an ad-hoc report

pitfalls.title: Connection storms on the workers
pitfalls.symptom: Workers hit `max_connections` during a burst of multi-shard queries.
pitfalls.cause: The adaptive executor opens up to `citus.max_adaptive_executor_pool_size` (default 16) connections per worker per session to run tasks in parallel.
pitfalls.fix: Pool clients in front of the coordinator, keep `citus.max_shared_pool_size` below the workers' `max_connections`, and lower the per-session pool size for many small queries.
pitfalls.sql:
ALTER SYSTEM SET citus.max_adaptive_executor_pool_size = 4;
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

pitfalls.title: A CTE that pulls everything to the coordinator
pitfalls.symptom: A query fails with an error about the maximum intermediate result size, or uses gigabytes of temp space on the coordinator.
pitfalls.cause: A subquery or CTE that cannot be pushed down is run first and its result is sent to the workers (push-pull). Results are capped by `citus.max_intermediate_result_size` (default 1 GB).
pitfalls.fix: Filter and aggregate inside the CTE so that it returns a few rows, or rewrite it so that it joins on the distribution column and can be pushed down.

pitfalls.title: Rebalancing a table without a replica identity
pitfalls.symptom: A rebalance stops with `cannot use logical replication to transfer shards of the relation … since it doesn't have a REPLICA IDENTITY or PRIMARY KEY`, or writes to that table block or fail during the move.
pitfalls.cause: Online moves stream changes with logical replication, which needs a primary key or replica identity. With the default `auto` mode such a table makes the move fail with an error; `block_writes` copies it while blocking writes, and `force_logical` makes concurrent updates and deletes fail.
pitfalls.fix: Give every distributed table a primary key before rebalancing. Preview with `get_rebalance_table_shards_plan()` and watch `citus_rebalance_status()`.

pointers: **Router** query: the filter pins the distribution column, so one task goes to one worker and any SQL works, much like [partition pruning](/m7/partitioning) on one node.
**Multi-shard** query: one task per shard in parallel, merged on the coordinator. Aggregates split into worker parts and a final step (avg → sum + count).
Joins on the distribution column of **colocated** tables push down; other joins need a **repartition** shuffle, which is off by default.
EXPLAIN shows `Custom Scan (Citus Adaptive)` with `Task Count` and one sample task plan from a worker.
Rebalancing moves whole colocated shard groups, online through logical replication when tables have a replica identity.

lessons.title: Distributed transactions and consistency
tldr: A transaction that writes on several nodes needs an **atomic commit protocol**, usually **two-phase commit** (prepare everywhere, then commit everywhere), plus a way to order events across machines whose clocks disagree.
Without them a crash can commit half a transfer, and the guarantees a single node gives for free (isolation, sequences, unique keys, foreign keys) each need a new answer.

visualizer.title: Two-phase commit, clocks and cross-node rules
visualizer.caption: Step through three 2PC scenarios, including a coordinator crash after PREPARE. Then send messages between two skewed clocks, and click the matrix to compare systems.

presets.label: Two-phase commit, both phases
presets.note: Between PREPARE and COMMIT PREPARED the balances still read 100 and 0: prepared work is invisible. After phase 2 they read 70 and 30, and nothing is left prepared.

presets.label: In doubt: locks with no session
presets.note: The prepared transaction holds its locks with `pid` NULL: no session owns them. NOWAIT reports the lock instead of waiting, SKIP LOCKED leaves row 3 out, and `backend_xmin` is held at the prepared xid. The preset resolves it at the end.

presets.label: Recovery from the decision log
presets.note: xfer-44 has a logged commit, so both halves are committed. xfer-45 never got a decision, so the safe choice is to roll it back. Any session may finish a prepared transaction.

presets.label: Two nodes, two clocks
presets.note: One logical transfer left two local xids with two commit timestamps. Each node orders its own history; nothing on a node knows the other node's xids. That is why distributed systems need a shared timestamp such as an HLC.

presets.label: Sequences across nodes
presets.note: Interleaved increments never collide, but every node must know the scheme forever. Snowflake ids embed time and node, so they sort roughly by time without coordination.

presets.label: Unique per node is not unique
presets.note: Each node's unique index only sees its own rows, so the same email exists twice. A single table that owns the value turns the second claim into an error before anything is written.

production.title: An orphaned prepared transaction that stopped VACUUM
production.context: A payments service moves money between accounts on different shards. Its transaction manager uses `PREPARE TRANSACTION` on each database and a decision log.
production.problem: A deploy killed the manager between the two phases. Weeks later table bloat grew on one shard, wraparound warnings appeared, and some account rows timed out on every update. A prepared transaction from that deploy still held its locks and its xmin.
production.solution: Alert on old prepared transactions, resolve each GID from the decision log, and make the manager run recovery on start-up. Keep `max_prepared_transactions` at 0 on databases that no transaction manager uses.
production.sql:
-- alert: anything prepared for more than 5 minutes
SELECT gid, prepared, now() - prepared AS age, owner, database
FROM pg_prepared_xacts WHERE prepared < now() - interval '5 minutes';

-- how far it holds back cleanup
SELECT gid, age(transaction) AS xid_age FROM pg_prepared_xacts ORDER BY xid_age DESC;

-- resolve from the decision log (from any session)
COMMIT PREPARED 'xfer-90211:w3';     -- decision = commit
ROLLBACK PREPARED 'xfer-90217:w3';   -- no decision logged
production.outcome: With the orphan resolved, VACUUM caught up and the locks were released. The alert now fires within minutes, long before bloat or wraparound pressure can build.

pitfalls.title: Forgotten prepared transactions
pitfalls.symptom: VACUUM removes nothing, `age(datfrozenxid)` climbs, and some rows are locked although no session is running.
pitfalls.cause: A prepared transaction survives restarts, keeps its locks and holds back the xmin horizon until someone commits or rolls it back.
pitfalls.fix: Monitor `pg_prepared_xacts`, resolve each GID from the transaction manager's log, and keep `max_prepared_transactions = 0` where nothing uses 2PC.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT gid, prepared, age(transaction) FROM pg_prepared_xacts ORDER BY prepared;

pitfalls.title: Assuming postgres_fdw commits atomically
pitfalls.symptom: After a network error, one server has the order and the other does not.
pitfalls.cause: `postgres_fdw` commits each remote transaction when the local one commits, without two-phase commit. A failure between those commits leaves partial results.
pitfalls.fix: Do not rely on cross-server atomicity through FDWs. Use a coordinator that runs `PREPARE TRANSACTION` on each server, or design with an outbox and idempotent retries.

pitfalls.title: Prepared transactions on a standby
pitfalls.symptom: A hot standby refuses to start after the primary raised `max_prepared_transactions`.
pitfalls.cause: A standby must have `max_prepared_transactions`, `max_connections` and a few other limits at least as high as the primary, because it replays the primary's prepared transactions.
pitfalls.fix: Raise the setting on standbys first, then on the primary. If you use 2PC, set it at least as high as `max_connections`.

pitfalls.title: Read Committed code on a Snapshot-only system
pitfalls.symptom: An application moved to a distributed SQL database gets serialization errors (SQLSTATE `40001`) that never happened on PostgreSQL.
pitfalls.cause: Some systems map READ COMMITTED to snapshot isolation unless a flag is set, so concurrent updates abort instead of waiting and re-reading.
pitfalls.fix: Enable the system's Read Committed mode where available (YugabyteDB: `yb_enable_read_committed_isolation`) and retry `40001` in the application in any case.

pointers: 2PC: **PREPARE TRANSACTION** on every participant, durably log the decision, then **COMMIT PREPARED** (or **ROLLBACK PREPARED**) everywhere. A failed PREPARE is a rollback.
If the coordinator dies after PREPARE, participants are **in doubt**: they hold locks and xmin until recovery reads the log and finishes. 2PC is a blocking protocol.
`max_prepared_transactions` is 0 by default, which disables 2PC. `pg_prepared_xacts` lists what is prepared, and any session can finish it.
A **hybrid logical clock** (physical, logical) orders causes before effects across nodes with skewed clocks. Commit timestamps decide "latest" in multi-master systems.

Across nodes, sequences, unique keys, foreign keys and [isolation](/m5/isolation-levels) all weaken unless the system adds global machinery for them. Old prepared transactions also block [wraparound protection](/m7/xid-wraparound).

lessons.title: Distributed SQL and multi-master
tldr: **Distributed SQL** systems such as YugabyteDB put a PostgreSQL-derived query layer on top of a sharded store where every shard (a **tablet**) is replicated with **Raft**, while **multi-master** systems such as EDB PGD and pgEdge Spock let every PostgreSQL node accept writes and replicate them to the others asynchronously.
Both remove the single primary, but the first pays with a consensus round trip on every write and the second with **conflicts** that must be resolved after commit.

visualizer.title: Raft tablets and a multi-master conflict
visualizer.caption: Write rows and fail nodes to watch tablet leaders move. Then make two nodes change the same row and pick a conflict resolution rule and a clock offset.

presets.label: Both nodes change the same row
presets.note: Each node read 100 and committed its own change. The log shows what each would replicate: old value, new value and a commit timestamp (`track_commit_timestamp = on`). This models two nodes with two schemas on one server.

presets.label: Last update wins
presets.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (id) id, origin AS winner, new_balance AS converged_balance,
       pg_xact_commit_timestamp(xid::text::xid)::text AS winning_commit,
       100 + 50 + 20 AS expected_if_nothing_lost
FROM change_log
ORDER BY id, pg_xact_commit_timestamp(xid::text::xid) DESC, origin DESC;
presets.note: The later commit timestamp wins on both nodes, so they agree on 120, and the +50 from node A is gone. That is the **lost update** of last-update-wins. The tie-breaker on origin covers equal timestamps.

presets.label: Delta-apply: replicate the difference
presets.note: Each node adds the other's difference instead of copying its value: both reach 170. `session_replication_role = replica` is how an apply worker keeps triggers from logging the replicated change again.

presets.label: Different columns, same row
presets.sql:
UPDATE node_a.accounts SET owner = 'bo k.' WHERE id = 2;   -- node A renames
UPDATE node_b.accounts SET balance = 55 WHERE id = 2;       -- node B changes the balance

WITH newest AS (
  SELECT origin FROM change_log WHERE id = 2
  ORDER BY pg_xact_commit_timestamp(xid::text::xid) DESC, origin DESC LIMIT 1
)
SELECT 'row level: newest row wins' AS resolution, r.owner, r.balance
FROM newest n, LATERAL (
  SELECT owner, balance FROM node_a.accounts WHERE id = 2 AND n.origin = 'node_a'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT owner, balance FROM node_b.accounts WHERE id = 2 AND n.origin = 'node_b') r
UNION ALL
SELECT 'column level: newest value per column', a.owner, b.balance
FROM node_a.accounts a JOIN node_b.accounts b USING (id) WHERE id = 2;
presets.note: The two nodes touched **different** columns, yet a row-level rule keeps one whole row: the later balance survives and the rename is lost (`bo`, 55). Tracking a change time per column merges both edits (`bo k.`, 55). EDB PGD resolves per row by default and can switch a table to column-level detection, which needs `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`.

presets.label: A unique key on two nodes
presets.note: Both inserts succeed locally. When A's row arrives at B, the email already exists with another id. PostgreSQL 18 counts such cases per subscription as `confl_insert_exists`, `confl_update_origin_differs` and five more.

presets.label: Replication needs a row identity
presets.note: A table without a primary key cannot publish UPDATE or DELETE, so the error comes from the publishing node itself. Multi-master tools need a primary key on every replicated table to match rows at all.

presets.label: Hash ranges into tablets
presets.sql:
CREATE TABLE orders_yb AS SELECT g AS id FROM generate_series(1, 3000) g;

SELECT CASE WHEN h < 21845 THEN 'tablet 1 (0x0000-0x5554)'
            WHEN h < 43690 THEN 'tablet 2 (0x5555-0xAAA9)'
            ELSE 'tablet 3 (0xAAAA-0xFFFF)' END AS tablet,
       count(*) AS rows
FROM (SELECT hashint4(id) & 65535 AS h FROM orders_yb) s
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
presets.note: YugabyteDB hashes the first primary key column into 0x0000–0xFFFF and gives each tablet one slice, as `SPLIT INTO 3 TABLETS` would. This uses PostgreSQL's own hash as a stand-in, so the counts show the idea, not YugabyteDB's exact placement.

production.title: Two regions, one wallet table
production.context: A consumer app runs in two regions and wants local writes in both, so it evaluates active-active PostgreSQL with Spock.
production.problem: A test with last-update-wins lost balance top-ups whenever a user's phone and a scheduled job changed the same wallet in different regions within a second, exactly the counter case.
production.solution: Home each user to one region for writes so most rows have one writer. Turn the remaining counters into delta-apply columns, enable commit timestamps, use globally unique ids, and keep NTP tight because "last" is decided by clocks. Tables that need strict invariants stay single-writer.
production.sql:
-- postgresql.conf on every node
--   wal_level = logical
--   track_commit_timestamp = on
--   shared_preload_libraries = 'spock'
--   spock.save_resolutions = on        -- log every resolution to spock.resolutions
ALTER SYSTEM SET spock.conflict_resolution = 'last_update_wins';

-- counters replicate their difference, not their value (column must be NOT NULL)
ALTER TABLE wallets ALTER COLUMN balance
  SET (log_old_value = true, delta_apply_function = spock.delta_apply);

-- find conflicts that were resolved automatically
SELECT * FROM spock.resolutions LIMIT 20;
production.outcome: Concurrent top-ups now add up on both nodes, and the few remaining overwrite conflicts are visible in the resolutions log instead of silently lost.

pitfalls.title: Last-update-wins on counters
pitfalls.symptom: Balances or stock counts drift below what the transactions add up to, with no error anywhere.
pitfalls.cause: Two nodes read the same value and each wrote its own result. Resolving by commit timestamp keeps one row and discards the other change.
pitfalls.fix: Write each counter on one node only, or use delta-apply columns (Spock), conflict-free replicated data types (EDB PGD ships counters such as `bdr.crdt_pncounter` and `bdr.crdt_delta_counter`), or an append-only ledger summed on read.

pitfalls.title: Clock skew deciding the winner
pitfalls.symptom: An older change overwrites a newer one after a conflict.
pitfalls.cause: Last-update-wins compares commit timestamps from different machines. A node whose clock runs behind loses even when it wrote last.
pitfalls.fix: Keep clocks synchronized tightly, monitor skew, and do not rely on last-update-wins for data where order matters.

pitfalls.title: Foreign keys and uniqueness during apply
pitfalls.symptom: Child rows reference parents that do not exist on another node, or the same email shows up twice across nodes.
pitfalls.cause: Each node checks constraints only against its own rows when it commits. Spock does not enforce foreign keys while applying remote changes, and unique conflicts are resolved by rule.
pitfalls.fix: Route writes for one entity to one node, use global id generators (snowflake-style sequences or UUIDs), and audit cross-node uniqueness regularly.

pitfalls.title: Treating distributed SQL as plain PostgreSQL
pitfalls.symptom: After moving to YugabyteDB, simple single-row workloads are fine but joins and new connections are slow, and some transactions fail with `40001`.
pitfalls.cause: Multi-tablet queries need RPCs between nodes, a new connection loads the catalog over the network, and isolation may run as Snapshot when Read Committed is not enabled.
pitfalls.fix: Keep hot transactions on one tablet (filter by the full hash key), colocate small tables, use a connection pooler, enable Read Committed and wait queues, and retry `40001`.
pitfalls.sql:
CREATE TABLE orders (customer_id int, order_id int, total numeric,
  PRIMARY KEY ((customer_id) HASH, order_id ASC)) SPLIT INTO 12 TABLETS;

pointers: YugabyteDB: YSQL reuses PostgreSQL's query layer over **DocDB**; tables split into **tablets**, each a **Raft** group with one leader. A write commits on a majority; a lost leader is replaced within seconds (about 3 s with default heartbeat settings).
Hash sharding uses a 16-bit space **0x0000–0xFFFF**, and by default only the first primary key column is hashed. Range sharding (`ASC`/`DESC`) suits range scans but risks hot spots.
Multi-master (PGD, Spock) commits locally and replicates later, so conflicts are detected on apply, for example (in PostgreSQL 18 terms) insert_exists, update_origin_differs, delete_missing.

Resolution rules (`last_update_wins`, `keep_local`, `apply_remote`, `error`) trade correctness for availability; delta-apply fixes counters; global sequences fix ids. See [logical replication](/m7/logical-replication) for the building block.
Use multi-master only for simple, partitionable write patterns; use distributed SQL when you need strong consistency across regions and can pay the write latency.

lessons.title: High-availability clusters in practice
tldr: An HA cluster is a primary with standbys plus a manager such as **Patroni** that holds a **leader key** in a consensus store (etcd, Consul, ZooKeeper), promotes a standby when the leader stops renewing it, and lets a proxy route clients to whoever holds the key.
PostgreSQL ships replication and `pg_promote()` but no failure detection or fencing, and getting those wrong means either long outages or two primaries.

visualizer.title: A Patroni failover, second by second
visualizer.caption: Step through a crash, a network cut and a planned switchover. Move the ttl, loop_wait and retry_timeout sliders to see the timings change and the split-brain rule break.

presets.label: Am I the primary?
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() AS is_standby,
       pg_current_wal_lsn() AS current_lsn,
       pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn()) AS wal_file,
       (SELECT timeline_id FROM pg_control_checkpoint()) AS timeline;
presets.note: This is the first question every health check asks. A promoted standby starts a new **timeline**, visible in the first 8 hex digits of the WAL file name. This single node is a primary on timeline 1.

presets.label: One slot per member
presets.note: With `use_slots` (the default) Patroni keeps a physical slot for each other member, so the primary retains the WAL a lagging replica still needs. Here no replica is connected, so both slots are inactive.

presets.label: How far behind is a replica?
presets.note: Lag is a WAL distance in bytes. Patroni compares it with `maximum_lag_on_failover` before letting a replica take over, and HAProxy can exclude laggards with `/replica?lag=…`. The inactive slots keep growing until dropped.

presets.label: Synchronous commit, per transaction
presets.note: `synchronous_standby_names` has context `sighup`: Patroni writes it into the configuration when `synchronous_mode` is on. Each transaction can still choose how long to wait. With no standbys listed, nothing waits here.

presets.label: Check the timing rule
presets.sql:
SELECT name, ttl, loop_wait, retry_timeout,
       loop_wait + 2 * retry_timeout AS worst_demote_s,
       loop_wait + 2 * retry_timeout <= ttl AS rule_ok,
       ttl + 2 + 2 * 3 AS approx_failover_s
FROM dcs_configs ORDER BY ttl;
presets.note: Patroni requires `loop_wait + 2 * retry_timeout <= ttl`; since 3.2 it lowers `loop_wait` (or `retry_timeout`) with a warning when the values break it. The "wrong" row breaks it: the old leader could still be primary when the key expires. The failover estimate adds an assumed 2 s promotion and two 3 s HAProxy checks to the TTL.

production.title: A three-node Patroni cluster with zero data loss
production.context: An order service needs automatic failover within a minute and must never lose an acknowledged order.
production.problem: Its first setup had one asynchronous standby and a script that promoted it when pings failed. A network blip produced two primaries, and a real crash lost the last seconds of orders.
production.solution: Run three PostgreSQL nodes under Patroni with a three-member etcd, `synchronous_mode` on, slots per member, `pg_rewind` for returning nodes, and HAProxy checking `/primary` for writes and `/replica?lag=…` for reads.
production.sql:
-- patroni.yml (bootstrap.dcs, applied at first initialization; later: patronictl edit-config)
--   ttl: 30
--   loop_wait: 10
--   retry_timeout: 10
--   maximum_lag_on_failover: 1048576   # bytes; also the default
--   synchronous_mode: true
--   postgresql: { use_pg_rewind: true, use_slots: true }
-- haproxy.cfg (example values, as in Patroni's sample config)
--   listen primary
--     bind *:5000
--     option httpchk GET /primary
--     http-check expect status 200
--     default-server inter 3s fall 3 rise 2 on-marked-down shutdown-sessions
--     server pg1 10.0.0.11:5432 check port 8008
--     server pg2 10.0.0.12:5432 check port 8008
--     server pg3 10.0.0.13:5432 check port 8008

-- on the primary: who is synchronous, and how far behind is everyone?
SELECT application_name, state, sync_state,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn)) AS replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;
production.outcome: A crash now costs well under a minute of write unavailability with the default timings (about 40 s in the worst case modelled above) and no acknowledged order is lost, because a commit returns only after a synchronous standby has it. The isolated old primary demotes itself before anyone else is promoted.

pitfalls.title: Split-brain from a home-made failover script
pitfalls.symptom: After a network blip, two nodes both accept writes, and their data diverges.
pitfalls.cause: The script promoted a standby because it could not reach the primary, but the primary was alive and still serving clients. Nothing fenced it.
pitfalls.fix: Use a manager with a leader lock in a consensus store (Patroni + etcd), so a node that cannot renew the lock demotes itself. Add a watchdog for the case where Patroni itself hangs, and never promote by hand while the old primary may be alive.

pitfalls.title: Timings that break the fencing rule
pitfalls.symptom: Failover tests pass, but under real network trouble the old leader keeps writing after a new one is promoted.
pitfalls.cause: With `loop_wait + 2 * retry_timeout > ttl` the leader key can expire before the isolated leader gives up and demotes. Patroni before 3.2 accepted such values silently; 3.2 and later adjust them and log a warning, which is easy to miss.
pitfalls.fix: Keep `loop_wait + 2 * retry_timeout <= ttl`. Change the values with `patronictl edit-config`; `bootstrap.dcs` only applies when the cluster is first created.

pitfalls.title: Synchronous mode with a single standby
pitfalls.symptom: Writes hang whenever the one synchronous standby restarts.
pitfalls.cause: A commit waits for a synchronous standby. With exactly one candidate and strict settings, there is nobody else to confirm.
pitfalls.fix: Run at least two replicas so another can become synchronous, or use quorum commit (`synchronous_mode: quorum`, `ANY n (...)`) so one standby can be down.

pitfalls.title: An old primary that cannot rejoin
pitfalls.symptom: After failover the old primary refuses to start as a replica because its timeline forked.
pitfalls.cause: It wrote WAL after the fork point that the new primary never received.
pitfalls.fix: Enable `use_pg_rewind` (it needs `wal_log_hints = on` or data checksums), or rebuild the node from a fresh base backup. See [streaming replication](/m7/streaming-replication) for timelines and standbys.

pointers: Patroni keeps a **leader key** with a TTL in a DCS (etcd, Consul, ZooKeeper, Kubernetes). Only the key holder runs as primary; a holder that cannot renew it **demotes itself**.
Defaults `ttl` 30 / `loop_wait` 10 / `retry_timeout` 10, and the rule **`loop_wait + 2 * retry_timeout <= ttl`**. A crash costs roughly the TTL plus promotion plus proxy checks.
HAProxy routes by HTTP checks against Patroni's REST API: `/primary` for writes, `/replica?lag=` for reads. A pooler such as [PgBouncer](/m7/connection-pooling) sits behind it or beside it.
`synchronous_mode` makes failover lose nothing acknowledged; asynchronous failover can lose the unreplicated tail.
Switchover is the planned, lossless version: rehearse it regularly. A returning old primary needs `pg_rewind` or a rebuild.

lessons.title: Geometry, geography and coordinate systems
tldr: PostGIS adds two spatial types to PostgreSQL: **geometry**, measured on a flat plane in the units of its coordinate system (its **SRID**), and **geography**, measured on the curved Earth in metres.
Every coordinate means nothing without its SRID, so picking the right type and coordinate system up front is what makes distances, areas and joins come out right.

visualizer.title: One pair of cities, three rulers
visualizer.caption: Switch the ruler and watch the grid morph from longitude/latitude to Web Mercator. **Next city pair** moves north and south; the checkbox shows what swapped coordinates do.

presets.label: Make a point
presets.sql:
SELECT ST_AsText(geom)  AS wkt,
       ST_AsEWKT(geom)  AS ewkt,
       ST_SRID(geom)    AS srid,
       geom::text       AS hexewkb,
       ST_AsGeoJSON(geom) AS geojson,
       ST_SRID(ST_MakePoint(-0.1276, 51.5072)) AS makepoint_srid
FROM cities WHERE name = 'London';
presets.note: The same point in four encodings. The default text output is **HEXEWKB**. `ST_MakePoint` alone has SRID **0** (unknown); `ST_Point(x, y, 4326)` sets it in one call.

presets.label: Coordinate systems
presets.note: **8500** coordinate systems ship in `spatial_ref_sys`. 4326 is longitude/latitude on WGS 84, 3857 is Web Mercator, and 3035, 27700 and 32618 are local projections in metres.

presets.label: Three rulers
presets.sql:
SELECT ST_Distance(a.geom, b.geom)                         AS geometry_degrees,
       ST_Distance(a.geom::geography, b.geom::geography) / 1000 AS geography_km,
       ST_Distance(ST_Transform(a.geom, 3857), ST_Transform(b.geom, 3857)) / 1000 AS mercator_km,
       ST_Distance(ST_Transform(a.geom, 3035), ST_Transform(b.geom, 3035)) / 1000 AS laea_europe_km
FROM cities a, cities b
WHERE a.name = 'London' AND b.name = 'Paris';
presets.note: geometry in 4326 returns **3.63 degrees**. geography returns **343.9 km**. Web Mercator says 537 km, about 56% too long at this latitude. The local equal-area projection 3035 is within 0.5 km.

presets.label: Swap lat and lon
presets.sql:
SELECT ST_AsText(ST_Point(51.5072, -0.1276, 4326)) AS swapped_london,
       ST_Distance(ST_Point(51.5072, -0.1276, 4326)::geography,
                   ST_Point(48.8566, 2.3522, 4326)::geography) / 1000 AS swapped_km,
       ST_AsText('SRID=4326;POINT(200 100)'::geography) AS out_of_range;
presets.note: Latitude first puts "London" in the Indian Ocean, and the distance comes out as **402.7 km**, with no error. Out-of-range geography input is silently wrapped to `POINT(-160 80)`.

presets.label: Area by latitude
presets.sql:
SELECT lat,
       ST_Area(cell)                                   AS square_degrees,
       round((ST_Area(cell::geography) / 1e6)::numeric) AS km2_true,
       round((ST_Area(ST_Transform(cell, 3857)) / 1e6)::numeric) AS km2_mercator
FROM unnest(ARRAY[0, 30, 45, 60, 70]) AS lat,
     LATERAL (SELECT ST_MakeEnvelope(0, lat, 1, lat + 1, 4326)) AS c(cell);
presets.note: A 1° × 1° cell is **1 square degree** everywhere, but its true area falls from 12 309 km² at the equator to 6 123 km² at 60°. Mercator grows it to 25 168 km².

presets.label: Typmods guard the column
presets.note: `geometry(Point, 4326)` rejects a wrong SRID and a wrong shape. A point that really is in 27700 must be **transformed**, not relabelled; the third insert works and lands on London.

presets.label: The antimeridian
presets.sql:
SELECT ST_Distance('SRID=4326;POINT(179.5 0)'::geometry,
                   'SRID=4326;POINT(-179.5 0)'::geometry)   AS geometry_degrees,
       ST_Distance('SRID=4326;POINT(179.5 0)'::geography,
                   'SRID=4326;POINT(-179.5 0)'::geography) / 1000 AS geography_km;
presets.note: Two points 1° apart across the date line. The plane thinks they are **359 degrees** apart; geography knows the Earth is round and says **111 km**.

production.title: A delivery app that measured in the wrong units
production.context: A delivery app stored courier and customer positions as `geometry(Point, 4326)` and charged a fee per kilometre. To get metres, a developer transformed both points to Web Mercator (3857) and called `ST_Distance`.
production.problem: Web Mercator stretches lengths by about 1/cos(latitude). At 51.5° N every distance came out about **1.6×** too long, so customers were overcharged. Moving the code to `ST_Distance(geom, geom)` in 4326 made it worse: the result was in **degrees**.
production.solution: Measure with **geography**, which works on the spheroid in metres. Store a geography column, or cast at query time. For heavy analysis in one city, transform once to a local projected SRID in metres.
production.outcome: For London–Paris the three answers are 537.3 km (3857), 3.63 (degrees) and 343.9 km (geography). The fee now uses the 343.9 km kind of number, and the local projection agrees to within half a kilometre.

pitfalls.title: Latitude written first
pitfalls.symptom: Points show up in the ocean or on the wrong continent, and distances are plausible but wrong. No error is raised.
pitfalls.cause: PostGIS coordinates are **x, y**, which for geodetic data means **longitude, latitude**. Many web APIs and spreadsheets write latitude first.
pitfalls.fix: Always pass longitude first to `ST_Point`/`ST_MakePoint`. Add a check constraint for your region to catch swaps.
pitfalls.sql:
ALTER TABLE cities ADD CONSTRAINT in_europe
  CHECK (ST_X(geom) BETWEEN -25 AND 45 AND ST_Y(geom) BETWEEN 34 AND 72);

pitfalls.title: Reading degrees as metres
pitfalls.symptom: `ST_Distance` returns 0.0036 for two shops 266 m apart, or `ST_DWithin(geom, pt, 500)` matches the whole country.
pitfalls.cause: geometry in SRID 4326 measures on the lon/lat plane, so its unit is the **degree**. A degree of longitude is 111 km at the equator and 72 km at 50° N.
pitfalls.fix: Cast to geography for metres, or transform to a projected SRID whose unit is metres.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT ST_DWithin(a.geom::geography, b.geom::geography, 500) FROM cities a, cities b;

pitfalls.title: ST_SetSRID where ST_Transform was needed
pitfalls.symptom: Points land within metres of 0° N 0° E (or of a national grid's origin), or `ST_Transform` fails with an invalid-coordinate error.
pitfalls.cause: `ST_SetSRID` only **relabels** coordinates. `ST_Transform` **recomputes** them into another system. Labelling metres as 4326 makes impossible degrees; labelling degrees as a metre-based SRID puts every point a few metres from that system's origin.
pitfalls.fix: Set the SRID the data was really produced in, then transform.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT ST_AsText(ST_Transform(ST_SetSRID(ST_MakePoint(530043, 180358), 27700), 4326));

pitfalls.title: Measuring in Web Mercator
pitfalls.symptom: Lengths and areas from tiles or map exports are 1.5–4× too large in northern cities.
pitfalls.cause: 3857 is made for drawing tiles, not for measuring. Its scale grows with latitude.
pitfalls.fix: Keep 3857 for display. Measure with geography or with a local equal-area or conformal projection.

pointers: **geometry**: planar, units of its SRID, the richest function set. **geography**: spheroid, metres, the right default for lon/lat data spread over a wide area.
Coordinates are **(x, y) = (longitude, latitude)**. `ST_Point(lon, lat, 4326)` builds a point with its SRID in one call.
`ST_Transform` changes coordinates; `ST_SetSRID` only changes the label.
Use typmods such as `geometry(Point, 4326)` so the column rejects the wrong SRID or shape.
Next: how a spatial index answers "what is near here" in [Spatial indexes](/e4/spatial-indexes).

lessons.title: Spatial indexes
tldr: A PostGIS **GiST** index is an R-tree of **bounding boxes**: each page stores boxes, and each box covers everything beneath it.
It lets a query skip whole regions with the cheap `&&` box test and run the exact, expensive geometry test only on the few rows that survive.

visualizer.title: Two-step filtering through a GiST tree
visualizer.caption: Drag the ✕, set the radius, and step the phases. Then switch to **geom::geography** to see the same query lose its index.

presets.label: Box overlap: &&
presets.note: `&&` is answered by the GiST index alone: **Bitmap Index Scan**, about 5 index buffers. The long hex string is the query box in WKB.

presets.label: ST_DWithin, indexed
presets.note: Read the **Index Cond**: `geom && st_expand(…, 0.005)`. Two-step filtering in one plan. The radius is **0.005 degrees**, because the column is geometry in 4326.

presets.label: The geography cast trap
presets.note: Metres at last, but the plan is a **Seq Scan** over the whole table: **19 995** rows removed by the filter. The index is on `geom`, not on `geom::geography`.

presets.label: Fix: expression index
presets.note: Same query, now a **Bitmap Index Scan** on `places_geog_gist` with `_st_expand` on geography. A few index pages, 8 heap blocks, and only 3 rows removed.

presets.label: ST_Distance is never indexed
presets.note: Same 5 rows, but **Seq Scan** even with the geography index: `ST_Distance` has no index support. Write radius filters with `ST_DWithin`.

presets.label: GiST vs SP-GiST vs BRIN
presets.note: GiST 864 kB, SP-GiST 968 kB, BRIN **24 kB**. BRIN is tiny because it stores one box per range of 4 pages. Whether it helps depends on row order (next preset).

presets.label: BRIN needs sorted rows
presets.note: On `places` the rows are scattered, so every range box covers the whole area: **lossy=171**, all pages. `ORDER BY geom` lays rows out along a space-filling curve, and BRIN then reads only about **16** pages.

production.title: A store finder that slowed down as it grew
production.context: A retail team stores 2 million store and pickup points as `geometry(Point, 4326)` with a GiST index. The "stores within 2 km" endpoint used `ST_DWithin(geom::geography, $1::geography, 2000)` to get metres.
production.problem: Latency grew in step with the table. `EXPLAIN` showed a **Seq Scan** with almost every row removed by the filter. The cast to geography made the filter an expression that the GiST index on `geom` cannot serve.
production.solution: Add an expression index on the cast, so the planner finds an index for the exact expression. Long term, migrate to a `geography` column (or a projected SRID in metres) and index that.
production.outcome: In the playground the same pattern goes from a Seq Scan that discards 19 995 of 20 000 rows to a Bitmap Index Scan that reads a few index pages and 8 heap blocks. The gap grows with the table: the seq scan is linear, the index descent is logarithmic.

pitfalls.title: Wrapping the indexed column in a cast or function
pitfalls.symptom: `EXPLAIN` shows `Seq Scan` and a huge `Rows Removed by Filter` even though a GiST index exists.
pitfalls.cause: An index matches only the exact indexed expression. `geom::geography`, `ST_Transform(geom, 3857)` or `ST_Buffer(geom, …)` on the column side are different expressions.
pitfalls.fix: Put the transformation on the **constant** side, or create an expression index that matches.
pitfalls.sql:
CREATE INDEX ON places USING gist (ST_Transform(geom, 27700));
SELECT * FROM places WHERE ST_DWithin(ST_Transform(geom, 27700), ST_Transform($1, 27700), 500);

pitfalls.title: Filtering with ST_Distance
pitfalls.symptom: `WHERE ST_Distance(a, b) < 500` is slow and gets slower as the table grows.
pitfalls.cause: `ST_Distance` has no index support. It runs for every row.
pitfalls.fix: Use `ST_DWithin(a, b, 500)`. It adds `&&` against the expanded box, so the index cuts the candidates first.

pitfalls.title: Using && when you mean "inside"
pitfalls.symptom: A map query returns features that are near the area but not in it, especially long diagonal lines.
pitfalls.cause: `&&` compares **bounding boxes** only. A diagonal road has a box much bigger than the road.
pitfalls.fix: Use `ST_Intersects` for the exact answer. It does the `&&` index step for you and then the exact test.

pitfalls.title: BRIN on unsorted or frequently updated data
pitfalls.symptom: A BRIN index exists, but `EXPLAIN` shows `Heap Blocks: lossy=` equal to the whole table.
pitfalls.cause: Each BRIN range stores one box covering its rows. If rows are scattered, every box covers everything.
pitfalls.fix: Use BRIN only for append-mostly data written in spatial order (or rewritten with `ORDER BY geom`). Use GiST otherwise.

pointers: Indexes store **boxes**; queries run in two steps: box filter (index) then exact test (recheck).
Index-aware: `&&`, `~`, `@`, `ST_Intersects`, `ST_Contains`, `ST_Within`, `ST_Covers`, `ST_DWithin` and friends. Not `ST_Distance`.
Casting the column (`geom::geography`) needs a matching **expression index** or the plan becomes a Seq Scan.
GiST is the default; SP-GiST suits points; BRIN is tiny but needs spatially sorted rows. Compare [GiST and SP-GiST](/m4/gist-spgist) and [BRIN](/m4/brin) internals.
Read the plan for `Index Cond` and `Rows Removed by Filter`, as in [EXPLAIN ANALYZE](/m4/explain-analyze).

lessons.title: Nearest-neighbour search
tldr: `ORDER BY geom <-> point LIMIT k` asks for the k nearest rows, and a GiST index answers it directly by returning rows in distance order.
It exists because "the closest five" has no radius to filter on, and sorting every row by distance gets slower as the table grows.

visualizer.title: Best-first search through the index
visualizer.caption: Pop entries off the priority queue and watch pages open and rows come out in order. Drag the ✕ or change **LIMIT k**, then compare the work with a full sort.

presets.label: KNN plan
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF)
SELECT id FROM places
ORDER BY geom <-> ST_Point(-0.1276, 51.5072, 4326)
LIMIT 5;
presets.note: **Index Scan** with `Order By: (geom <-> …)`. No Sort node: the index hands rows over already in distance order, after about 10 buffers.

presets.label: Degrees can mis-rank
presets.sql:
SELECT id, kind,
       round((geom <-> ST_Point(-0.1276, 51.5072, 4326))::numeric, 5) AS degrees,
       round(ST_Distance(geom::geography, ST_Point(-0.1276, 51.5072, 4326)::geography)::numeric, 1) AS metres
FROM places
ORDER BY geom <-> ST_Point(-0.1276, 51.5072, 4326)
LIMIT 6;

SELECT id, round(ST_Distance(geom::geography, ST_Point(-0.1276, 51.5072, 4326)::geography)::numeric, 1) AS metres
FROM places
ORDER BY geom::geography <-> ST_Point(-0.1276, 51.5072, 4326)::geography
LIMIT 6;
presets.note: The first five agree, but the 6th differs: ordering in **degrees** picks #9976 at 652 m, while the true 6th nearest is #11179 at **524 m**. At 51.5° N a degree east is shorter than a degree north.

presets.label: Geography KNN
presets.note: Without a geography index the plan is **Seq Scan + Sort**. With the expression index it becomes an ordered Index Scan. Geography `<->` measures on a sphere, in metres.

presets.label: KNN with a filter
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF)
SELECT id FROM places
WHERE kind = 'pharmacy'
ORDER BY geom <-> ST_Point(-0.1276, 51.5072, 4326)
LIMIT 3;
presets.note: The index walks outward in distance order and the filter throws away non-pharmacies: **Rows Removed by Filter: 11**. A rare kind would mean walking much further.

presets.label: Nearest per row: LATERAL
presets.sql:
SELECT r.id AS rider, p.id AS pharmacy,
       round(ST_Distance(r.geom::geography, p.geom::geography)) AS metres
FROM riders r
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT id, geom FROM places
  WHERE kind = 'pharmacy'
  ORDER BY places.geom <-> r.geom
  LIMIT 1) p
ORDER BY r.id LIMIT 5;

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF)
SELECT r.id, p.id FROM riders r
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT id FROM places WHERE kind = 'pharmacy' ORDER BY places.geom <-> r.geom LIMIT 1) p;
presets.note: For each rider, `r.geom` is a constant inside the subquery, so every probe is an index KNN scan: **Index Searches: 50**, one per rider.

presets.label: Trap: join without LATERAL
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT p.id FROM places p, riders r
WHERE r.id = 1
ORDER BY p.geom <-> r.geom
LIMIT 3;
presets.note: The distance is between two **columns**, so no index can order it: Seq Scan on `places`, then Sort. Rewrite with LATERAL or a scalar subquery.

presets.label: Radius and order
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF)
SELECT id FROM places
WHERE ST_DWithin(geom, ST_Point(-0.1276, 51.5072, 4326), 0.01)
ORDER BY geom <-> ST_Point(-0.1276, 51.5072, 4326)
LIMIT 5;

SELECT 'LINESTRING(0 0, 10 10)'::geometry <-> 'POINT(10 0)'::geometry AS exact_distance,
       'LINESTRING(0 0, 10 10)'::geometry <#> 'POINT(10 0)'::geometry AS box_distance;
presets.note: With a radius the planner filters through the index and **top-N sorts** the 14 survivors. `<#>` is box distance: 0 for a point inside a diagonal line's box, even though the line is 7.07 away.

production.title: Assigning the nearest courier
production.context: A food delivery platform assigns each new order to the nearest free courier. Courier positions are `geometry(Point, 4326)` with a GiST index, updated every few seconds.
production.problem: The first version joined orders to couriers and sorted by `ST_Distance` with a 5 km `ST_DWithin` cap. On busy evenings every order computed distances to hundreds of couriers, and quiet suburbs found nobody inside 5 km.
production.solution: Use a LATERAL KNN probe per order. Order by `<->` so the index walks outward until it finds one free courier, with no fixed radius. Re-rank the few candidates in metres for the final pick.
production.sql:
SELECT o.id, c.id AS courier, ST_Distance(o.geom::geography, c.geom::geography) AS m
FROM new_orders o
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT id, geom FROM couriers
  WHERE status = 'free'
  ORDER BY couriers.geom <-> o.geom
  LIMIT 3) c
ORDER BY o.id, m;
production.outcome: Each order costs one short index descent instead of a scan. In the playground, 50 riders find their nearest pharmacy with 50 index probes in a few milliseconds. Taking 3 by degrees and re-ranking in metres fixes the degree mis-ranking.

pitfalls.title: <-> between two columns
pitfalls.symptom: A nearest-neighbour join is a Seq Scan plus Sort, and gets slower with every row.
pitfalls.cause: The index orders by distance to **one fixed point**. `a.geom <-> b.geom` with both sides from the join has no fixed point.
pitfalls.fix: Use `CROSS JOIN LATERAL (… ORDER BY t.geom <-> outer.geom LIMIT k)`. Inside the subquery the outer value is a constant.

pitfalls.title: Nearest in degrees
pitfalls.symptom: The "nearest" store is sometimes the second or third nearest, mostly in east–west directions.
pitfalls.cause: In SRID 4326, `<->` measures degrees. Away from the equator a degree of longitude is shorter than a degree of latitude.
pitfalls.fix: Order by geography (`geom::geography <-> $1::geography` with a matching index), use a projected SRID, or fetch a few extra rows and re-rank by `ST_Distance` on geography.

pitfalls.title: Ordering by ST_Distance
pitfalls.symptom: `ORDER BY ST_Distance(geom, $1) LIMIT 5` returns correct rows but reads the whole table.
pitfalls.cause: `ST_Distance` is a plain function. Only distance **operators** such as `<->` and `<#>` can drive an ordered index scan.
pitfalls.fix: Order by `geom <-> $1`; select `ST_Distance` in the column list for display.

pitfalls.title: A selective filter on top of KNN
pitfalls.symptom: A KNN query with `WHERE kind = 'rare'` is fast for common kinds and slow for rare ones.
pitfalls.cause: The index returns rows in distance order and the filter rejects them one by one. A rare kind means walking far.
pitfalls.fix: Use a partial index per hot filter value, or a separate table for the rare kind.
pitfalls.sql: CREATE INDEX ON places USING gist (geom) WHERE kind = 'pharmacy';

pointers: `ORDER BY geom <-> constant LIMIT k` is an **index-ordered scan**: rows leave the index already sorted, with no Sort node.
The scan is **best-first** over a priority queue: boxes are keyed by a lower-bound distance, rows by their exact distance.
geometry `<->` uses SRID units (degrees in 4326); geography `<->` gives metres on a sphere and needs a geography index.
`<#>` orders by **bounding-box** distance; nearest-per-row needs **LATERAL**. The same idea for vectors is in [Distance metrics and exact search](/e1/distance-and-exact-search).

lessons.title: Everyday spatial queries
tldr: Most map features are built from a handful of spatial operations: point-in-polygon joins, buffers, unions, clusters and GeoJSON output.
Running them inside PostgreSQL keeps the data, its indexes and its validity rules in one place, so the answers stay correct and fast as the data grows.

visualizer.title: A point-in-polygon join and a DBSCAN run, step by step
visualizer.caption: Step the join zone by zone: box candidates first, then the exact test. Switch to **ST_ClusterDBSCAN**, set eps and minpoints, and watch core, border and noise points appear.

presets.label: Orders per zone
presets.sql:
SELECT z.name, count(o.id) AS orders
FROM zones z
JOIN orders o ON ST_Contains(z.geom, o.geom)
GROUP BY z.name
ORDER BY orders DESC
LIMIT 5;

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF)
SELECT z.name, count(*) FROM zones z
JOIN orders o ON ST_Contains(z.geom, o.geom)
GROUP BY z.name;
presets.note: Z25, Z15 and Z07 hold the hubs (about 1 000 orders each). The plan loops over 33 zones and probes the orders index with `Index Cond: (geom @ z.geom)`, then `Filter: st_contains`: **Rows Removed by Filter: 44** per zone on average.

presets.label: Contains vs covers
presets.sql:
WITH v AS (SELECT ST_PointN(ST_ExteriorRing(geom), 2) AS p FROM zones WHERE id = 12)
SELECT ST_AsText(p) AS shared_corner,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM zones z WHERE ST_Contains(z.geom, v.p))   AS contains,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM zones z WHERE ST_Covers(z.geom, v.p))     AS covers,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM zones z WHERE ST_Intersects(z.geom, v.p)) AS intersects
FROM v;
presets.note: A point exactly on a zone corner: `ST_Contains` says **0** zones (a polygon does not contain its own boundary), `ST_Covers` and `ST_Intersects` say **2**. Pick the one that matches your counting rule.

presets.label: Buffer, length, area
presets.sql:
SELECT r.name,
       round(ST_Length(r.geom)) AS length_m,
       round((ST_Area(ST_Buffer(r.geom, 300)) / 1e6)::numeric, 2) AS corridor_km2,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE ST_DWithin(o.geom, r.geom, 300)) AS orders_within_300m,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM zones z WHERE ST_Intersects(z.geom, r.geom))  AS zones_crossed
FROM route r;
presets.note: The road is **15 097 m** long; its 300 m corridor covers 9.34 km². To count orders near it, `ST_DWithin` (index-aware) beats testing against a buffer polygon.

presets.label: ST_Union vs ST_Collect
presets.sql:
-- Z15 and the six zones around it
SELECT string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name)  AS zones,
       sum(ST_NPoints(geom))               AS input_vertices,
       ST_GeometryType(ST_Union(geom))      AS union_type,
       ST_NPoints(ST_Union(geom))           AS union_vertices,
       round((ST_Area(ST_Union(geom)) / 1e6)::numeric, 2) AS union_km2,
       ST_GeometryType(ST_Collect(geom))    AS collect_type,
       ST_NumGeometries(ST_Collect(geom))   AS collect_parts
FROM zones
WHERE ST_Intersects(geom, (SELECT geom FROM zones WHERE name = 'Z15'));
presets.note: `ST_Union` **dissolves** the shared edges: 7 hexagons (49 vertices) become one Polygon of 19 vertices and 40.92 km² (7 × 5.85). `ST_Collect` only bundles them into a 7-part collection: much cheaper, but the inner edges stay.

presets.label: Clusters: DBSCAN and k-means
presets.sql:
SELECT cid, count(*) AS orders,
       round((ST_Area(ST_ConvexHull(ST_Collect(geom))) / 1e6)::numeric, 2) AS hull_km2
FROM (SELECT ST_ClusterDBSCAN(geom, eps => 100, minpoints => 10) OVER () AS cid, geom FROM orders) s
GROUP BY cid ORDER BY cid NULLS FIRST;

SELECT k, count(*) AS orders, ST_AsText(ST_SnapToGrid(ST_Centroid(ST_Collect(geom)), 1)) AS centre
FROM (SELECT ST_ClusterKMeans(geom, 4) OVER () AS k, geom FROM orders) s
GROUP BY k ORDER BY k;
presets.note: DBSCAN finds the **4 hubs** (about 800 orders each), one small extra cluster, and **1 745** noise orders with a NULL id. k-means returns exactly k clusters (more only if you pass `max_radius`), so every order is forced into one of 4.

presets.label: GeoJSON for a web map
presets.sql:
SELECT json_build_object(
         'type', 'FeatureCollection',
         'features', json_agg(ST_AsGeoJSON(t.*, id_column => 'id', maxdecimaldigits => 6)::json))
FROM (SELECT z.id, z.name, count(o.id) AS orders, ST_Transform(z.geom, 4326) AS geom
      FROM zones z LEFT JOIN orders o ON ST_Contains(z.geom, o.geom)
      WHERE z.id <= 2 GROUP BY z.id) t;

SELECT length(ST_AsGeoJSON(ST_Transform(ST_Union(geom), 4326)))                       AS full_chars,
       length(ST_AsGeoJSON(ST_Transform(ST_Simplify(ST_Union(geom), 500), 4326), 6)) AS simplified_chars
FROM zones;
presets.note: GeoJSON coordinates must be **longitude/latitude (4326)**, so transform first. Six decimals is about 0.1 m. Simplifying the outline by 500 m and trimming decimals cuts the payload from 1 285 to 752 characters.

presets.label: Validity
presets.sql:
SELECT ST_IsValid(g)                AS valid,
       ST_IsValidReason(g)          AS reason,
       ST_Area(g)                   AS area_as_drawn,
       ST_AsText(ST_MakeValid(g))   AS repaired,
       ST_Area(ST_MakeValid(g))     AS area_repaired
FROM (SELECT 'POLYGON((0 0, 2 2, 2 0, 0 2, 0 0))'::geometry AS g) s;

SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT ST_IsValid(geom)) AS invalid_zones FROM zones;
presets.note: A "bow-tie" ring crosses itself at (1 1). Its signed areas cancel, so `ST_Area` says **0**. `ST_MakeValid` splits it into two triangles with area **2**. PostGIS does not validate on insert.

production.title: A delivery-zone dashboard
production.context: A grocery delivery team shows orders per zone on a live web map. Zones are hand-drawn polygons; orders arrive as GPS points in longitude/latitude.
production.problem: Counts were wrong in two ways. Orders on a shared zone border were counted twice, because the query used `ST_Intersects`. A few hand-drawn zones were self-intersecting, and their `ST_Area` and contains tests silently gave nonsense.
production.solution: Repair zones once with `ST_MakeValid` and add a check constraint so bad shapes are rejected. Count with `ST_Contains`, or assign each border order to exactly one zone. Serve the map as one GeoJSON FeatureCollection in 4326, simplified for the zoom level.
production.outcome: Every order is counted at most once, the constraint blocks new invalid zones, and the map loads one compact JSON document. In the playground the 33-zone join runs in about 10 ms through the orders index.

pitfalls.title: Double counting on shared borders
pitfalls.symptom: The per-zone counts add up to more than the number of orders.
pitfalls.cause: `ST_Intersects` and `ST_Covers` include the boundary, so a point on a shared edge matches **both** zones.
pitfalls.fix: Use `ST_Contains` (excludes the boundary) and decide what to do with exact-boundary points, or pick one zone per point with `DISTINCT ON`.

pitfalls.title: Invalid polygons in, nonsense out
pitfalls.symptom: A zone reports area 0, or a point clearly inside it is "not contained".
pitfalls.cause: PostGIS does not check validity on insert. Self-intersecting rings make area and predicates unreliable.
pitfalls.fix: Repair once, then enforce.
pitfalls.sql:
UPDATE zones SET geom = ST_MakeValid(geom) WHERE NOT ST_IsValid(geom);
ALTER TABLE zones ADD CONSTRAINT zones_valid CHECK (ST_IsValid(geom));

pitfalls.title: Simplify breaking shapes
pitfalls.symptom: After `ST_Simplify` some polygons vanish, overlap their neighbours, or fail `ST_IsValid`.
pitfalls.cause: Douglas-Peucker removes vertices without checking topology. Small shapes collapse and neighbours stop sharing edges.
pitfalls.fix: Use `ST_SimplifyPreserveTopology` for validity, or `ST_CoverageSimplify` to keep shared edges between neighbours. Simplify in a metric SRID with a tolerance in metres.

pitfalls.title: Buffering to find what is near
pitfalls.symptom: `WHERE ST_Intersects(geom, ST_Buffer($1, 500))` is slow and its circle edges are polygons.
pitfalls.cause: Building a buffer is costly, and its 32-segment circle is only an approximation.
pitfalls.fix: Use `ST_DWithin(geom, $1, 500)`. It is exact and index-aware.

pointers: Point-in-polygon join: `JOIN … ON ST_Contains(zone, point)`. The index probe uses the zone box, then the exact test filters.
`ST_Contains` excludes the boundary; `ST_Covers` and `ST_Intersects` include it.
`ST_Union` dissolves into one shape; `ST_Collect` only bundles. `ST_ClusterDBSCAN` returns NULL for noise; `ST_ClusterKMeans` makes exactly k clusters unless given `max_radius`.
GeoJSON output is longitude/latitude: `ST_AsGeoJSON(ST_Transform(geom, 4326), 6)`.
Check `ST_IsValid` on load and enforce it with a constraint. Start again from [Spatial indexes](/e4/spatial-indexes) when a query is slow.
